title: JavaScript
tagline: From variables to the event loop - the complete JavaScript revision roadmap.
description: Revise JavaScript topic by topic from absolute basics to advanced concepts: data types, functions, arrays, objects, closures, prototypes, async programming, the DOM, browser APIs, modern ES2015+ features and tricky interview questions. Every topic has a clear explanation, runnable examples and interview Q&As.

topics.title: What is JavaScript and How It Runs
topics.summary: JavaScript is a single-threaded, interpreted/JIT-compiled language that runs in browsers and in Node.js.
topics.description:
JavaScript (JS) is the programming language of the web. It runs inside every browser and, with **Node.js**, also on servers and your own machine. It is **dynamically typed** (a variable can hold any type), **single-threaded** (one thing at a time) and **multi-paradigm** (you can write procedural, object-oriented or functional code).

### How the engine runs your code
Every browser ships a JavaScript engine (V8 in Chrome and Node, SpiderMonkey in Firefox, JavaScriptCore in Safari). The engine does this:

1. **Parsing** - the lexer breaks the source into tokens, the parser builds an **AST** (abstract syntax tree).
2. **Compilation** - the AST is turned into bytecode and hot code is optimised by a **JIT** (just-in-time) compiler.
3. **Execution** - the engine creates an **execution context**, pushes it on the **call stack** and runs it.

### Where data lives
- **Call stack** - keeps track of which function is running now (LIFO: last in, first out). Primitives and references usually live here.
- **Heap** - a large memory area for objects, arrays and functions.
- **Web APIs / event loop** - timers, DOM events and network calls are handled outside the stack and their callbacks are queued (see the Event Loop topic).

### Running JavaScript
- In a browser: add `<script src="app.js"></script>` or use the DevTools console.
- In Node.js: `node file.js`.
- Use `console.log()` to print values while learning.

JavaScript is not Java. The name was a marketing decision; they are different languages. The official standard is **ECMAScript (ES)**, and new versions have been released every year since ES2015.
keyPoints: JS is dynamically typed, single-threaded and has first-class functions
Engine = parse to AST, compile (JIT), execute using a call stack and heap
ECMAScript is the standard, JavaScript is the implementation you use
Same language runs in browsers (with DOM/BOM) and in Node.js (with fs, http...)
pitfalls: Java and JavaScript are unrelated languages
Single-threaded does not mean it cannot do async work - the browser/Node provide that

examples.title: Your first program
examples.explanation: console.log prints to the console. The call stack runs these lines from top to bottom.

interview.q: Is JavaScript compiled or interpreted?
interview.a: Modern engines do both: they parse to bytecode, interpret it and use a JIT compiler to optimise hot code into machine code at runtime. So it is best described as JIT-compiled.

interview.q: What does single-threaded mean?
interview.a: There is only one call stack, so one piece of JavaScript runs at a time. Async work is delegated to the browser or Node and results come back through the event loop.

interview.q: What is the difference between JavaScript and ECMAScript?
interview.a: ECMAScript is the language specification (ECMA-262). JavaScript is the implementation of that spec in browsers and Node, plus host APIs like the DOM.

topics.title: Variables: var, let and const
topics.summary: Variables store values; use const by default, let when reassignment is needed and avoid var.
topics.description:
A **value** is a piece of data (a number, text, true/false...). A **variable** is a named container that holds a value so you can use it later.

### Declaring variables
```js
var oldWay = 1;      // function scoped, can be redeclared (avoid)
let counter = 0;     // block scoped, can be reassigned
const PI = 3.14159;  // block scoped, cannot be reassigned
```

| Feature | `var` | `let` | `const` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scope | function | block | block |
| Redeclare | yes | no | no |
| Reassign | yes | yes | no |
| Hoisted value | `undefined` | TDZ (error) | TDZ (error) |

### Naming rules
- May contain letters, digits, `_` and `$`.
- Cannot start with a digit (`123age` is invalid).
- No spaces or special characters like `@` or `-`.
- Case sensitive: `age` and `Age` are different.
- Cannot use reserved words (`class`, `let`, `return`...).
- Convention: `camelCase` for variables, `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` for constants, `PascalCase` for classes.

### const does not mean frozen
`const` stops **re-assignment of the binding**. If it holds an object or array, the contents can still change.

### Best practice
Use `const` by default. Switch to `let` only if you need to reassign. Do not use `var` in modern code.
keyPoints: const by default, let when you must reassign, avoid var
let/const are block scoped, var is function scoped
const prevents re-assignment, not mutation of objects
Names: letters, digits, _ and $, cannot start with a digit
pitfalls: Declaring a global variable without a keyword (x = 5) creates an accidental global
Using const with an object and expecting it to be immutable
var inside a loop leaks outside the loop block

examples.title: Valid names and const mutation
examples.explanation: const protects the variable binding, not the object it points to.

examples.title: var vs let in a block

interview.q: Difference between var, let and const?
interview.a: var is function scoped, hoisted as undefined and can be redeclared. let and const are block scoped and live in the temporal dead zone until declared. const cannot be reassigned.

interview.q: Can we change an object declared with const?
interview.a: Yes. const only prevents re-assigning the variable. You can still add, change or delete properties unless you use Object.freeze.

interview.q: What happens if you assign to an undeclared variable?
interview.a: In sloppy mode it creates a global variable. In strict mode it throws a ReferenceError.

topics.title: Data Types and typeof
topics.summary: JavaScript has 7 primitive types plus objects; typeof tells you the type of a value.
topics.description:
Every value in JavaScript has a **type**. There are two groups:

### Primitive types (immutable, copied by value)
| Type | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `number` | `42`, `3.14`, `NaN`, `Infinity` | one type for ints and floats (64-bit) |
| `string` | `"hi"`, `'hi'`, `` `hi` `` | sequence of UTF-16 characters |
| `boolean` | `true`, `false` | |
| `undefined` | `let x;` | variable declared but no value |
| `null` | `let x = null;` | intentional empty value |
| `bigint` | `123n` | arbitrary size integers |
| `symbol` | `Symbol("id")` | unique identifier |

### Non-primitive (reference types)
`object`, including arrays, functions, dates, maps, sets... They are stored in the heap and variables hold a **reference**.

### typeof operator
`typeof` returns a string describing the type. Two oddities everyone must know:
- `typeof null` is `"object"` - a historic bug that can never be fixed.
- `typeof []` is `"object"` - use `Array.isArray(value)`.
- `typeof function(){}` is `"function"` (functions are objects, but get their own answer).

### null vs undefined
- `undefined` - "no value has been assigned yet" (the engine's default).
- `null` - "there is deliberately no value" (set by the programmer).

Because JavaScript is dynamically typed, the same variable can hold a number now and a string later. That is flexible but can cause bugs, so TypeScript is popular for big projects.
keyPoints: 7 primitives: number, string, boolean, undefined, null, bigint, symbol
Everything else is an object (arrays, functions, dates...)
typeof null === "object" is a known historic bug
Use Array.isArray to detect arrays
undefined = not assigned, null = intentionally empty
pitfalls: typeof on an undeclared variable returns "undefined" but reading it throws a ReferenceError
NaN has type number and is not equal to itself

examples.title: typeof cheat sheet

interview.q: What is the result of typeof null and why?
interview.a: It is "object". It is a bug from the first version of JavaScript where null used the same type tag as objects. It is kept for backward compatibility.

interview.q: What are primitive data types?
interview.a: number, string, boolean, undefined, null, bigint and symbol. They are immutable and compared/copied by value.

interview.q: Difference between null and undefined?
interview.a: undefined means a variable has not been given a value; null is an explicit "no value" assigned by the developer. null == undefined is true, null === undefined is false.

topics.title: Type Conversion, Coercion and Truthy/Falsy
topics.summary: JavaScript silently converts types in expressions; learn the rules so the output never surprises you.
topics.description:
**Type coercion** is the automatic conversion of a value from one type to another. **Explicit conversion** is when you do it yourself with `Number()`, `String()`, `Boolean()`.

### The + operator
- If **either** operand is a string, `+` concatenates: `"5" + 3` is `"53"`.
- Otherwise it adds numbers.
- Operators `- * / %` always convert to numbers: `"9" - 5` is `4`.

### Conversion rules
| Value | to Number | to Boolean |
|---|---|---|
| `""` | `0` | `false` |
| `"12"` | `12` | `true` |
| `"abc"` | `NaN` | `true` |
| `null` | `0` | `false` |
| `undefined` | `NaN` | `false` |
| `true` / `false` | `1` / `0` | - |
| `[]` | `0` | `true` |

### Falsy values
Exactly **eight** values are falsy: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`. Everything else is **truthy**, including `"0"`, `"false"`, `[]`, `{}` and `function(){}`.

### Explicit conversions
```js
Number("42");     // 42
+"42";            // 42
String(42);       // "42"
42 + "";          // "42"
Boolean("hi");    // true
!!"hi";           // true (double NOT trick)
```

Prefer explicit conversion in real code so your intention is clear.
keyPoints: + concatenates if any side is a string, other math operators convert to numbers
8 falsy values: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN
Empty array and empty object are truthy
Use Number(), String(), Boolean() for explicit conversion
pitfalls: [] + {} and similar tricks are rarely useful, avoid relying on them
Number(null) is 0 but Number(undefined) is NaN

examples.title: Interview coercion puzzles
examples.code:
console.log(10 + "20");        // "1020"
console.log(9 - "5");          // 4
console.log("Java" + "Script");
console.log(true + true);      // 2
console.log(false - true);     // -1
console.log("vinod" - "thapa");// NaN
console.log(typeof (" " + 0)); // string
console.log("20" + 10 + 10);   // "201010"
console.log(10 + 10 + "20");   // "2020"
console.log(typeof ("5" - 3)); // number

examples.title: Truthy and falsy table

interview.q: What is the output of "5" + 3 and "5" - 3?
interview.a: "53" and 2. The + operator prefers string concatenation when one side is a string, while - converts both sides to numbers.

interview.q: List the falsy values in JavaScript.
interview.a: false, 0, -0, 0n, "" (empty string), null, undefined and NaN. Everything else is truthy.

interview.q: What does !!value do?
interview.a: The first ! converts value to a boolean and negates it, the second ! negates it back, giving the boolean truthiness of value.

topics.title: parseInt, parseFloat and NaN
topics.summary: Convert strings to numbers safely and understand why NaN is never equal to itself.
topics.description:
### parseInt and parseFloat
Both read a string from the left and stop at the first invalid character.

- `parseInt(string, radix)` returns an **integer**. Always pass the radix (usually `10`).
- `parseFloat(string)` returns a **decimal** number.
- `Number(string)` is stricter: the **whole** string must be a valid number, otherwise `NaN`.

```js
parseInt("42px");   // 42
Number("42px");     // NaN
parseInt("1.9");    // 1  (truncates)
parseFloat("1.9");  // 1.9
parseInt("  123 "); // 123 (whitespace ignored)
```

### NaN
`NaN` means "Not a Number". It is the result of an impossible numeric operation such as `"hello" / 2` or `parseInt("xyz")`. Strangely, `typeof NaN` is `"number"`.

**NaN is not equal to anything, even itself**, so `NaN === NaN` is `false`. To test for it use:
- `Number.isNaN(value)` - true only for the actual NaN value (recommended).
- `isNaN(value)` - first converts to number, so `isNaN("abc")` is `true`.
- `Object.is(value, NaN)`.

### Related checks
- `Number.isFinite(x)` - false for `Infinity` and `NaN`.
- `Number.isInteger(x)` - true for whole numbers.
- `Number.isSafeInteger(x)` - within +/- 2^53 - 1.
keyPoints: parseInt stops at the first invalid char, Number needs a fully valid string
Always give parseInt a radix: parseInt(s, 10)
NaN !== NaN, so use Number.isNaN()
typeof NaN is "number"
pitfalls: ["1","2","3"].map(parseInt) gives [1, NaN, NaN] because map passes the index as radix
Global isNaN("abc") returns true because it coerces first

examples.title: Parsing and NaN checks

interview.q: Why is NaN === NaN false?
interview.a: By the IEEE 754 floating point rule NaN is unordered and never equal to any value, including itself. Use Number.isNaN or Object.is to detect it.

interview.q: Difference between parseInt and Number?
interview.a: parseInt reads as many valid leading characters as it can ("42px" gives 42). Number requires the entire string to be numeric and returns NaN otherwise.

interview.q: Why does ["1","2","3"].map(parseInt) return [1, NaN, NaN]?
interview.a: map passes (value, index, array), so parseInt receives the index as its radix: parseInt("2", 1) and parseInt("3", 2) are NaN.

topics.title: Arithmetic, Assignment and Unary Operators
topics.summary: Operators combine values into expressions: math, assignment, increment/decrement and type conversion.
topics.description:
An **expression** is any piece of code that produces a value. It is built from **operands** (the values) and **operators** (the symbols). For `5 + 3`, the operands are `5` and `3` and the operator is `+`.

### Arithmetic
`+ - * / % **` (add, subtract, multiply, divide, remainder, exponent). `%` gives the remainder (`17 % 5` is `2`) and is perfect for even/odd checks and wrapping around. `**` was added in ES2016 (`2 ** 5` is `32`).

### Assignment
`=` assigns. Compound forms update in place: `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`, `**=`. Modern versions add logical assignment `||=`, `&&=` and `??=`.

### Unary operators (one operand)
- `+x` converts to number, `-x` negates.
- `typeof x`, `!x`, `delete obj.key`, `void 0`.
- `++x` / `--x` (**prefix**): change first, then return the new value.
- `x++` / `x--` (**postfix**): return the old value, then change.

```js
let x = 5;
let y = x++; // y = 5, x = 6
let z = ++x; // x = 7, z = 7
```

### Operator precedence
`**` binds tighter than `* /`, which bind tighter than `+ -`. Use parentheses to make intent obvious: `(a + b) * c`.

### Floating point precision
Numbers are IEEE 754 doubles, so `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`. For money, work in the smallest unit (paise/cents) or use `toFixed()` only for display.
keyPoints: % returns remainder, ** is exponent
Prefix ++x returns the new value, postfix x++ returns the old one
Unary + converts to number: +"5" is 5
0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3 because of floating point
Use parentheses instead of memorising precedence
pitfalls: "hello" / 2 gives NaN, not an error
Dividing by 0 gives Infinity, not an exception
toFixed returns a string, not a number

examples.title: Prefix vs postfix

interview.q: What is the difference between x++ and ++x?
interview.a: Both add 1. x++ returns the value before the increment, ++x returns the value after the increment.

interview.q: Why is 0.1 + 0.2 not equal to 0.3?
interview.a: Binary floating point cannot represent 0.1 and 0.2 exactly, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004. Compare with a tolerance (Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON) or use integers.

interview.q: What does unary + do?
interview.a: It converts its operand to a number, so +"5" is 5, +true is 1 and +"abc" is NaN.

topics.title: Comparison and Equality (== vs ===)
topics.summary: Prefer === (strict equality); know exactly what == coerces and when Object.is differs.
topics.description:
Comparison operators return a **boolean**: `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `==`, `!=`, `===`, `!==`.

### Loose equality `==`
Converts types before comparing, using a complicated set of rules. `5 == "5"` is `true`, `0 == false` is `true`, `null == undefined` is `true`.

### Strict equality `===`
Compares **type and value** with no conversion. `5 === "5"` is `false`. This is what you want almost always.

### Special cases
- `NaN === NaN` is `false`.
- `+0 === -0` is `true`.
- `Object.is(NaN, NaN)` is `true` and `Object.is(+0, -0)` is `false` - it is the "same value" check.
- Objects, arrays and functions are compared by **reference**: `{} === {}` is `false`.
- `null == 0` is `false` but `null >= 0` is `true` (relational operators convert null to 0, equality does not).

### Relational comparisons
- Strings compare **alphabetically** by UTF-16 code: `"apple" < "banana"` and `"10" < "9"` (string compare!).
- Mixed string and number: the string is converted to a number.
- Chained comparisons do not work like maths: `1 < 5 < 3` is `true` because `(1 < 5)` becomes `true`, then `true < 3` is `1 < 3`.

### Rule of thumb
Use `===` and `!==`. The only common use of `==` is `value == null`, which checks `null` or `undefined` together.
keyPoints: === checks type and value, == coerces first
Objects/arrays compare by reference
NaN is not equal to itself, use Number.isNaN or Object.is
value == null is true for both null and undefined
Strings compare alphabetically, not numerically
pitfalls: 2 < 12 < 5 is true because of left-to-right evaluation
"10" > "9" is false (string comparison) but 10 > "9" is true
[] == false is true and [] is truthy at the same time

examples.title: Equality gallery

interview.q: Difference between == and ===?
interview.a: == converts operands to a common type before comparing; === compares both type and value and never converts.

interview.q: What is the output of console.log(2 < 12 < 5)?
interview.a: true. 2 < 12 is true, then true is coerced to 1 and 1 < 5 is true.

interview.q: How are two objects compared in JavaScript?
interview.a: By reference. Two separate objects with the same content are not equal; only two variables pointing to the same object are equal.

topics.title: Logical Operators and Short-Circuiting
topics.summary: &&, || and ! return one of their operands, which enables default values and guard patterns.
topics.description:
The logical operators are `&&` (AND), `||` (OR) and `!` (NOT). With booleans they behave as in school logic, but with other types they have an important twist: **`&&` and `||` return one of the operands, not necessarily a boolean.**

### Rules
- `a || b` returns `a` if `a` is truthy, otherwise `b`.
- `a && b` returns `a` if `a` is falsy, otherwise `b`.
- `!a` always returns a boolean.

### Short-circuit evaluation
The right side runs only when needed. That makes these patterns common:

```js
const name = userInput || "Guest";        // default value
user && user.login();                     // run only if user exists
const isAdult = age >= 18 && hasId;       // combine conditions
```

### Nullish coalescing `??`
`||` treats `0`, `""` and `false` as "missing". `??` only treats `null` and `undefined` as missing, so it is safer for defaults:

```js
const count = 0;
count || 10;   // 10 (wrong if 0 is valid)
count ?? 10;   // 0
```

### Logical assignment (ES2021)
`a ||= b`, `a &&= b`, `a ??= b` assign only when the short-circuit rule says so.

### Mixing
You cannot mix `??` with `||` or `&&` without parentheses. `&&` has higher precedence than `||`.
keyPoints: && and || return an operand, not always a boolean
|| gives the first truthy value, && gives the first falsy value
Use ?? when 0, "" or false are valid values
||=, &&= and ??= are logical assignment shortcuts
Short-circuit stops evaluation early
pitfalls: Using || for defaults breaks when 0 or "" is legitimate input
a ?? b || c is a syntax error without parentheses

examples.title: Defaults and guards

interview.q: What does console.log(null || "hi" && 0) print?
interview.a: 0. && runs first: "hi" && 0 is 0. Then null || 0 returns the last operand, 0.

interview.q: Difference between || and ???
interview.a: || falls back for any falsy value (0, "", false...). ?? falls back only for null and undefined.

interview.q: What is short-circuit evaluation?
interview.a: The second operand of && or || is evaluated only if the first operand does not already decide the result.

topics.summary: Choose which code runs using if/else chains, switch statements and the ternary operator.
keyPoints: if/else chains run the first truthy branch only
switch uses === and needs break to avoid fall-through
Ternary is an expression, if is a statement
default handles the no-match case
An object lookup can replace a big switch

switch(true) tricks and deep nested ternaries hurt readability
Declaring let/const directly inside a case without braces shares one scope

interview.q: Why do we write break in switch?
interview.a: Without break, execution continues into the next case (fall-through). break exits the switch after the matching case runs.

interview.q: Which equality does switch use?
interview.a: Strict equality (===), so switch("5") will not match case 5.

interview.q: When should you use the ternary operator?
interview.a: For short two-way choices that produce a value, such as assigning or returning. Use if/else when you need multiple statements or complex logic.

topics.title: Loops: for, while, do-while, break and continue
topics.summary: Repeat work with for, while and do...while and control the flow with break and continue.
topics.description:
Loops execute a block of code repeatedly while a condition is true.

### for
```js
for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { console.log(i); }
```
Three parts: **initialisation**, **condition** (checked before every run), **update** (after every run). Any part can be left empty; `for (;;) {}` is an infinite loop.

### while
Use when you do not know the number of iterations upfront:
```js
let n = 1;
while (n <= 10) { n++; }
```

### do...while
Runs the body **at least once**, then checks the condition. Good for "ask, then validate" flows.

### break, continue and labels
- `break` leaves the loop completely.
- `continue` skips to the next iteration.
- A **label** lets you break out of nested loops: `outer: for (...) { for (...) { break outer; } }`.

### Common practice problems
Times tables, sum 1 to N, prime check, leap year, star patterns. Use `let` in loops: each iteration gets its own binding, which matters for closures and callbacks.

### Choosing a loop
- Known count: `for`.
- Unknown count / waiting for a condition: `while`.
- Run once first: `do...while`.
- Iterating arrays: `for...of`, `forEach` or `map` (see arrays).
keyPoints: for = init; condition; update
do...while always runs at least once
break exits the loop, continue skips one iteration
Labels allow breaking out of nested loops
Always make sure the condition eventually becomes false
pitfalls: Infinite loops from forgetting to update the counter
Off-by-one errors with < vs <=
Using var in a loop with async callbacks shares one variable

examples.title: Table, sum and prime
Star pattern, break/continue and label

interview.q: Difference between while and do...while?
interview.a: while checks the condition before each iteration and may never run. do...while runs the body once first and checks the condition afterwards.

interview.q: What is the difference between break and continue?
interview.a: break terminates the whole loop; continue stops only the current iteration and moves to the next one.

interview.q: How do you exit from nested loops at once?
interview.a: Use a labelled break (break outer;), or put the loops in a function and return.

topics.title: for...in vs for...of vs forEach
topics.summary: for...of iterates values of iterables, for...in iterates enumerable keys of objects.
topics.description:
Three similar-looking ways to loop over collections often confuse beginners.

### for...of
Iterates over the **values** of any **iterable**: arrays, strings, Map, Set, NodeList, generators. You can use `break`, `continue` and `await` inside.

```js
for (const fruit of ["apple", "mango"]) console.log(fruit);
for (const ch of "JS") console.log(ch);
```

### for...in
Iterates over the **enumerable property keys** (as strings) of an object, **including inherited ones**. Use it for plain objects, and prefer `Object.keys/entries` for arrays.

```js
for (const key in { a: 1, b: 2 }) console.log(key);
```

### Array.prototype.forEach
Calls a function for each element. It returns `undefined`, cannot be stopped with `break`, and does not wait for `async` callbacks.

### Which one to use
| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| values of an array/string/Map/Set | `for...of` |
| keys of a plain object | `Object.keys` / `Object.entries` + `for...of` |
| side effects for every item, no early exit | `forEach` |
| early exit | `for...of` / `some` / `every` / classic `for` |
| `await` inside | `for...of` |

### Remember
Plain objects are **not iterable**: `for (const x of {a:1})` throws a TypeError. Use `Object.entries(obj)` first.
keyPoints: for...of gives values, for...in gives keys (strings)
for...in also walks the prototype chain
Plain objects are not iterable - use Object.entries
forEach cannot break or await properly
Use for...of when you need break or await
pitfalls: Using for...in on arrays gives string indexes and may include extra properties
forEach(async ...) does not wait for the promises
Adding to an array while iterating with for...of can cause endless loops

interview.q: Difference between for...in and for...of?
interview.a: for...in loops over enumerable keys (including inherited ones) as strings. for...of loops over values of an iterable object.

interview.q: Can you use break inside forEach?
interview.a: No. forEach cannot be stopped except by throwing. Use a for...of loop, or some()/every() for early exit.

interview.q: Why does for...of fail on a plain object?
interview.a: Plain objects do not implement Symbol.iterator. Convert with Object.keys, Object.values or Object.entries.
