interview.q: What is the difference between a function declaration and a function expression?
interview.a: A declaration is fully hoisted and can be called before it is defined. An expression is a value assigned to a variable and exists only after that line executes.

interview.q: What does a function return when it has no return statement?
interview.a: undefined.

interview.q: What are first-class functions?
interview.a: Functions are treated like any other value: they can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments and returned from other functions.

topics.title: Arrow Functions
topics.summary: Arrow functions are a short syntax with lexical this and no own arguments object.
topics.description:
Arrow functions (ES2015) are a compact way to write function expressions.

### Syntax
```js
const add = (a, b) => a + b;         // implicit return
const square = n => n * n;           // one param: () optional
const hello = () => "hi";            // no params: () required
const make = (n) => { return { n }; }; // block body needs return
const obj = () => ({ ok: true });    // wrap object literal in ()
```

### What is different from normal functions
1. **Lexical `this`** - an arrow does not create its own `this`; it uses the `this` of the surrounding code. Great for callbacks inside methods.
2. **No `arguments` object** - use rest parameters (`...args`).
3. **Cannot be used with `new`** - not a constructor, no `prototype`.
4. **Cannot be a generator**.
5. `call`, `apply` and `bind` cannot change its `this`.

### When not to use arrows
- Object methods that need `this` to be the object.
- Prototype methods and constructors.
- Event handlers where you need `this` to be the element (use `event.currentTarget` instead).

### When to use arrows
Short callbacks for `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `setTimeout`, promise chains, and any function that should keep the outer `this`.
keyPoints: Concise syntax with implicit return for single expressions
Wrap an object literal in parentheses to return it
Arrows capture this from the surrounding scope
No arguments object, not constructible
Not suitable for object methods that rely on this
pitfalls: const f = () => { a: 1 } returns undefined (it is a block with a label)
Using an arrow as an object method makes this point to the outer scope

examples.title: Arrow vs normal this

interview.q: What is the main difference between arrow functions and regular functions?
interview.a: Arrow functions have no own this, arguments or prototype; they inherit this lexically and cannot be used as constructors.

interview.q: Why does an arrow function used as an object method give wrong this?
interview.a: Because arrows do not bind this to the object. They use the this of the enclosing scope (often the module or window), not the object.

interview.q: How do you return an object literal from an arrow function directly?
interview.a: Wrap it in parentheses: () => ({ key: value }).

topics.title: Default, Rest Parameters and the arguments Object
topics.summary: Give parameters default values and collect extra arguments with rest syntax.
topics.description:
### Default parameters
A parameter gets its default only when the argument is `undefined` (not for `null`, `0` or `""`).

```js
function greet(name = "Guest", greeting = "Hello") {
  return `${greeting}, ${name}`;
}
greet();            // Hello, Guest
greet("Asha");      // Hello, Asha
```
Defaults can use earlier parameters and any expression, and are evaluated on every call.

### Rest parameters `...`
Collect all remaining arguments into a **real array**:
```js
const sum = (first, ...others) => others.reduce((a, b) => a + b, first);
sum(1, 2, 3, 4); // 10
```
Rules: only **one** rest parameter and it must be **last**.

### The `arguments` object
Old-style functions have an array-like `arguments`. It has `length` and indexes but no array methods. Arrow functions do not have it. Prefer rest parameters.

### Spread when calling
The opposite of rest: `Math.max(...numbers)` expands an array into separate arguments.

### Named parameters via destructuring
For many options, accept one object and destructure it with defaults:
```js
function createUser({ name, role = "user", active = true } = {}) { }
```
This makes call sites readable and order-independent.
keyPoints: Defaults apply only for undefined
Rest collects remaining args into a real array and must be last
arguments is array-like and missing in arrow functions
Spread (...) expands an array when calling
Destructured options object = named parameters
pitfalls: Passing null does not trigger a default value
Objects passed as arguments are references, so mutating them inside the function changes the caller's data

examples.title: Defaults, rest and spread

interview.q: When is a default parameter value used?
interview.a: Only when the argument is undefined or missing. null, 0, "" and false are used as given.

interview.q: Difference between rest and spread?
interview.a: Rest collects many values into one array in a parameter list or destructuring. Spread expands one iterable into many values in a call or literal.

interview.q: Why prefer rest parameters over arguments?
interview.a: Rest gives a real array with all array methods, works in arrow functions and is explicit in the signature.

topics.title: IIFE (Immediately Invoked Function Expression)
topics.summary: An IIFE runs immediately after being defined and creates a private scope.
topics.description:
An **IIFE** is a function that is defined and called at the same time:

```js
(function () {
  // private scope
})();

(() => { /* arrow IIFE */ })();
```

The wrapping parentheses turn the `function` keyword into an **expression** so it can be invoked straight away.

### Why use an IIFE?
1. **Avoid polluting the global scope.** Before ES modules and `let/const`, IIFEs were the only way to make private variables.
2. **Module pattern.** Return an object with public methods while internal state stays hidden through closures.
3. **Run once setup code**, such as reading config.
4. **Async top-level helper**: `(async () => { await ... })();` to use `await` where top-level await is unavailable.

### Passing arguments
```js
const result = (function (a, b) { return a + b; })(5, 10);
```

### Modern alternatives
ES modules and block scopes (`{ let x; }`) solve most of the original problems, but IIFEs are still common in older code, bundled output and interviews.

### A semicolon warning
When a line starts with `(`, the previous line must end with `;`, otherwise JavaScript may treat it as a function call on the previous expression.
keyPoints: Function expression wrapped in () and invoked immediately
Creates a private scope, keeps variables out of global
Basis of the module pattern with closures
Can take arguments and return a value
Async IIFE is used to await in non-module scripts
pitfalls: A missing semicolon on the previous line breaks the IIFE
Without the wrapping parentheses it is a syntax error

examples.title: Module pattern with IIFE

interview.q: What is an IIFE and why use it?
interview.a: A function that runs immediately after it is defined. It creates a private scope so variables do not leak globally and enables the module pattern.

interview.q: Why are the parentheses needed around a function in an IIFE?
interview.a: A statement starting with function is parsed as a declaration, which needs a name and cannot be invoked. Wrapping makes it an expression.

interview.q: Do we still need IIFEs?
interview.a: Less so, because ES modules and let/const give scope isolation. They still appear in legacy code and for async wrappers.

topics.title: First-Class, Higher-Order and Callback Functions
topics.summary: Functions can be passed around; a higher-order function takes or returns a function, and a callback is the function passed in.
topics.description:
In JavaScript functions are **first-class citizens**: they are values just like numbers or strings.

### Higher-order function (HOF)
A function that **takes a function as an argument** or **returns a function**. `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `setTimeout` and `addEventListener` are all higher-order functions.

### Callback function
A function passed to another function to be **called later** - either immediately (synchronous callback, e.g. `arr.map(cb)`) or after some work finishes (asynchronous callback, e.g. `setTimeout(cb)`).

```js
function operate(a, b, operation) {
  return operation(a, b);   // operation is the callback
}
operate(5, 15, (x, y) => x + y);
```

### Returning functions
HOFs can build specialised functions. The returned function remembers its environment through a **closure**:
```js
const multiplier = (factor) => (n) => n * factor;
const double = multiplier(2);
double(5); // 10
```

### Why this matters
- Removes duplicate code (pass behaviour in as data).
- Enables functional style: `compose`, `pipe`, `curry`.
- Callbacks are the base of async JavaScript, later improved by Promises and async/await.

### Callback conventions
Node.js uses **error-first callbacks**: `(err, data) => {}`. Always check `err` first.
keyPoints: Functions are first-class values
HOF takes and/or returns a function
Callback is a function passed to be invoked later
Returned functions keep access to outer variables (closure)
map/filter/reduce/forEach are HOFs
pitfalls: Passing fn() instead of fn runs it immediately
Deeply nested callbacks become callback hell
Losing this when passing a method as a callback

examples.title: Callbacks and a function factory

interview.q: What is a higher-order function?
interview.a: A function that accepts another function as an argument, returns a function, or both. Examples are map, filter and reduce.

interview.q: What is a callback?
interview.a: A function passed as an argument to another function, to be executed later by it - either synchronously or after an async task.

interview.q: What happens if you write setTimeout(fn(), 1000)?
interview.a: fn runs immediately and its return value is passed to setTimeout. You must pass the function reference: setTimeout(fn, 1000) or setTimeout(() => fn(), 1000).

topics.title: Pure Functions, Currying and Composition
topics.summary: Write predictable functions without side effects and combine small functions into bigger ones.
topics.description:
### Pure functions
A function is **pure** when:
1. The same input always gives the same output.
2. It has **no side effects** (no mutation of outside data, no I/O, no `Math.random()`, no `Date.now()`).

Pure functions are easy to test, cache (memoize), run in parallel and reason about. React reducers and selectors rely on them.

```js
// impure - mutates input
const addItem = (arr, x) => { arr.push(x); return arr; };
// pure - returns a new array
const addItemPure = (arr, x) => [...arr, x];
```

### Currying
Transform `f(a, b, c)` into `f(a)(b)(c)`. Each call returns a function that waits for the next argument. It enables **partial application**:
```js
const add = (a) => (b) => a + b;
const add10 = add(10);
add10(5); // 15
```

### Composition
Combine functions so the output of one becomes the input of the next:
```js
const compose = (...fns) => (x) => fns.reduceRight((v, f) => f(v), x);
const pipe = (...fns) => (x) => fns.reduce((v, f) => f(v), x);
```
`pipe` reads left to right and is usually easier to follow.

### Immutability
Prefer `map`, `filter`, spread and `structuredClone` over in-place mutation to keep functions pure.
keyPoints: Pure = same input gives same output and no side effects
Currying turns f(a, b) into f(a)(b)
Partial application pre-fills some arguments
compose/pipe chain small functions
Pure code is easier to test and memoize
pitfalls: Mutating arguments (arrays/objects) makes a function impure
Over-currying can hurt readability

examples.title: Pure, curry and pipe

interview.q: What is a pure function?
interview.a: A function whose output depends only on its inputs and which causes no side effects, so calling it with the same arguments always returns the same result.

interview.q: What is currying?
interview.a: Converting a function with multiple arguments into a chain of functions that each take one argument, e.g. add(1)(2).

interview.q: Write a function sum(1)(2)(3)... that returns the total when called with no arguments.
interview.a: const sum = (a) => (b) => b === undefined ? a : sum(a + b); then sum(1)(2)(3)() returns 6.

topics.title: Recursion
topics.summary: A function that calls itself needs a base case and a smaller problem each time.
topics.description:
**Recursion** is when a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem. Every recursive function needs:

1. **Base case** - a condition where it returns without calling itself.
2. **Recursive case** - a call with an input that moves closer to the base case.

```js
function factorial(n) {
  if (n <= 1) return 1;        // base case
  return n * factorial(n - 1); // recursive case
}
```

### How it works
Each call is pushed on the **call stack**. When the base case returns, the stack unwinds and results are multiplied back up. Too many nested calls cause `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` (stack overflow).

### Good use cases
- Tree and graph traversal (DOM tree, folder structure).
- Flattening nested arrays, deep clone, deep equality.
- Divide and conquer: merge sort, quick sort, binary search.
- Permutations, combinations, backtracking.

### Recursion vs loops
Anything recursive can be written with a loop. Loops are faster and use no stack; recursion is often clearer for hierarchical data. JavaScript engines do not reliably optimise tail calls, so avoid very deep recursion (more than a few thousand calls).

### Optimisation
Memoize repeated sub-problems (Fibonacci) or convert to iteration.
keyPoints: Needs a base case and progress toward it
Each call uses call stack memory
Missing base case causes stack overflow
Great for trees and nested data
Memoization avoids repeated work
pitfalls: Forgetting the base case or never reaching it
Naive recursive Fibonacci is exponential time
Deep recursion on big inputs overflows the stack

examples.title: Factorial, sum of nested array, Fibonacci

interview.q: What is a base case?
interview.a: The condition under which a recursive function stops calling itself and returns a value directly. Without it the recursion never ends.

interview.q: What causes a stack overflow in recursion?
interview.a: Too many nested calls (usually from a missing or unreachable base case) exceed the call stack limit, giving a RangeError.

interview.q: How can you make recursive Fibonacci efficient?
interview.a: Use memoization (cache results) or an iterative loop, reducing time from exponential O(2^n) to linear O(n).

topics.title: Array Basics and CRUD Methods
topics.summary: Create arrays, read by index and add, remove or replace elements with push, pop, shift, unshift, splice and slice.
topics.description:
An **array** is an ordered, zero-indexed list that can hold any mix of values. It is a special kind of object with a `length` property, so `typeof []` is `"object"` - use `Array.isArray()`.

### Creating
```js
const fruits = ["apple", "orange", "banana"]; // literal (preferred)
const empty = [];
const five = new Array(5);   // 5 empty slots (careful!)
const nums = Array.of(5);    // [5]
```

### Reading and writing
`fruits[0]` is the first item, `fruits[fruits.length - 1]` the last, `fruits.at(-1)` also the last. Reading an index that does not exist gives `undefined`. Assigning `fruits[2] = "mango"` replaces an item.

### Add / remove at the ends
| Method | Effect | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `push(x)` | add at end | new length |
| `pop()` | remove last | removed item |
| `unshift(x)` | add at start | new length |
| `shift()` | remove first | removed item |

### splice and slice
- `splice(start, deleteCount, ...items)` **mutates**: remove/replace/insert anywhere and returns the removed items.
- `slice(start, end)` **does not mutate**: returns a shallow copy of a portion (end is excluded).

### Other basics
`arr.length`, `concat`, `join(", ")`, `indexOf`, `includes`, `reverse()` (mutates), spread `[...a, ...b]`.

Mutating methods (`push`, `pop`, `shift`, `unshift`, `splice`, `sort`, `reverse`) change the original array - important in React state, where you should create a new array instead.
keyPoints: Arrays are zero-indexed objects with a length
push/pop work at the end, unshift/shift at the start
splice mutates and can insert, delete and replace
slice returns a copy and does not mutate
Use Array.isArray to detect arrays
pitfalls: new Array(3) creates empty slots, not three undefined values
Setting arr.length = 0 clears the array (also for other references)
Confusing splice (mutates) with slice (copy)

examples.title: CRUD with push, pop and splice

interview.q: Difference between slice and splice?
interview.a: slice returns a shallow copy of part of the array and leaves the original untouched. splice changes the original array by removing, replacing or adding items and returns the removed items.

interview.q: What does push return?
interview.a: The new length of the array.

interview.q: How do you check whether a value is an array?
interview.a: Array.isArray(value). typeof returns "object" for arrays.

topics.title: Iterating: forEach, map and for...of
topics.summary: Loop over arrays with for...of or forEach, and transform every item into a new array with map.
topics.description:
### forEach
Runs a callback for each element, returns `undefined`. Use it for **side effects** such as logging or updating the DOM.

```js
[1, 2, 3].forEach((value, index, array) => console.log(index, value));
```

### map
Creates a **new array** by applying a callback to every element. The original array is not changed and the length stays the same. Use it to **transform** data.

```js
const doubled = [1, 2, 3].map((n) => n * 2); // [2, 4, 6]
```

### Key differences
| | `forEach` | `map` |
|---|---|---|
| Returns | `undefined` | new array |
| Chainable | no | yes |
| Purpose | side effects | transformation |

### Callback arguments
Every array callback receives `(element, index, array)`. Use only what you need.

### Choosing
- Need the result as an array: `map`.
- Need to stop early: `for...of` with `break`, or `some`/`every`.
- Need to `await` in order: `for...of`.

### Chaining
Because `map` and `filter` return arrays, you can chain: `users.filter(isActive).map(toName)`.

### Real example
Rendering a list in the UI is a `map` from data to HTML strings or elements.
keyPoints: forEach returns undefined, map returns a new array
map keeps array length and does not mutate
Callbacks receive (element, index, array)
Chain map and filter for pipelines
forEach cannot be broken out of
pitfalls: Using map just for side effects creates a useless array
forEach(async fn) does not wait for the async work
A map callback without return fills the array with undefined

examples.title: forEach vs map

interview.q: Difference between forEach and map?
interview.a: forEach just runs a function for each item and returns undefined. map returns a new array of the callback results and can be chained.

interview.q: Does map mutate the original array?
interview.a: No. It returns a new array of the same length; the original stays unchanged (unless your callback mutates the objects inside).

interview.q: Can you break out of a forEach loop?
interview.a: Not with break or return. Use a for loop, for...of, some or every instead.

topics.title: Searching and Filtering: find, filter, some, every
topics.summary: Locate items with indexOf, includes and find, and select subsets with filter, some and every.
topics.description:
### Searching for a value
- `indexOf(x, from)` - first index or `-1`.
- `lastIndexOf(x)` - last index or `-1`.
- `includes(x)` - `true`/`false`. Handles `NaN` correctly, `indexOf` does not.

These use strict equality, so they are good for primitives only.

### Searching with a condition
- `find(cb)` - **first element** that passes, or `undefined`.
- `findIndex(cb)` - its index, or `-1`.
- `findLast(cb)` / `findLastIndex(cb)` (ES2023) - search from the end.

### Filtering
`filter(cb)` returns a **new array** with all elements for which `cb` returns truthy. Typical uses: remove an item from a cart, search boxes, keeping active users.

```js
const cart = [1, 2, 3, 6, 5, 6];
cart.filter((id) => id !== 6); // [1, 2, 3, 5]
```

### Boolean checks
- `some(cb)` - at least one passes (stops early).
- `every(cb)` - all pass (stops early; `[]` gives `true`).

### Unique values
`arr.filter((v, i, a) => a.indexOf(v) === i)` or `[...new Set(arr)]`.

### Choosing
| Need | Method |
|---|---|
| does it exist? | `includes` / `some` |
| the item | `find` |
| its position | `findIndex` / `indexOf` |
| all matches | `filter` |
| are all valid? | `every` |
keyPoints: includes returns a boolean, indexOf returns a position
find returns the first match, filter returns all matches
some/every short-circuit and return booleans
findLast and findLastIndex search from the end
Set gives the quickest unique values
pitfalls: indexOf cannot find NaN, includes can
find returns undefined (not -1) when nothing matches
Objects are compared by reference in includes/indexOf

examples.title: Search and filter products

interview.q: Difference between find and filter?
interview.a: find returns only the first matching element (or undefined). filter returns a new array containing all matching elements (empty array if none).

interview.q: Difference between some and every?
interview.a: some is true if at least one element passes the test; every is true only if all elements pass.

interview.q: How do you remove duplicates from an array?
interview.a: Use [...new Set(arr)] for primitives, or filter with indexOf for a manual approach.

topics.title: Sorting Arrays
topics.summary: sort() converts to strings by default, so pass a compare function for numbers and objects.
topics.description:
`Array.prototype.sort()` sorts **in place** (mutates) and returns the same array.

### Default behaviour
Without a compare function, items are converted to **strings** and compared by UTF-16 code. That is why `[10, 9, 1].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 9]`.

### Compare function
`sort((a, b) => ...)` must return:
- **negative** number - `a` goes before `b`
- **positive** number - `b` goes before `a`
- **0** - keep order

```js
nums.sort((a, b) => a - b); // ascending
nums.sort((a, b) => b - a); // descending
```

### Sorting objects and strings
```js
users.sort((a, b) => a.age - b.age);
names.sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b)); // correct for accents and case
```

### Stable sort
Since ES2019 `sort` is **stable**: equal elements keep their original relative order. Sort by one key and then another works as expected.

### Non-mutating versions (ES2023)
`toSorted()`, `toReversed()` return new arrays, so they are safe for React state.

### Related
`reverse()` mutates; `toReversed()` does not. To sort a copy in older code: `[...arr].sort(...)`.

### Performance
Sorting is O(n log n). Do not sort inside a render loop for large arrays without memoising.
keyPoints: sort mutates the array
Default sort is alphabetical by string value
Compare function returns negative, zero or positive
Use localeCompare for strings
toSorted returns a copy (ES2023)
pitfalls: [10, 9, 1].sort() does not sort numerically
Compare function returning a boolean does not work reliably
Sorting state arrays in place in React causes bugs

examples.title: Numbers, strings and objects

interview.q: Why does [10, 9, 1].sort() return [1, 10, 9]?
interview.a: The default sort converts elements to strings and compares them lexicographically, so "10" comes before "9".

interview.q: How do you sort numbers in descending order?
interview.a: arr.sort((a, b) => b - a).

interview.q: Does sort mutate the array?
interview.a: Yes, it sorts in place and returns the same array. Use toSorted() or copy first with [...arr] when you need the original.

topics.title: reduce() Explained
topics.summary: reduce folds an array into a single value - sum, object, grouped data or even another array.
topics.description:
`reduce` walks through the array, carrying an **accumulator** and returning a single result.

```js
array.reduce((accumulator, current, index, array) => {
  return newAccumulator;
}, initialValue);
```

### How it runs
1. Start with `accumulator = initialValue`.
2. For each element call the callback with `(accumulator, element)`.
3. Whatever you return becomes the next accumulator.
4. The final accumulator is the result.

If you omit `initialValue`, the first element is used as the accumulator and iteration starts at the second element. Calling `reduce` on an **empty array without an initial value throws a TypeError**. Always pass an initial value.

### Typical uses
- Sum, product, min, max.
- Counting occurrences: `{ apple: 2, mango: 1 }`.
- Grouping items by a key.
- Converting an array to an object (`id -> item`).
- Flattening arrays or building pipelines.

### reduceRight
Same but from right to left (used for function composition).

### Readability tip
`reduce` is powerful but can be hard to read. If a simple `map`/`filter`/`for...of` is clearer, use it. A good reducer is a **pure** function that returns a new accumulator (or mutates only its own fresh accumulator).
keyPoints: Accumulator carries the result between iterations
Always provide an initial value
Return the accumulator every time
Can build numbers, objects or arrays
reduceRight goes from right to left
pitfalls: Forgetting to return the accumulator gives undefined on the next step
Empty array without initial value throws TypeError
Mutating the accumulator when it is the original input

examples.title: Sum, count and group

interview.q: What are the arguments of reduce?
interview.a: A callback (accumulator, currentValue, index, array) and an optional initial value for the accumulator.

interview.q: What happens if you call reduce on an empty array without an initial value?
interview.a: It throws a TypeError: "Reduce of empty array with no initial value".

interview.q: How would you count the occurrences of each item using reduce?
interview.a: Start with an empty object and increment acc[item] = (acc[item] || 0) + 1 for every element, returning acc.

topics.title: flat, flatMap, at, Array.from and Immutable Methods
topics.summary: Modern array helpers for flattening, negative indexing, creating arrays and non-mutating updates.
topics.description:
Modern JavaScript added many helpful array methods.

### Flattening
- `flat(depth)` - flattens nested arrays one level by default; `flat(Infinity)` flattens fully.
- `flatMap(cb)` - `map` followed by `flat(1)`. Great when each item maps to several items.

### Access
- `at(index)` (ES2022) - supports negative indexes: `arr.at(-1)` is the last item.

### Creating arrays
- `Array.from(iterable | arrayLike, mapFn)` - from a string, Set, NodeList or `{ length: 3 }`.
- `Array.of(...items)`.
- `new Array(3).fill(0)` - prefilled array.
- `[...Array(5).keys()]` - `[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]`.

### Immutable versions (ES2023)
These return a **new array** instead of mutating:
| Mutating | Non-mutating |
|---|---|
| `reverse()` | `toReversed()` |
| `sort()` | `toSorted()` |
| `splice()` | `toSpliced()` |
| `arr[i] = v` | `with(i, v)` |

Also `findLast()` and `findLastIndex()` (ES2023), `Object.groupBy()` / `Map.groupBy()` (ES2024) for grouping.

### Other useful ones
`join`, `concat`, `fill`, `copyWithin`, `entries`, `keys`, `values`, `Array.prototype.includes`.

These non-mutating methods fit perfectly with immutable state updates in React and Redux.
keyPoints: flat and flatMap remove nesting
at(-1) reads from the end
Array.from converts iterables and array-likes
toSorted/toReversed/toSpliced/with return new arrays
Object.groupBy groups items by key (ES2024)
pitfalls: flat() only goes one level deep by default
Array(3).map(...) skips empty slots - use Array.from({length:3}, fn)
ES2023 methods need a recent browser/Node (Node 20+)

examples.title: flat, flatMap, at and Array.from
Non-mutating methods (ES2023)

interview.q: What is the difference between map and flatMap?
interview.a: flatMap maps each element and then flattens the result by one level, so callbacks that return arrays produce a single flat array.

interview.q: Why use arr.at(-1) instead of arr[arr.length - 1]?
interview.a: It is shorter and works with negative indexes counting from the end.

interview.q: How do toSorted and with help in React?
interview.a: They return new arrays without mutating the original, which fits the immutable state update rule.

topics.title: Common Array Patterns and Interview Recipes
topics.summary: Reusable recipes: unique, chunk, group, intersect, rotate, remove, and quick statistics.
topics.description:
These short recipes appear again and again in interviews and real projects. Learn the idea behind each one rather than memorising code.

### Unique values
`[...new Set(arr)]` - a Set stores each value once.

### Chunk into groups
Slice the array in steps of `size`:
```js
const chunk = (arr, n) =>
  Array.from({ length: Math.ceil(arr.length / n) }, (_, i) => arr.slice(i * n, i * n + n));
```

### Group by a key
`reduce` into an object of arrays, or `Object.groupBy(arr, fn)` in new engines.

### Intersection / difference
```js
const common = a.filter((x) => b.includes(x));
const onlyInA = a.filter((x) => !b.includes(x));
```
Use a `Set` of `b` for large arrays so lookup is O(1).

### Remove an item immutably
`arr.filter((x) => x.id !== id)`.

### Update an item immutably
`arr.map((x) => (x.id === id ? { ...x, done: true } : x))`.

### Copy an array
`[...arr]`, `arr.slice()`, `Array.from(arr)` - all shallow copies. Use `structuredClone(arr)` for a deep copy.

### Swap and rotate
`[a[0], a[1]] = [a[1], a[0]]` swaps. Rotate left: `[...a.slice(k), ...a.slice(0, k)]`.

### Max / min
`Math.max(...nums)` works until the array is huge; `reduce` has no argument limit.
keyPoints: Set makes unique values and fast lookups
filter removes, map updates immutably
Shallow copy with spread; deep copy with structuredClone
reduce can group or count
Destructuring swaps two values
pitfalls: Spread copies are shallow - nested objects are still shared
includes inside filter is O(n^2) for large arrays
Math.max(...hugeArray) can throw a RangeError

examples.title: Recipe collection

interview.q: How do you find the common elements of two arrays?
interview.a: Put one array in a Set and filter the other with set.has(item). This is O(n + m).

interview.q: How do you update one object in an array without mutating it?
interview.a: Use map and return a new object for the matching item with spread: arr.map(x => x.id === id ? { ...x, ...changes } : x).

interview.q: How can you swap two variables without a temp variable?
interview.a: Use array destructuring: [a, b] = [b, a].

topics.title: Strings and Template Literals
topics.summary: Strings are immutable sequences of characters; template literals make interpolation and multi-line text easy.
topics.description:
A **string** is a sequence of UTF-16 characters written in single quotes, double quotes or backticks. Single and double quotes behave the same; backticks create **template literals**.

### Basic facts
- `str.length` counts UTF-16 code units (spaces included).
- Access characters with `str[0]` or `str.at(-1)`.
- Strings are **immutable**: `str[0] = "x"` silently does nothing. Methods always return a **new** string.
- Strings are iterable: `[..."INDIA"]` gives an array of characters.

### Escape characters
| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `\'` `\"` | quote |
| `\\` | backslash |
| `\n` | new line |
| `\t` | tab |
| `\u{1F600}` | Unicode code point |

### Template literals (ES2015)
```js
const name = "Ravi", n = 5;
const msg = `Hi ${name}, 5 * ${n} = ${5 * n}`;
const multi = `line one
line two`;
```
- `${expression}` can contain any JavaScript expression.
- Multi-line strings need no `\n`.
- **Tagged templates** (a function name written right before a template literal) pass the text pieces and values to that function; libraries like styled-components use this.

### Concatenation
`+` joins strings; if either side is a string the other is converted. Prefer template literals for readability. `"5" + 3` is `"53"`.

### Comparing
Use `===`. For locale-aware ordering use `a.localeCompare(b)`.

### Emoji caveat
Some characters take two code units, so `"😀".length` is `2`. Use `[..."😀"].length` to count real characters.
keyPoints: Strings are immutable - methods return new strings
Template literals use backticks, ${} and allow multiple lines
Index with str[i] or str.at(-1)
Strings are iterable with for...of and spread
length counts UTF-16 code units, not always visible characters
pitfalls: Trying to modify str[0] does nothing
Mixing quotes without escaping causes a syntax error
Concatenating numbers and strings with + gives unexpected results

examples.title: Template literals and immutability

interview.q: Are strings mutable in JavaScript?
interview.a: No. Strings are immutable primitives; every method such as replace or toUpperCase returns a new string.

interview.q: What are the advantages of template literals?
interview.a: They allow expression interpolation with ${}, multi-line strings without escapes, and tagged templates.

interview.q: What does "5" + 3 return and why?
interview.a: "53". When either operand of + is a string, JavaScript concatenates instead of adding.

topics.title: Essential String Methods
topics.summary: Search, extract, replace, pad, split and clean strings with the built-in methods.
topics.description:
### Searching
- `indexOf(text, from)` / `lastIndexOf(text)` - position or `-1` (case sensitive).
- `includes(text)`, `startsWith(text, pos)`, `endsWith(text)` - booleans.
- `search(regex)` - index of first regex match.
- `match(regex)` - array of matches (with `g`) or match details; `matchAll(regex)` - iterator of all matches with groups.

### Extracting
- `slice(start, end)` - supports **negative** indexes. Preferred.
- `substring(start, end)` - negatives treated as 0, swaps arguments if start > end.
- `substr()` is **deprecated**.
- `charAt(i)`, `charCodeAt(i)`, `at(i)`.

### Replacing
- `replace(search, replacement)` - first match only (for a string search).
- `replaceAll(search, replacement)` (ES2021) - all matches.
- Both accept a regex or a function as the replacement.

### Transforming
`toUpperCase()`, `toLowerCase()`, `trim()`, `trimStart()`, `trimEnd()`, `padStart(len, ch)`, `padEnd(len, ch)`, `repeat(n)`, `concat()`.

### Splitting and joining
`"a,b,c".split(",")` gives an array; `array.join("-")` builds a string. Reverse a string: `str.split("").reverse().join("")`.

### Char codes
`"a".charCodeAt(0)` is 97 and `String.fromCharCode(97)` is `"a"`. Useful for loops from "a" to "z" and Caesar ciphers.

All of these return **new** values; the original string never changes.
keyPoints: slice supports negative indexes, substring does not
replace changes only the first match, replaceAll changes all
includes/startsWith/endsWith return booleans
split and join convert between strings and arrays
padStart is great for 0-padded numbers
pitfalls: indexOf is case sensitive
replace("a", "b") with a string only replaces the first occurrence
includes does not accept a regex (it throws)

examples.title: Extract, replace, pad
Count vowels and pangram

interview.q: Difference between slice and substring?
interview.a: Both extract part of a string, but slice accepts negative indexes (counting from the end) while substring treats negatives as 0 and swaps arguments if start is greater than end.

interview.q: How do you replace all occurrences of a word?
interview.a: Use replaceAll("a", "b") or replace with a global regex: replace(/a/g, "b").

interview.q: How do you reverse a string?
interview.a: str.split("").reverse().join("") or [...str].reverse().join("") to handle Unicode characters better.

topics.title: Regular Expressions
topics.summary: Describe text patterns with regex literals, flags, groups and use them with test, match and replace.
topics.description:
A **regular expression** (regex) is a pattern used to search, validate and replace text.

### Creating
```js
const re1 = /ab+c/gi;             // literal
const re2 = new RegExp("ab+c", "gi"); // constructor (dynamic patterns)
```

### Flags
| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `g` | global - find all matches |
| `i` | ignore case |
| `m` | `^`/`$` match at each line |
| `s` | dot matches newline |
| `u` | full Unicode |
| `y` | sticky |

### Building blocks
- Character classes: `\d` digit, `\w` word char, `\s` space, `.` any char, `[abc]`, `[^abc]`, `[a-z]`.
- Quantifiers: `*` (0+), `+` (1+), `?` (0 or 1), `{2,4}`.
- Anchors: `^` start, `$` end, `\b` word boundary.
- Groups: `( )` capture, `(?: )` non-capture, `(?<year>\d{4})` named group.
- Alternation: `cat|dog`. Lookahead: `a(?=b)`.

### Methods
- `regex.test(str)` - boolean.
- `regex.exec(str)` - match details (stateful with `g`).
- `str.match(regex)`, `str.matchAll(regex)`, `str.replace(regex, fn)`, `str.split(regex)`, `str.search(regex)`.

### Notes
- Quantifiers are **greedy** by default; add `?` to make them lazy (`.*?`).
- A regex with the `g` flag keeps `lastIndex`, so calling `test` twice can give surprising results.
- Do not validate full email addresses or HTML with regex; keep patterns simple.
keyPoints: Literal /pattern/flags or new RegExp(string, flags)
g finds all matches, i ignores case
test returns boolean, match/matchAll return matches
Use capture groups and named groups to extract parts
Quantifiers are greedy unless followed by ?
pitfalls: Reusing a /g regex with test() keeps lastIndex and alternates results
Forgetting to escape special characters like . or ?
Catastrophic backtracking with nested quantifiers

examples.title: Validate and extract

interview.q: What does the g flag do?
interview.a: It makes the regex global so match/replace find all matches instead of stopping after the first, and test/exec keep track of lastIndex.

interview.q: What is the difference between greedy and lazy quantifiers?
interview.a: Greedy quantifiers (.*) match as much as possible; lazy ones (.*?) match as little as possible.

interview.q: How do you extract capturing groups?
interview.a: Use match/exec/matchAll and read result[1], result[2] or result.groups.name for named groups.

topics.title: Numbers and the Math Object
topics.summary: Work with number methods, rounding, random numbers and floating point limits.
topics.description:
### The Number type
All numbers are 64-bit floating point. Useful constants: `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53 - 1), `Number.EPSILON`, `Infinity`. For integers larger than the safe limit use **BigInt** (`123n`).

### Number methods
- `n.toFixed(2)` - string with 2 decimals (rounds).
- `n.toString(2)` - binary string; `n.toString(16)` - hex.
- `Number.isInteger`, `Number.isFinite`, `Number.isNaN`, `Number.parseFloat`.
- `toLocaleString()` - formatting like `1,23,456.78`.

### Math object
| Method | Result |
|---|---|
| `Math.round(3.5)` | 4 (nearest) |
| `Math.ceil(3.1)` | 4 (up) |
| `Math.floor(3.9)` | 3 (down) |
| `Math.trunc(-3.7)` | -3 (remove decimals) |
| `Math.abs(-5)` | 5 |
| `Math.max(...)`, `Math.min(...)` | extremes |
| `Math.pow(2, 5)` or `2 ** 5` | 32 |
| `Math.sqrt(25)` | 5 |
| `Math.PI` | 3.14159... |
| `Math.sign(-8)` | -1 |

`Math.floor(-3.1)` is `-4` while `Math.trunc(-3.1)` is `-3`.

### Random numbers
`Math.random()` returns a number from 0 (inclusive) to 1 (exclusive).
```js
const randInt = (min, max) => Math.floor(Math.random() * (max - min + 1)) + min;
```
It is **not** cryptographically secure; use `crypto.getRandomValues()` for tokens.

### Floating point
`0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3`. Compare with `Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON` or use integers (paise/cents).
keyPoints: All numbers are 64-bit floats
toFixed returns a string
floor rounds down, ceil up, trunc removes decimals
Math.random is in [0, 1) and not secure
BigInt handles integers beyond 2^53 - 1
pitfalls: toFixed(2) of 1.005 is "1.00" because of binary representation
Mixing BigInt and Number throws a TypeError

examples.title: Rounding and random

interview.q: Difference between Math.floor and Math.trunc?
interview.a: They are equal for positive numbers. For negative numbers floor goes down (-3.1 gives -4) while trunc just drops the decimals (-3.1 gives -3).

interview.q: How do you generate a random integer between min and max inclusive?
interview.a: Math.floor(Math.random() * (max - min + 1)) + min.

interview.q: How do you deal with floating point errors in money calculations?
interview.a: Store amounts as integers in the smallest unit (cents/paise), or round with toFixed for display only, or use a decimal library.

topics.title: Date and Time
topics.summary: Create, read, change and compare dates, and remember that months start at 0.
topics.description:
The `Date` object stores **milliseconds since 1 January 1970 UTC** (the Unix epoch).

### Creating dates
```js
new Date();                          // now
new Date("2024-02-19");              // ISO string (parsed as UTC)
new Date("2024-02-19T10:44:09Z");
new Date(2024, 1, 19, 10, 44);       // year, MONTH(0-11), day, h, m
new Date(1708339449000);             // from milliseconds
Date.now();                          // current timestamp (number)
```

### Getters
`getFullYear()`, `getMonth()` (**0-11**), `getDate()` (1-31), `getDay()` (0 = Sunday), `getHours()`, `getMinutes()`, `getSeconds()`, `getTime()`. UTC versions: `getUTCHours()` etc.

### Setters
`setFullYear`, `setMonth`, `setDate`, `setHours`... They **mutate** the date and automatically roll over: `d.setDate(d.getDate() + 7)` adds a week even across months.

### Formatting
- `toISOString()` - `2024-02-19T10:44:09.274Z` (best for storage/APIs).
- `toLocaleDateString("en-IN")`, `toLocaleTimeString()`, `toLocaleString()`.
- For full control use `Intl.DateTimeFormat` (next topic).

### Arithmetic
Subtracting two dates returns milliseconds:
```js
const days = Math.round((d2 - d1) / (24 * 60 * 60 * 1000));
```

### Gotchas
- Months are zero-based; days of month are one-based.
- Date-only ISO strings are UTC, date-time strings without `Z` are local time.
- Time zones and daylight saving make date math tricky; the upcoming Temporal API will fix many issues.
keyPoints: A Date is a number of ms since 1970-01-01 UTC
Months are 0-11, getDay returns 0 for Sunday
Setters mutate and handle overflow automatically
Subtracting dates gives milliseconds
Use toISOString for machine-readable output
pitfalls: new Date(2024, 1, 29) is February, not January
Date strings in non-ISO formats parse differently across browsers
Mutating a Date that is shared between functions

examples.title: Add days and difference between dates

interview.q: Why does new Date(2024, 0, 1) give January and not 0th month?
interview.a: Months are zero-based in JavaScript (0 = January, 11 = December), while the day of the month starts at 1.

interview.q: How do you find the difference in days between two dates?
interview.a: Subtract the dates to get milliseconds and divide by 24*60*60*1000, then round.

interview.q: What does Date.now() return?
interview.a: The current timestamp as the number of milliseconds since the Unix epoch.

topics.title: Intl: Formatting Dates, Numbers and Currency
topics.summary: The built-in Intl API formats dates, numbers, currency, lists and region names for any locale.
topics.description:
`Intl` is the **Internationalization API** built into every modern browser and Node.js. It formats values according to a locale without any library.

### Intl.DateTimeFormat
```js
const fmt = new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", {
  weekday: "long", year: "numeric", month: "long", day: "numeric",
  hour: "numeric", minute: "numeric",
});
fmt.format(new Date());
```
Shortcut: `date.toLocaleDateString("en-IN", options)`.

### Intl.NumberFormat
```js
new Intl.NumberFormat("en-IN", { style: "currency", currency: "INR" }).format(1234567.5);
// "₹12,34,567.50"
```
Options: `style` (`decimal`, `currency`, `percent`, `unit`), `minimumFractionDigits`, `notation: "compact"` (`1.2M`).

### Intl.DisplayNames
Turns codes into names - used in the weather app project to show a country name:
```js
new Intl.DisplayNames(["en"], { type: "region" }).of("IN"); // "India"
```

### Other helpers
- `Intl.RelativeTimeFormat` - "yesterday", "in 3 days".
- `Intl.ListFormat` - "A, B, and C".
- `Intl.PluralRules`, `Intl.Collator` (locale aware sorting).

### Why use it
It handles currency symbols, digit grouping, month names and right-to-left languages for you, and is faster and more correct than hand-written formatting.

Remember to create a formatter **once** and reuse it if you format many values.
keyPoints: Intl formats by locale: dates, numbers, currency, lists
DateTimeFormat and NumberFormat take locale + options
DisplayNames converts region codes to names
toLocaleString methods use Intl under the hood
Reuse formatter instances for performance
pitfalls: Output depends on the runtime's locale data and may differ slightly
Passing an invalid currency code throws a RangeError

examples.title: Dates, currency and names

interview.q: How do you format a number as currency in JavaScript?
interview.a: Use Intl.NumberFormat(locale, { style: "currency", currency: "USD" }).format(value) or number.toLocaleString with the same options.

interview.q: What is Intl.DisplayNames used for?
interview.a: To convert codes such as region (IN), language (en) or currency (USD) into human-readable names in a chosen language.

interview.q: Why prefer Intl over manual formatting?
interview.a: It follows locale conventions automatically (separators, symbols, order, translations) and avoids bugs and extra libraries.

topics.title: Objects: Creating, Accessing and Methods
topics.summary: Objects store related data as key-value pairs and can hold functions as methods.
topics.description:
An **object** is a collection of key-value pairs (properties). Keys are strings or symbols; values can be anything, including functions (**methods**) and other objects.

### Creating
```js
const person = {
  name: "Vinod",
  age: 30,
  "is-student": false,       // quotes needed for odd names
  greet() { return `Hi ${this.name}`; },  // method shorthand
};
```
Other ways: `new Object()`, `Object.create(proto)`, constructor functions and classes.

### Accessing
- Dot notation: `person.name`.
- Bracket notation: `person["is-student"]` or `person[key]` when the key is dynamic.

### Add, update, delete, check
```js
person.job = "dev";       // add
person.age = 31;          // update
delete person.job;        // delete
"age" in person;          // true (also inherited keys)
Object.hasOwn(person, "age"); // true (own keys only)
```

### Shorthand and computed keys (ES2015)
```js
const name = "Asha", age = 25;
const user = { name, age };          // shorthand properties
const field = "email";
const form = { [field]: "a@b.com" }; // computed key
```

### Methods and this
Inside a method `this` points to the object that called it (see the `this` topic). Do not use arrow functions for methods that need `this`.

### Data modelling
Objects model real things - a car, user or product - with properties for data and methods for behaviour. Arrays of objects are the most common data shape from APIs.
keyPoints: Key-value pairs; keys are strings or symbols
Dot vs bracket notation (bracket for dynamic or odd keys)
Shorthand properties and computed keys from ES2015
delete removes a property; in/hasOwn check existence
Methods use this to reach the object
pitfalls: Using an arrow function as a method breaks this
Property order: integer-like keys are sorted first
Accessing a missing property gives undefined, not an error

examples.title: Create, read and update

interview.q: How can you add a dynamic key to an object?
interview.a: Use computed property names in the literal ({ [key]: value }) or bracket notation (obj[key] = value).

interview.q: Dot notation vs bracket notation?
interview.a: Dot notation needs a valid identifier name. Bracket notation accepts any string, including variables, spaces and special characters.

interview.q: How do you check if a property exists?
interview.a: Use "key" in obj (includes inherited), Object.hasOwn(obj, key) for own properties, or obj.key !== undefined when undefined is not a valid value.

topics.title: Object.keys, values, entries, assign and friends
topics.summary: The Object static methods let you iterate, merge, transform and inspect objects.
topics.description:
### Inspecting
- `Object.keys(obj)` - array of own enumerable **keys**.
- `Object.values(obj)` - array of **values**.
- `Object.entries(obj)` - array of `[key, value]` pairs.
- `Object.hasOwn(obj, key)` (ES2022) - modern replacement for `obj.hasOwnProperty(key)`.

### Transforming
`Object.fromEntries(entries)` (ES2019) is the reverse of `entries`. Together they let you "map" an object:

```js
const prices = { a: 10, b: 20 };
Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(prices).map(([k, v]) => [k, v * 2]));
// { a: 20, b: 40 }
```

### Merging and copying
- `Object.assign(target, ...sources)` - copies own enumerable props **into target** (mutates target).
- Spread `{ ...a, ...b }` - creates a new object; later keys win.

### Grouping (ES2024)
`Object.groupBy(items, (x) => x.category)` returns an object of arrays.

### Creating with prototype
- `Object.create(proto)` and `Object.create(null)` (no prototype - a clean dictionary).
- `Object.getPrototypeOf`, `Object.setPrototypeOf`.

### Iteration order
Integer-like keys ascending first, then string keys in insertion order, then symbols.

### Why hasOwn
`Object.create(null)` objects have no `hasOwnProperty` method, so `Object.hasOwn(obj, key)` is safer.
keyPoints: keys/values/entries return arrays for easy looping
fromEntries turns entries back into an object
assign mutates the target, spread creates a new object
Object.hasOwn is the safe own-property check
Object.groupBy groups an array by a key (ES2024)
pitfalls: Object.assign and spread are shallow copies
Object.keys ignores symbols and non-enumerable properties
Using the same target object in assign changes it permanently

examples.title: Iterate, transform and merge

interview.q: What does Object.entries return?
interview.a: An array of [key, value] pairs for the object's own enumerable string-keyed properties.

interview.q: Output of Object.assign({}, {a:1,b:2}, {b:3,c:4})?
interview.a: { a: 1, b: 3, c: 4 }. Later sources overwrite earlier keys with the same name.

interview.q: Why use Object.hasOwn instead of hasOwnProperty?
interview.a: It works on objects without a prototype (Object.create(null)) and cannot be shadowed by an own property called hasOwnProperty.

topics.title: Value vs Reference, Shallow and Deep Copy
topics.summary: Primitives are copied by value, objects by reference; know how to make shallow and deep copies.
topics.description:
### Primitives: copied by value
```js
let a = 10;
let b = a;   // independent copy
b = 20;      // a is still 10
```

### Objects and arrays: copied by reference
A variable stores a **reference** (address) to the object in the heap. Assigning copies the reference, so both names point to the same object:
```js
const obj = { name: "kody" };
const obj1 = obj;
obj1.name = "thapa";
obj.name; // "thapa"
```

### Passing to functions
JavaScript is always pass-by-value, but for objects the value is the reference. A function can **mutate** the caller's object, but re-assigning the parameter does not affect the caller.

### Comparison
`{} === {}` is `false`. Two objects are equal only if they are the same reference.

### Shallow copy
Copies the top level only; nested objects are still shared.
- `{ ...obj }`, `Object.assign({}, obj)`
- `[...arr]`, `arr.slice()`

### Deep copy
- `structuredClone(obj)` - built-in (handles Date, Map, Set, cycles; not functions).
- `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))` - quick but loses `undefined`, functions, Dates (become strings), Map/Set.
- Libraries like lodash `cloneDeep`.

### Deep equality
No built-in operator. Compare recursively, or `JSON.stringify` for simple cases (key order matters).
keyPoints: Primitives copy by value, objects by reference
Spread and Object.assign make shallow copies
structuredClone makes a deep copy
=== on objects checks identity, not content
Functions can mutate objects passed in
pitfalls: Spread on nested data still shares inner objects
JSON clone drops functions, undefined and turns Dates into strings
const does not stop an object from being mutated

examples.title: Reference, shallow and deep copy

interview.q: Is JavaScript pass by value or pass by reference?
interview.a: Always pass by value. For objects, the value passed is a copy of the reference, so mutations are visible to the caller but reassigning the parameter is not.

interview.q: Difference between shallow and deep copy?
interview.a: A shallow copy duplicates only the top level and nested objects remain shared. A deep copy duplicates every nested level.

interview.q: How do you deep clone an object?
interview.a: structuredClone(obj) in modern environments, or JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) for simple JSON-safe data, or a library function.

topics.title: Property Descriptors, freeze and seal
topics.summary: Control whether properties can be changed, listed or deleted using descriptors, freeze and seal.
topics.description:
Each property has hidden **attributes** described by a *property descriptor*:

| Attribute | Meaning | Default (literal) |
|---|---|---|
| `value` | the stored value | - |
| `writable` | can be changed | `true` |
| `enumerable` | appears in loops and `Object.keys` | `true` |
| `configurable` | can be deleted / redefined | `true` |

Accessor properties use `get` and `set` instead of `value`/`writable`.

### Reading and defining
```js
Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(obj, "id");
Object.defineProperty(obj, "id", { value: 1, writable: false, enumerable: false });
```
Properties added with `defineProperty` default to `false` for all three flags.

### Locking objects
| Method | Add | Delete | Change values |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Object.preventExtensions(o)` | no | yes | yes |
| `Object.seal(o)` | no | no | yes |
| `Object.freeze(o)` | no | no | no |

Check with `Object.isFrozen`, `Object.isSealed`, `Object.isExtensible`.

### Important details
- `freeze` is **shallow**; nested objects stay mutable. Write a recursive `deepFreeze` if needed.
- In sloppy mode writes to frozen objects fail **silently**; in strict mode (modules, classes) they throw a `TypeError`.
- Getters and setters via `get`/`set` in literals or classes allow computed or validated properties.

### Use cases
Constants, configuration objects, enums (`Object.freeze({ UP: "UP" })`), hiding internals, library APIs and immutable state in Redux-style code.
keyPoints: Descriptor flags: writable, enumerable, configurable
defineProperty defaults all flags to false
freeze = no add, delete or change; seal allows changes
freeze is shallow
Strict mode throws errors where sloppy mode silently ignores
pitfalls: Assuming Object.freeze makes nested data immutable
Silent failure in non-strict code hides bugs
Frozen objects cannot be unfrozen

examples.title: freeze, seal and defineProperty

interview.q: Difference between Object.freeze and Object.seal?
interview.a: freeze makes properties read-only and prevents adding or deleting. seal prevents adding and deleting but still allows changing existing values.

interview.q: Is Object.freeze deep?
interview.a: No. It only freezes the top level; nested objects can still be modified unless frozen recursively.

interview.q: What do writable, enumerable and configurable mean?
interview.a: writable allows value changes, enumerable shows the property in loops and Object.keys, configurable allows deleting or redefining the property.

topics.title: JSON: stringify and parse
topics.summary: JSON is a text format for data exchange; convert with JSON.stringify and JSON.parse.
topics.description:
**JSON** (JavaScript Object Notation) is a lightweight text format used to exchange data between server and client and to store it as text (localStorage, files).

### Rules of JSON
- Keys must be in **double quotes**.
- Strings use double quotes only.
- Allowed values: object, array, string, number, `true`, `false`, `null`.
- No comments, no trailing commas, no `undefined`, no functions.

### JSON.stringify(value, replacer, space)
Converts a JavaScript value to a JSON string.
```js
JSON.stringify({ name: "Vinod", age: 30 });          // '{"name":"Vinod","age":30}'
JSON.stringify(data, null, 2);                        // pretty printed
JSON.stringify(user, ["name"]);                       // only chosen keys
```
- `undefined`, functions and symbols are **skipped** in objects (become `null` in arrays).
- `Date` becomes an ISO string. `NaN` and `Infinity` become `null`.
- Objects can define `toJSON()` to customise output.
- Circular references throw a `TypeError`.

### JSON.parse(text, reviver)
Converts JSON text back to a value. Invalid JSON throws a `SyntaxError`, so wrap in `try...catch`. A **reviver** function can transform values (for example turn date strings back into `Date`).

### Typical uses
- `fetch().then(r => r.json())` calls `JSON.parse` for you.
- Storing objects in `localStorage`.
- Quick deep copy for simple data.
- Sending a request body: `body: JSON.stringify(payload)`.
keyPoints: stringify: value to JSON text; parse: text to value
JSON has no undefined, functions, comments or single quotes
Always wrap JSON.parse of external data in try/catch
localStorage only stores strings, so stringify objects
toJSON and replacer customise the output
pitfalls: Dates are stringified and not restored automatically
Circular objects cannot be stringified
Single-quoted or unquoted keys make JSON.parse throw

examples.title: Round trip and edge cases

interview.q: Difference between JSON and a JavaScript object?
interview.a: JSON is a text format with strict syntax (double-quoted keys and strings, no functions or undefined). A JavaScript object is a live in-memory value.

interview.q: What happens to undefined and functions in JSON.stringify?
interview.a: They are omitted from objects and replaced by null inside arrays.

interview.q: How do you store an object in localStorage?
interview.a: localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(obj)) and read it back with JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(key)).

topics.title: Map and Set
topics.summary: Map stores key-value pairs with any key type; Set stores unique values.
topics.description:
### Map
A **Map** holds key-value pairs where keys can be **any type** (objects, functions, numbers) and insertion order is preserved.

```js
const m = new Map();
m.set("a", 1).set({ id: 1 }, "obj");
m.get("a");     // 1
m.has("a");     // true
m.delete("a");
m.size;         // number of entries
for (const [k, v] of m) {}
```

Why Map instead of a plain object?
| | Object | Map |
|---|---|---|
| Key types | string / symbol | anything |
| Order | mostly insertion | insertion |
| Size | `Object.keys(o).length` | `map.size` |
| Prototype keys | yes (`toString`) | none |
| Performance for frequent add/delete | ok | better |

### Set
A **Set** stores **unique values** of any type.
```js
const s = new Set([1, 2, 2, 3]); // {1, 2, 3}
s.add(4); s.has(2); s.delete(1); s.size;
```
Use it to remove duplicates (`[...new Set(arr)]`) and for fast membership checks.

### Converting
`new Map(Object.entries(obj))`, `Object.fromEntries(map)`, `[...map.keys()]`, `Array.from(set)`.

### Equality
Set and Map use **SameValueZero**: `NaN` equals `NaN`, but two different objects are different even if their content matches.

### Set operations (new in 2024-2025)
`union`, `intersection`, `difference`, `symmetricDifference`, `isSubsetOf` exist in the latest engines. Otherwise use filter.
keyPoints: Map: any key type, ordered, has size
Set: unique values, fast has()
Iterate with for...of or forEach
Convert between arrays/objects and Map/Set easily
Objects as keys are compared by reference
pitfalls: map[key] = value on a Map does not store an entry
Two equal-looking objects are two different Set members
JSON.stringify(map) gives {}

examples.title: Count words with a Map and dedupe with a Set

interview.q: Difference between Map and Object?
interview.a: Map accepts any type as key, keeps insertion order, has a size property and no inherited keys. Object keys are strings or symbols and inherit from Object.prototype.

interview.q: How do you remove duplicates from an array?
interview.a: [...new Set(array)].

interview.q: How does Set compare values?
interview.a: With SameValueZero: primitives by value (NaN equals NaN) and objects by reference.

topics.title: WeakMap, WeakSet, Symbol and BigInt
topics.summary: Weak collections allow garbage collection, symbols create unique keys and BigInt handles huge integers.
topics.description:
### WeakMap and WeakSet
- Keys (WeakMap) / values (WeakSet) must be **objects**.
- References are **weak**: if nothing else references the object, it can be garbage collected and its entry disappears.
- Not iterable and have no `size` - you cannot list entries.

```js
const privateData = new WeakMap();
class User { constructor(n) { privateData.set(this, { n }); } }
```
Use cases: private data for objects, caching computed results per object, tracking DOM nodes without memory leaks.

### Symbol
A **Symbol** is a unique, immutable primitive often used as a hidden property key.
```js
const id = Symbol("id");
const user = { name: "A", [id]: 123 };
```
- `Symbol("x") !== Symbol("x")`.
- Symbol keys are skipped by `for...in`, `Object.keys` and `JSON.stringify`.
- `Symbol.for("key")` creates/reads a global registry symbol.
- `symbol.description` (ES2019) returns the text.
- **Well-known symbols** customise behaviour: `Symbol.iterator`, `Symbol.toPrimitive`, `Symbol.asyncIterator`, `Symbol.hasInstance`.

### BigInt
Integers of arbitrary size, written with `n`: `123456789012345678901234567890n`.
```js
BigInt(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER) + 10n;
```
You cannot mix BigInt and Number in arithmetic (`1n + 1` throws), and `Math` functions do not accept BigInt. Use it for big IDs, factorials and cryptography.
keyPoints: WeakMap/WeakSet hold objects weakly and are not iterable
Symbols are unique primitive keys, hidden from normal enumeration
Symbol.iterator makes an object iterable
BigInt: whole numbers of any size, written with n
BigInt and Number cannot be mixed directly
pitfalls: You cannot loop or get the size of a WeakMap
JSON.stringify throws on BigInt values
Two Symbol("same") values are not equal

examples.title: Symbol, WeakMap and BigInt

interview.q: What is the difference between Map and WeakMap?
interview.a: WeakMap keys must be objects and are held weakly, so entries are garbage collected when the key is unreachable. WeakMap is not iterable and has no size.

interview.q: Why use Symbols as property keys?
interview.a: They are unique, so they avoid name collisions and are not exposed by normal enumeration, which makes them suitable for metadata and protocols like Symbol.iterator.

interview.q: When do you need BigInt?
interview.a: When integers exceed Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (2^53 - 1), such as large IDs, timestamps in nanoseconds or cryptographic calculations.

topics.title: Destructuring
topics.summary: Unpack values from arrays and properties from objects into variables in one line.
topics.description:
**Destructuring** extracts values from arrays or objects into separate variables with a short, readable syntax.

### Array destructuring (by position)
```js
const [first, second, , fourth] = [10, 20, 30, 40];
const [a, b = 5, ...rest] = [1, undefined, 3, 4];
[x, y] = [y, x];     // swap without a temp variable
```

### Object destructuring (by name)
```js
const user = { name: "Vinod", age: 30, address: { city: "Pune" } };
const { name, age } = user;
const { name: fullName } = user;           // rename
const { role = "guest" } = user;           // default
const { address: { city } } = user;        // nested
const { name: n, ...others } = user;       // rest
```

### In function parameters
```js
function show({ name, age = 18 } = {}) {}
const total = ({ price, qty }) => price * qty;
```
This is the standard way to receive props in React components and options objects.

### In loops and imports
```js
for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(obj)) {}
import { useState } from "react";
```

### Rules and tips
- Object patterns match **names**; array patterns match **positions**.
- Destructuring `null` or `undefined` throws a `TypeError`; give a default `= {}`.
- Defaults apply only for `undefined`.
- Computed names are allowed: `const { [key]: value } = obj`.
- When assigning to existing variables in an object pattern, wrap in parentheses: `({ a, b } = obj);`.

### Why it matters
Less repetition (`user.name`, `user.age`), clearer function signatures and elegant swapping or returning multiple values from a function.
keyPoints: Arrays match by position, objects match by key name
Rename with a colon and default with =
Rest collects the remaining items or properties
Works in parameters, loops and imports
Destructuring null/undefined throws
pitfalls: Order matters for arrays but not for objects
Forgetting parentheses around an assignment pattern at statement start
A default is not used for null values

examples.title: Arrays and objects

interview.q: How do you swap two variables without a third variable?
interview.a: Use array destructuring: [a, b] = [b, a].

interview.q: How do you rename a property while destructuring?
interview.a: Use a colon: const { name: fullName } = user.

interview.q: What happens when you destructure undefined?
interview.a: It throws a TypeError. Provide a default value (= {}) for parameters that may be missing.

topics.title: Spread and Rest Operators
topics.summary: The three dots expand iterables or objects (spread) and collect leftovers (rest).
topics.description:
The `...` syntax has two roles depending on where it appears.

### Spread - expand
Used in **calls, array literals and object literals**.

```js
// arrays
const all = [...numbers1, ...numbers2];
const copy = [...fruits];
const chars = [..."INDIA"];
// function calls
Math.max(...nums);
fruits.push(...["guava", "grapes"]);
// objects (ES2018)
const merged = { ...defaults, ...options };    // later keys win
const updated = { ...user, age: 31 };
```

### Rest - collect
Used in **parameters and destructuring patterns**.

```js
function sum(...nums) {}             // all arguments as an array
const [head, ...tail] = [1, 2, 3];
const { id, ...others } = obj;       // others = remaining props
```
Rest must always be the **last** element, and there can be only one.

### Spread vs rest
| | Spread | Rest |
|---|---|---|
| Position | right side / call | left side / parameter |
| Action | expands one value into many | gathers many into one |

### Shallow copy
Spread copies only the first level. Nested objects and arrays are shared between the copy and the original.

### Common patterns
- Immutable updates in React/Redux: `{ ...state, loading: true }`.
- Merging config with defaults.
- Removing a key: `const { password, ...safeUser } = user`.
- Converting a `Set` or `NodeList` to an array: `[...set]`.
keyPoints: Spread expands arrays, strings, sets and objects
Rest collects remaining items into an array/object
Rest must be last
Spread makes shallow copies
Later spread properties override earlier ones
pitfalls: Spreading a plain object into an array throws (objects are not iterable)
Nested data is still shared after spreading
Large arrays in function-call spread can overflow the stack

examples.title: Spread and rest in practice

interview.q: What is the difference between spread and rest?
interview.a: Spread expands an iterable/object into individual elements; rest collects multiple elements into a single array or object. Same syntax, different position.

interview.q: How do you merge two objects?
interview.a: { ...obj1, ...obj2 } or Object.assign({}, obj1, obj2). Properties of the later object win.

interview.q: Is spread a deep copy?
interview.a: No, it is shallow. Nested objects are copied by reference.

topics.title: Optional Chaining (?.) and Nullish Coalescing (??)
topics.summary: Safely read deep properties and apply defaults only for null or undefined.
topics.description:
### Optional chaining `?.` (ES2020)
Stops evaluation and returns `undefined` if the value before `?.` is `null` or `undefined`, instead of throwing a `TypeError`.

```js
user?.address?.city        // property
user.getName?.()           // method that may not exist
items?.[0]                 // array / dynamic key
```
Without it you would write `user && user.address && user.address.city`.

Important: `?.` short-circuits the **entire chain**, and it only guards the part immediately before it. Do not overuse it - if a value must exist, let the error surface.

### Nullish coalescing `??` (ES2020)
Returns the right side only when the left is `null` or `undefined`:
```js
const count = 0;
count || 10;   // 10  (0 is falsy)
count ?? 10;   // 0   (0 is valid)
```

### Together
```js
const city = person.address?.city ?? "city is not present";
```

### Logical assignment (ES2021)
```js
user.nickname ??= "friend";   // assign if null/undefined
settings.volume ||= 50;       // assign if falsy
isOn &&= toggle();            // assign if truthy
```

### Differences
| Operator | Falls back when left is |
|---|---|
| `\|\|` | any falsy value |
| `??` | only `null` or `undefined` |

### Notes
- `?.` cannot be used on the left of an assignment (`a?.b = 1` is invalid).
- Combining `??` with `||` or `&&` requires parentheses.
keyPoints: ?. returns undefined if the left side is null or undefined
Works for properties, methods and indexes
?? treats only null and undefined as missing
??= ||= &&= assign conditionally
Prefer ?? over || for defaults
pitfalls: Overusing ?. hides real bugs
Mixing ?? with || without parentheses is a syntax error
?. does not protect against a value that is not null but not an object either

examples.title: Safe access and defaults

interview.q: What does optional chaining do?
interview.a: It short-circuits and returns undefined when the part before ?. is null or undefined, instead of throwing an error.

interview.q: Difference between || and ???
interview.a: || uses the right side for every falsy value; ?? uses it only for null and undefined, so 0, "" and false are preserved.

interview.q: Can you write user?.name = "x"?
interview.a: No. Optional chaining is not allowed on the left side of an assignment.

topics.title: ES2015 to ES2019 Feature Tour
topics.summary: A year-by-year list of the features that shaped modern JavaScript between ES2015 and ES2019.
topics.description:
ECMAScript releases a new version every year. These are the features you must know.

### ES2015 (ES6) - the big one
- `let`, `const`, block scope
- Arrow functions, default / rest parameters, spread
- Template literals, destructuring, shorthand properties
- Classes, modules (`import`/`export`)
- Promises, `Symbol`, iterators and generators
- `Map`, `Set`, `WeakMap`, `WeakSet`
- `for...of`, `Array.from`, `Object.assign`, `String.includes/startsWith`, `Math.trunc`

### ES2016
- `**` exponent operator
- `Array.prototype.includes()`

### ES2017
- `async` / `await`
- `Object.values()`, `Object.entries()`
- `padStart()`, `padEnd()`
- Trailing commas in function parameter lists
- `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptors`

### ES2018
- Object **rest / spread** properties
- `Promise.prototype.finally()`
- Async iteration (`for await...of`)
- Regex: named groups, lookbehind, `s` flag

### ES2019
- `Array.prototype.flat()` and `flatMap()`
- `Object.fromEntries()`
- `trimStart()`, `trimEnd()`
- Optional catch binding: `catch { }`
- `Symbol.prototype.description`
- Stable `Array.prototype.sort`

### How to use this list
Check support in your target browsers (caniuse.com or MDN) and let a build tool such as Babel or esbuild transpile when you must support old ones.
keyPoints: ES2015 introduced let/const, classes, modules, promises, arrow functions
ES2017 gave us async/await and Object.entries/values
ES2018 brought object spread and Promise.finally
ES2019 added flat, flatMap and Object.fromEntries
A new ECMAScript version ships every year
pitfalls: ES versions are not browser versions - check actual support
Features like top-level await need modules

interview.a: It modernised the language: let/const, arrow functions, classes, modules, promises, template literals, destructuring, spread/rest, Map/Set, symbols and generators.

interview.q: Which ES version introduced async/await?
What does Object.fromEntries do?
interview.a: It converts an iterable of [key, value] pairs (such as Object.entries output or a Map) into an object.

topics.title: ES2020 to ES2024 Feature Tour
topics.summary: The newest features: optional chaining, BigInt, at(), hasOwn, immutable array methods, groupBy and more.
topics.description:
### ES2020
- Optional chaining `?.` and nullish coalescing `??`
- `BigInt` (`123n`)
- `Promise.allSettled()`
- `globalThis`, dynamic `import()`
- `String.prototype.matchAll()`

### ES2021
- `String.prototype.replaceAll()`
- Logical assignment `||=`, `&&=`, `??=`
- Numeric separators `1_000_000`
- `Promise.any()` and `AggregateError`
- `WeakRef`

### ES2022
- `Array.prototype.at()` and `String.prototype.at()`
- `Object.hasOwn()`
- Class fields and **private** `#fields`, static blocks
- **Top-level await** in modules
- `Error` `cause` option

### ES2023
- `findLast()`, `findLastIndex()`
- `toSorted()`, `toReversed()`, `toSpliced()`, `with()`
- Hashbang `#!` support

### ES2024
- `Object.groupBy()` and `Map.groupBy()`
- `Promise.withResolvers()`
- `Array.fromAsync()`
- `String.prototype.isWellFormed()`
- Regex `v` flag, resizable `ArrayBuffer`

### Looking ahead
Temporal API (a modern replacement for `Date`), iterator helpers (`map`, `filter`, `take` on iterators), `Set` methods (`union`, `intersection`) and decorators are being rolled out.

Always check runtime support before relying on the newest features.

interview.a: Promise.any resolves with the first fulfilled promise and ignores rejections (rejecting with AggregateError only if all reject). Promise.race settles with the first promise to settle, fulfilled or rejected.

interview.q: Name the non-mutating array methods added in ES2023.

topics.summary: Iterables produce values one by one; generator functions make writing them easy with yield.

interview.q: What is an iterator?
interview.a: An object with a next() method that returns { value, done }. Iterables expose one through [Symbol.iterator]().

interview.q: What is a generator function?
interview.a: A function declared with function* that can pause with yield and resume later; it returns an iterator and produces values lazily.

interview.q: Why are generators useful?
interview.a: They produce values on demand (memory efficient, can be infinite), simplify writing iterators and underpin async iteration.

topics.title: ES Modules: import and export
topics.summary: Split code into files with export and import; each module has its own scope.
topics.description:
**ES modules** (ES2015) are the standard way to split JavaScript into reusable files. Each file is a module with its **own scope**; nothing is global unless exported.

### Exporting
```js
// math.js
export const PI = 3.14159;                 // named exports
export function add(a, b) { return a + b; }
export default function multiply(a, b) { return a * b; } // one default per file
```

### Importing
```js
import multiply, { PI, add } from "./math.js";
import { add as sum } from "./math.js";     // rename
import * as math from "./math.js";          // namespace object
```

### Using modules in the browser
```html
<script type="module" src="main.js"></script>
```
Modules are deferred by default, run in **strict mode**, and need a server (they do not work with `file://` due to CORS).

### Key properties
- Imports are **live read-only bindings**, not copies.
- Modules run **once** and are cached.
- Static `import` statements are hoisted and analysed at build time, which enables **tree-shaking** (removing unused exports).
- **Dynamic import**: `const mod = await import("./heavy.js")` loads on demand (code splitting).
- **Top-level await** works in modules.

### CommonJS vs ES modules
| | CommonJS | ES modules |
|---|---|---|
| Syntax | `require` / `module.exports` | `import` / `export` |
| Loading | sync | async, static |
| Default in | older Node | browsers, modern tooling |

In Node.js use `"type": "module"` in package.json or the `.mjs` extension.
keyPoints: Named exports use braces, default exports do not
Each module has its own scope and runs once
Imports are live bindings and read-only
Dynamic import() loads code lazily
Browsers need type="module" and a server
pitfalls: Forgetting the file extension or ./ in browser imports
Circular dependencies can produce undefined values
Mixing require and import in the same file
