interview.q: Difference between named and default exports?
interview.a: A module can have many named exports (imported with braces and the exact name) but only one default export, which can be imported under any name.

interview.q: What is tree shaking?
interview.a: A build optimisation that removes unused exports from the bundle; it works because ES module imports and exports are static.

interview.q: Difference between CommonJS and ES modules?
interview.a: CommonJS uses require/module.exports and loads synchronously. ES modules use import/export, are statically analysable, asynchronous and the official standard.

sections.title: Under the Hood: Scope, Closures and this

topics.title: Execution Context and the Call Stack
topics.summary: Every run of code happens inside an execution context created in two phases and tracked on the call stack.
topics.description:
When JavaScript runs code it creates an **execution context** - an environment that stores variables, functions, the scope chain and the value of `this`.

### Types of contexts
- **Global execution context** - created first; `this` is `window` (browser) or `globalThis`/`module.exports` in Node.
- **Function execution context** - created every time a function is called.
- **Eval context** - rarely used.

### Two phases
1. **Creation (memory) phase**
   - Creates the variable environment.
   - `var` variables are stored with the value `undefined`.
   - Function declarations are stored with their whole body.
   - `let`/`const` are registered but **uninitialised** (temporal dead zone).
   - Sets up the scope chain and `this`.
2. **Execution phase** - runs line by line, assigning values and calling functions.

### The call stack
A **LIFO** (last in, first out) stack of execution contexts. Calling a function **pushes** a context; returning **pops** it. The global context stays at the bottom.

```js
function first() { second(); }
function second() { third(); }
function third() { console.log("done"); }
first();
// stack: global -> first -> second -> third, then unwinds
```

### Stack overflow
Too many nested calls (usually infinite recursion) throw `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`.

### Heap
Objects, arrays and functions live in the **heap**; the stack only keeps references and primitives. Async callbacks (timers, events) wait outside the stack and are moved back by the event loop only when the stack is empty.
keyPoints: Global and function execution contexts
Creation phase hoists declarations, execution phase runs code
Call stack is LIFO; functions are pushed and popped
Stack overflow comes from endless recursion
Heap stores objects, stack stores execution contexts
pitfalls: Thinking hoisting physically moves code - it is memory allocation in the creation phase
Blocking the stack with heavy loops freezes the page

examples.title: Watching the stack order

interview.q: What is an execution context?
interview.a: The environment where code is evaluated, holding variable environment, scope chain and this. There is a global context and one per function call.

interview.q: What happens in the creation phase?
interview.a: Memory is allocated: var variables are set to undefined, function declarations are stored fully, let/const are reserved but uninitialised, and scope chain and this are set.

interview.q: What is the call stack?
interview.a: A LIFO structure that tracks which function is currently executing and where to return after it finishes.

topics.title: Scope and the Scope Chain
topics.summary: Scope decides where a variable is visible: global, function or block, resolved by lexical scoping.
topics.description:
**Scope** is the area of code where a variable can be accessed.

### Kinds of scope
- **Global scope** - declared outside any function/block; visible everywhere.
- **Function scope** - variables declared inside a function (`var`, `let`, `const`) are visible only inside it.
- **Block scope** - `let` and `const` inside `{ }` (if, for, while, plain block) stay inside the block. `var` ignores blocks.
- **Module scope** - top level of an ES module is not global.

### Lexical scoping
The scope of a variable is decided by **where it is written** in the source, not where the function is called. An inner function can read variables of the functions that **enclose** it.

### Scope chain
When a variable is used, the engine looks in the current scope; if not found it goes to the outer scope, and so on up to global. If nothing is found, a `ReferenceError` is thrown. Inner variables **shadow** outer variables with the same name.

```js
const x = "global";
function outer() {
  const x = "outer";
  function inner() { console.log(x); } // "outer"
  inner();
}
```

### Global leaks
Assigning to an undeclared name (`count = 1`) creates a global (error in strict mode). Variables declared with `var` at the top of a script become properties of `window`; `let` and `const` do not.

### Best practices
Keep variables in the smallest scope, avoid globals, and prefer `const`.
keyPoints: Global, function, block (and module) scope
let/const are block scoped, var is function scoped
Lexical scope: determined by where code is written
Scope chain searches inner to outer

interview.q: What is lexical scoping?

interview.q: What is the scope chain?
interview.a: The ordered list of scopes the engine walks, from the current one outward to global, when resolving an identifier.

interview.q: Difference between function scope and block scope?
interview.a: var is function scoped (visible in the entire function). let and const are block scoped (visible only inside the nearest { }).

topics.title: Hoisting and the Temporal Dead Zone
topics.summary: Declarations are registered before code runs: var is undefined, functions are usable, let/const are in the TDZ.
topics.description:
**Hoisting** is the behaviour where declarations are processed before the code runs, so they appear "moved to the top" of their scope. Nothing really moves; the engine allocates memory during the creation phase.

### What hoists how
| Declaration | Before its line |
|---|---|
| `var x = 5` | exists, value `undefined` |
| `function f(){}` | fully usable |
| `let` / `const` | in **TDZ** - ReferenceError |
| `class C {}` | in TDZ - ReferenceError |
| `var f = function(){}` | `f` is `undefined`, calling it is a TypeError |
| `const f = () => {}` | TDZ - ReferenceError |

### Temporal dead zone (TDZ)
The time between entering a scope and the line where a `let`/`const` is declared. Accessing the variable there throws `ReferenceError: Cannot access 'x' before initialization`. It exists to catch bugs, which is one reason `var` is discouraged.

### Function vs variable priority
When a function declaration and a `var` share a name, the function is hoisted first; the `var` assignment later overwrites it at run time.

### Rules of thumb
- Declare variables at the top of their scope.
- Prefer `const`/`let`.
- Define functions before use, even though declarations allow otherwise.
- Function **expressions** and arrow functions are not hoisted like declarations.

Hoisting is one of the most asked interview topics, usually with output-based questions.

Function declarations are hoisted with their body
let/const/class are hoisted but in the TDZ until declared

interview.a: JavaScript processes declarations during the creation phase before executing code, so variables and functions can be referenced earlier in their scope. var is undefined until assigned, functions are fully available, let/const are in the TDZ.

interview.q: What is the temporal dead zone?
interview.a: The period from the start of a block until a let/const/class declaration is evaluated, in which accessing the binding throws a ReferenceError.

interview.q: Are let and const hoisted?
interview.a: Yes, they are hoisted but not initialised, so they cannot be accessed before their declaration line.

topics.title: Closures
topics.summary: A closure is a function together with the variables from the scope where it was created.
topics.description:
A **closure** is created when a function remembers the variables of its **lexical scope** even after the outer function has finished. Every function in JavaScript forms a closure; it becomes interesting when the inner function outlives the outer one.

```js
function makeCounter() {
  let count = 0;            // private variable
  return function () {      // closure over count
    count++;
    return count;
  };
}
const counter = makeCounter();
counter(); // 1
counter(); // 2
```

The call stack frame of `makeCounter` is gone, but `count` lives on in memory because the returned function still references it. The garbage collector frees it only when the closure itself is unreachable.

### Why closures matter
- **Data privacy** (module pattern, private state).
- **Function factories** (`multiplier(2)`).
- **Callbacks and event handlers** that remember context.
- **Memoization, debounce, throttle, once, curry**.
- **React hooks** rely on closures.

### Each call gets its own copy
`makeCounter()` called twice gives two independent counters.

### Closures capture variables, not values
The inner function sees the **current** value of the variable, not a snapshot. This is the cause of the classic `var` in a loop bug - fixed by `let` (new binding per iteration) or an IIFE.

### Cost
Closed-over variables stay in memory. Avoid capturing huge objects you do not need and remove event listeners when done to prevent leaks.

Each call to the outer function creates a new closure
Used for private state, factories and callbacks

interview.a: A function bundled with references to its surrounding (lexical) scope, which lets it access outer variables even after the outer function has returned.

interview.q: Give a practical use of closures.
interview.a: Data hiding (private variables), function factories, memoization, debounce/throttle, and keeping state in callbacks and event handlers.

interview.q: Why does a var loop with setTimeout print the same number?
interview.a: All callbacks close over the same function-scoped variable, which has its final value when they run. let creates a fresh binding per iteration.

topics.title: The this Keyword
topics.summary: this is decided by how a function is called, not where it is written - except in arrow functions.
topics.description:
`this` is a keyword that refers to the object that is **executing** the current code. Its value depends on **how the function is called** (the call site).

### Rules in order of priority
1. **`new` binding** - `new Fn()`: `this` is the newly created object.
2. **Explicit binding** - `fn.call(obj)`, `apply`, `bind`: `this` is `obj`.
3. **Implicit binding** - `obj.method()`: `this` is the object before the dot.
4. **Default binding** - plain call `fn()`: `this` is the global object (`window`), or `undefined` in strict mode and modules.
5. **Arrow functions** - no own `this`; it is taken lexically from the enclosing scope.

### Other contexts
- Global scope: `window` in browsers, `module.exports`/`{}` in Node modules.
- DOM event handler (normal function): the element (`event.currentTarget`).
- Class methods: the instance - but only if called as `instance.method()`.

### Losing this
```js
const user = { name: "Asha", hi() { return this.name; } };
const f = user.hi;
f();                 // undefined - detached method
setTimeout(user.hi, 0); // same problem
```
Fixes: `user.hi.bind(user)`, an arrow wrapper `() => user.hi()`, or arrow-function class fields.

### Quick tip
Look at what is on the **left of the dot** at the moment of the call. No dot means default binding.

Plain function calls give undefined (strict) or window

topics.title: call, apply and bind
topics.summary: Borrow methods and fix this with call, apply and bind.
topics.description:
Every function has three methods to set `this` explicitly.

### call
Invokes the function **immediately** with a given `this` and arguments passed one by one.
```js
greet.call(person, "Hello", "!");
```

### apply
Same as `call`, but arguments are passed as an **array**.
```js
greet.apply(person, ["Hello", "!"]);
```
With the spread operator, `call(person, ...args)` has largely replaced `apply`.

### bind
Returns a **new function** with `this` (and optionally some arguments) permanently fixed. It does **not** call the function.
```js
const greetJohn = greet.bind(person, "Hi");
greetJohn("?");
```

### Summary
| Method | Calls now? | Arguments | Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| `call` | yes | comma separated | function result |
| `apply` | yes | array | function result |
| `bind` | no | comma separated (partial) | new function |

### Use cases
- **Method borrowing**: `Array.prototype.slice.call(arguments)`, or using `greet` of one object on another.
- **Fixing this** in callbacks and event handlers.
- **Partial application**: `const double = multiply.bind(null, 2)`.
- `Math.max.apply(null, arr)` before spread existed.

### Details
- A bound function's `this` cannot be changed again by `call`/`apply`.
- `bind` on an arrow function does not change `this`.
- Passing `null`/`undefined` as `this` uses the global object (sloppy mode) or stays `undefined` (strict).

apply: invoke now, arguments in an array

interview.q: Can you change the this of a bound function?
interview.a: No. Once bound, later call/apply/bind cannot override this.

interview.a: Return a function that calls the original with the stored this and the combined arguments: Function.prototype.myBind = function (ctx, ...a) { const fn = this; return function (...b) { return fn.apply(ctx, [...a, ...b]); }; };

topics.title: Prototypes and the Prototype Chain
topics.summary: Objects inherit properties from other objects through their prototype link.
topics.description:
Every JavaScript object has a hidden link, `[[Prototype]]`, to another object (or `null`). When you read a property the engine looks at the object itself first, then follows the link up the **prototype chain** until it finds the property or reaches `null`.

```js
const animal = { eats: true, walk() { return "walking"; } };
const dog = Object.create(animal);   // dog's prototype is animal
dog.barks = true;
dog.eats;      // true - found on the prototype
dog.walk();    // "walking"
```

### Important pieces
- `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)` (or the legacy `obj.__proto__`) reads the prototype.
- `Fn.prototype` is the object that becomes the `[[Prototype]]` of instances created with `new Fn()`.
- `Object.prototype` sits at the top of nearly every chain; its prototype is `null`.
- Arrays inherit from `Array.prototype`, which inherits from `Object.prototype`. That is why `[].map` and `[].hasOwnProperty` both work.

### Own vs inherited
- Writing `dog.eats = false` creates an **own** property that shadows the inherited one.
- `Object.hasOwn(dog, "eats")` tests own properties.
- `for...in` also lists inherited enumerable properties.

### Why prototypes
Methods live **once** on the prototype and are shared by all instances, saving memory compared with copying them to every object.

### Classes are sugar
ES2015 `class` syntax is a cleaner way to write the same prototype mechanism; the engine still uses prototypes underneath.

### Dictionaries
`Object.create(null)` makes an object with **no** prototype - a pure key-value store without inherited keys like `toString`.

topics.title: Classes
topics.summary: class syntax gives a clear way to define constructors, methods, getters and setters.
topics.description:
**Classes** (ES2015) are a cleaner syntax over prototypes and constructor functions.

```js
class User {
  constructor(name, age) {
    this.name = name;
    this.age = age;
  }
  greet() {                 // on User.prototype
    return `Hi, ${this.name}`;
  }
  get isAdult() { return this.age >= 18; }       // getter
  set nickname(v) { this._nick = v.trim(); }     // setter
  static create(name) { return new User(name, 18); }  // static
}
const u = new User("Asha", 25);
```

### Key facts
- `constructor` runs on `new`; a class can have only one.
- Methods are placed on the prototype and are **non-enumerable**.
- Class declarations are **not hoisted** like functions (TDZ).
- Class bodies run in **strict mode**.
- Calling a class without `new` throws a `TypeError`.
- `typeof User` is `"function"`.

### Class fields (ES2022)
```js
class Counter {
  count = 0;                // public field
  inc = () => { this.count++; };   // arrow keeps this
}
```

### Class expressions
`const A = class { }` or a named class expression.

### instanceof
`u instanceof User` is `true`.

### Method `this`
Methods lose `this` when detached (`const f = u.greet`). Bind in the constructor or use arrow class fields (useful in React class components).

### Static members
`static` methods and properties belong to the class, not the instances - utility methods and factories.

topics.title: Error Handling: try, catch, finally and throw
topics.summary: Handle runtime errors gracefully with try/catch/finally and throw meaningful Error objects.
topics.description:
Errors will happen: bad input, missing data, network failure. **Error handling** keeps the app running and gives useful feedback.

### try...catch...finally
```js
try {
  riskyCode();            // may throw
} catch (error) {
  console.error(error.message);   // handle it
} finally {
  cleanup();              // always runs
}
```
- `catch` receives the error; the binding is optional since ES2019 (`catch { }`).
- `finally` runs whether or not an error happened - ideal for hiding loaders or closing resources.

### throw
You can throw **anything**, but throw `Error` objects so you get a stack trace:
```js
if (!email) throw new Error("Email is required");
```

### Built-in error types
`Error`, `TypeError` (wrong type, calling undefined), `ReferenceError` (undeclared variable), `SyntaxError` (invalid code or JSON), `RangeError` (out of range, stack overflow), `URIError`, `AggregateError`.

### Custom errors
```js
class ValidationError extends Error {
  constructor(msg, field) { super(msg); this.name = "ValidationError"; this.field = field; }
}
```
Use `instanceof` or `error.name` in `catch` to react differently. Since ES2022 you can pass a cause: `new Error("failed", { cause: err })`.

### Rethrow
If you cannot handle an error, rethrow it: `catch (e) { if (!(e instanceof ValidationError)) throw e; }`.

### Async errors
- With promises use `.catch()`.
- With `async/await` use `try/catch` around `await`.
- A `try/catch` does **not** catch errors thrown inside a callback that runs later (setTimeout).
- `fetch` only rejects on network failure; check `response.ok` for 404/500.

topics.title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous Code and Timers
topics.summary: Async code lets the program continue while waiting; setTimeout and setInterval schedule work for later.
topics.description:
### Synchronous vs asynchronous
- **Synchronous**: each line waits for the previous one. A slow task blocks everything.
- **Asynchronous**: start a long task (timer, network, file) and keep running; the result comes back later through a callback, promise or `await`.

JavaScript has one thread, so it relies on the browser/Node to do the waiting and on the **event loop** to run the callback when the stack is free.

### setTimeout
Runs a function **once** after a delay (milliseconds).
```js
const id = setTimeout(() => console.log("later"), 2000);
clearTimeout(id);       // cancel
```
Pass extra arguments after the delay: `setTimeout(fn, 1000, arg1)`.

### setInterval
Runs repeatedly until cancelled.
```js
const id = setInterval(tick, 1000);
clearInterval(id);
```

### Important details
- The delay is a **minimum**: the callback runs only when the call stack is empty.
- `setTimeout(fn, 0)` still runs after the current code finishes.
- Browsers throttle timers in background tabs.
- Nested `setTimeout` is often better than `setInterval` because the next run is scheduled only after the current one finishes (no overlap).
- Always clear timers in cleanup (React `useEffect`), otherwise you leak memory and run stale code.
- `requestAnimationFrame(fn)` is the right tool for animations.

interview.a: The callback is placed in the task queue and runs only after the current synchronous code and microtasks have completed and the stack is empty.

topics.title: Promises
topics.summary: A Promise represents a future value and is pending, fulfilled or rejected.
topics.description:
A **Promise** is an object that represents the eventual **completion or failure** of an asynchronous operation and its resulting value. Think of it as a receipt: you get something now that will be exchanged for the real result later.

### States
- **pending** - initial state.
- **fulfilled** - finished successfully with a value.
- **rejected** - failed with a reason (error).
A promise settles **once** and never changes again.

### Creating
```js
const p = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  setTimeout(() => {
    Math.random() > 0.5 ? resolve("done") : reject(new Error("failed"));
  }, 100);
});
```
The function passed in is the **executor**; it runs immediately.

### Consuming
```js
p.then((value) => value)     // success
 .catch((err) => {})         // failure
 .finally(() => {});         // always
```
- `.then()` returns a **new promise**, so you can chain. Returning a value passes it down; returning a promise waits for it.
- A throw inside `.then` turns into a rejection handled by the next `.catch`.
- `.catch(fn)` is `.then(undefined, fn)`.

### Shortcuts
`Promise.resolve(value)`, `Promise.reject(error)`.

### Microtasks
Promise callbacks run as **microtasks**, before timers and other macrotasks.

### Always handle rejections
An unhandled rejection logs an error in the browser and can crash Node. Put a `.catch()` at the end of every chain.

interview.a: Pending, fulfilled and rejected. Once fulfilled or rejected (settled) it cannot change.

interview.q: What does .then() return?
interview.a: A new promise that resolves with the return value of the handler (or follows the promise it returns), which is what makes chaining possible.

interview.q: What is the difference between .catch and the second argument of .then?
interview.a: .catch also handles errors thrown inside the previous then handler, while the second argument of the same then only handles rejections of the earlier promise.

topics.title: Promise.all, allSettled, race and any
topics.summary: Run promises in parallel and choose how to combine their results.
topics.description:
These static methods take an iterable of promises and return one promise.

| Method | Fulfills when | Rejects when |
|---|---|---|
| `Promise.all` | **all** fulfil (array of values, same order) | **any** rejects (first rejection) |
| `Promise.allSettled` | **all** settle (array of `{status, value/reason}`) | never |
| `Promise.race` | the **first** promise settles | the first settled one is a rejection |
| `Promise.any` | the **first fulfilled** | all reject (`AggregateError`) |

### When to use which
- **all** - you need every result, and one failure means the whole thing fails (load user + settings).
- **allSettled** - independent tasks; you want to report each success/failure (bulk upload).
- **race** - timeout pattern: race a request against a `setTimeout` rejection.
- **any** - try several mirrors/servers, take the first that works.

### Parallel vs sequential
`await a(); await b();` runs one after another. `await Promise.all([a(), b()])` runs both at the same time, so it is faster for independent tasks.

### Other helpers
- `Promise.withResolvers()` (ES2024) returns `{ promise, resolve, reject }`.
- Non-promise values in the array are treated as already resolved.

### Concurrency control
`Promise.all` with thousands of requests can overload a server. Process in chunks or use a small pool.

topics.title: Event Loop, Microtasks and Macrotasks
topics.summary: The event loop moves queued callbacks onto the call stack, running microtasks before macrotasks.
topics.description:
JavaScript runs on a single thread, yet handles timers, clicks and network requests without freezing. The **event loop** makes this possible.

### The pieces
- **Call stack** - where synchronous code runs.
- **Web APIs / Node APIs** - do the waiting (timers, fetch, DOM events) outside the stack.
- **Macrotask (task) queue** - callbacks from `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, DOM events, I/O.
- **Microtask queue** - `Promise.then/catch/finally`, `queueMicrotask`, `MutationObserver`, `await` continuations.
- **Event loop** - checks: if the stack is empty, run **all** microtasks, then take **one** macrotask, (render if needed), repeat.

### Order of execution
1. All synchronous code.
2. All queued **microtasks** (even those added while draining).
3. The next **macrotask**, then microtasks again, and so on.

```js
console.log("1");
setTimeout(() => console.log("4"), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("3"));
console.log("2");
// 1, 2, 3, 4
```

### Consequences
- Promise callbacks always beat `setTimeout(0)`.
- A long synchronous loop blocks everything, including rendering and clicks.
- A microtask that keeps scheduling microtasks can starve the macrotask queue.
- Heavy work should be chunked, moved to a Web Worker, or yielded with `setTimeout`.

### Node.js extras
`process.nextTick` runs before promise microtasks; `setImmediate` runs in the check phase.
keyPoints: Single thread with one call stack
Microtasks (promises) run before macrotasks (timers)
Event loop runs when the stack is empty
Long tasks block rendering and events
await continues as a microtask

Blocking the main thread with big loops
Infinite microtask loops freeze the page

examples.title: Predict the order

interview.q: What is the output order of sync code, setTimeout(0) and a resolved promise?
interview.a: Synchronous code first, then the promise callback (microtask), then the setTimeout callback (macrotask).

interview.q: What is the difference between microtasks and macrotasks?
interview.a: Microtasks (promise reactions, queueMicrotask) run immediately after the current script/task and before the next macrotask. Macrotasks (timers, events, I/O) run one per event loop turn.

interview.q: Why can a heavy loop freeze the UI?
interview.a: The loop occupies the single call stack, so the event loop cannot run event handlers or let the browser render until it finishes.

topics.title: Fetch API and AbortController
topics.summary: fetch makes HTTP requests that return promises; AbortController cancels them.
topics.description:
`fetch(url, options)` is the modern browser (and Node 18+) API for HTTP requests. It returns a **promise of a Response**.

### Basic GET
```js
const res = await fetch("https://api.example.com/users");
if (!res.ok) throw new Error("HTTP " + res.status);
const data = await res.json();      // also .text(), .blob(), .formData()
```

### Important behaviour
- `fetch` **rejects only on network failure**. A 404 or 500 still resolves, so always check `res.ok`.
- Reading the body (`res.json()`) is another async step and can only be done once.
- Cross-origin requests need **CORS** headers from the server.

### POST with JSON
```js
await fetch("/api/users", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify({ name: "Asha" }),
});
```
Other options: `credentials: "include"` for cookies, `cache`, `mode`, `signal`.

### Cancelling with AbortController
```js
const controller = new AbortController();
fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal });
controller.abort();                 // rejects with AbortError
```
Use it to cancel when a component unmounts, when a new search replaces the old one, or for timeouts: `AbortSignal.timeout(5000)`.

### Weather app pattern
Build the URL with a template literal, `await fetch`, destructure the JSON, then update the DOM. Wrap in `try/catch` and show a friendly message on failure. Never put secret API keys in front-end code.

Check response.ok - HTTP errors do not reject

interview.a: Create an AbortController, pass controller.signal in the fetch options and call controller.abort(); the promise rejects with an AbortError.

interview.q: Why does response.json() return a promise?
interview.a: The body is a stream that must be read and parsed asynchronously, so you await it after the headers arrive.

topics.title: DOM Tree and Navigation
topics.summary: The DOM is a tree of nodes that JavaScript can walk through using parent, child and sibling properties.
topics.description:
When a browser loads an HTML page it parses it and builds the **DOM (Document Object Model)** - a tree of objects representing the document. JavaScript uses this tree to read and change the page. The DOM is an **API**, not part of the JavaScript language itself.

### Node types
- **Document** node (`document`) - the root.
- **Element** nodes - HTML tags (`div`, `p`...).
- **Text** nodes - text content (including whitespace and new lines).
- **Comment** nodes, **Attribute** nodes, DocumentType.

### Key entry points
`document`, `document.documentElement` (`<html>`), `document.head`, `document.body`.

### Navigating the tree
| Need | Elements only | All nodes (incl. text) |
|---|---|---|
| parent | `parentElement` | `parentNode` |
| children | `children` | `childNodes` |
| first / last child | `firstElementChild`, `lastElementChild` | `firstChild`, `lastChild` |
| siblings | `nextElementSibling`, `previousElementSibling` | `nextSibling`, `previousSibling` |

Use the **Element** versions in most cases; the others also return whitespace text nodes.

### closest()
`el.closest(".card")` walks **up** from the element (including itself) and returns the first ancestor matching the selector, or `null`. Very useful in event delegation.

### Live vs static
`children`, `childNodes` and `getElementsBy*` return **live** collections that update automatically; `querySelectorAll` returns a **static** NodeList.

### Changes are temporary
Edits you make to the DOM exist only in memory; reloading the page rebuilds the DOM from the HTML.

topics.title: Selecting Elements
topics.summary: Find elements with getElementById, querySelector and querySelectorAll.
topics.description:
Before changing an element you must **select** it.

### Methods
| Method | Returns | Live? |
|---|---|---|
| `getElementById("id")` | one element or `null` | - |
| `getElementsByClassName("c")` | HTMLCollection | live |
| `getElementsByTagName("li")` | HTMLCollection | live |
| `querySelector(css)` | first match or `null` | - |
| `querySelectorAll(css)` | NodeList | static |

`querySelector` and `querySelectorAll` accept **any CSS selector** (`#id`, `.class`, `ul > li:nth-child(2)`, `[data-id="3"]`). They can also be called on an element to search only inside it.

### Iterating
- NodeList supports `forEach` and `for...of`.
- HTMLCollection does not have `forEach`; convert with `[...collection]` or `Array.from(collection)`.

### Reading content
| Property | What you get |
|---|---|
| `innerHTML` | markup inside the element (as a string) |
| `innerText` | rendered text; respects CSS, ignores hidden elements |
| `textContent` | all raw text, including hidden, faster |

### Tips
- Do **not** include `#` in `getElementById("heading")`.
- Cache selections in variables instead of querying repeatedly.
- Make sure the script runs after the DOM exists: place it at the end of body, use `defer`, or `DOMContentLoaded`.
- Prefer `data-*` attributes and classes for JS hooks.

topics.title: Events and addEventListener
topics.summary: React to user actions by attaching listeners and reading the event object.
topics.description:
An **event** is a signal that something happened: a click, key press, form submit, page load, resize.

### addEventListener
```js
button.addEventListener("click", function (event) {
  console.log(event.type, event.target);
}, { once: false });
button.removeEventListener("click", handler);   // needs the same function reference
```
Prefer `addEventListener` to `onclick="..."` attributes or `el.onclick = fn`, because you can attach **many** listeners and control options.

### The event object
| Property / method | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `type` | event name |
| `target` | element that triggered the event (deepest) |
| `currentTarget` | element the listener is attached to |
| `preventDefault()` | stop the default action (link, submit) |
| `stopPropagation()` | stop bubbling |
| `key`, `code` | keyboard events |
| `clientX`, `clientY` | mouse position |

### Common events
- Mouse: `click`, `dblclick`, `mouseover`, `mousemove`, `contextmenu`
- Keyboard: `keydown`, `keyup`
- Form: `submit`, `input`, `change`, `focus`, `blur`
- Document: `DOMContentLoaded`, `load`, `scroll`, `resize`
- Touch / pointer: `pointerdown`, `touchstart`

### Listener options
`{ once: true }` (auto remove), `{ passive: true }` (better scroll performance), `{ capture: true }`, `{ signal }` (remove via AbortController).

### this in listeners
In a normal function, `this` is the element (`currentTarget`). In an arrow function it is not - use `event.currentTarget`.

### Cleanup
Remove listeners for elements or components that disappear to avoid memory leaks.

interview.a: target is the element that actually triggered the event (the innermost one); currentTarget is the element the handler is attached to.

interview.q: Why prefer addEventListener over onclick?
interview.a: It allows multiple handlers for the same event, supports options (capture, once, passive) and can be removed with removeEventListener.

interview.q: What does preventDefault do?
interview.a: It cancels the browser's default action for the event, such as following a link or submitting a form, without stopping propagation.

topics.title: Event Propagation: Capturing and Bubbling
topics.summary: Events travel down (capture), hit the target and bubble back up, and you can stop them anywhere on the way.
topics.description:
When you click an element inside other elements, the event does not only run on that element. It travels through the DOM in **three phases**:

1. **Capturing phase** - from `window` down to the target's parent.
2. **Target phase** - the element that was clicked.
3. **Bubbling phase** - from the target back up to `window`.

By default listeners run in the **bubbling** phase. Pass `true` or `{ capture: true }` as the third argument to listen during capturing.

```js
outer.addEventListener("click", handler, true); // capturing
```

### Stopping propagation
- `event.stopPropagation()` - stops the event from moving on to other elements.
- `event.stopImmediatePropagation()` - also stops other listeners on the same element.
- `event.preventDefault()` - different: cancels the default action only.

### Which events bubble?
Most do (`click`, `input`, `keydown`). Some do **not**: `focus`, `blur`, `mouseenter`, `mouseleave`, `load`. Use `focusin`/`focusout` for bubbling focus events.

### target vs currentTarget
While the event travels, `target` stays the same (original element) and `currentTarget` changes to the element whose listener is running.

### Order example
With three nested divs and bubbling listeners, a click on the inner one logs: inner, middle, outer. With capture listeners the order is reversed: outer, middle, inner.

### Practical tips
- Avoid `stopPropagation` unless needed; it can break analytics and other widgets.
- Bubbling is what makes **event delegation** possible.

interview.q: What are event bubbling and capturing?
interview.a: Bubbling means an event fires on the target and then travels up through its ancestors; capturing means it travels from the root down to the target first. Listeners run in bubbling by default.

interview.q: How do you stop an event from bubbling?
interview.a: Call event.stopPropagation() inside the handler.

interview.q: Which common events do not bubble?
interview.a: focus, blur, mouseenter, mouseleave and load (use focusin/focusout or mouseover/mouseout equivalents).

topics.title: Event Delegation
topics.summary: Attach one listener to a parent and use event.target to handle many children, even ones added later.
topics.description:
**Event delegation** uses bubbling: instead of adding a listener to every child, add **one listener to a common ancestor** and find out which child was clicked with `event.target`.

```js
list.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  const item = event.target.closest("li");   // robust against inner elements
  if (!item || !list.contains(item)) return;
  console.log(item.dataset.id);
});
```

### Why use it
- **Less memory**: one listener instead of hundreds.
- **Dynamic content**: elements added later work automatically, no re-attaching.
- **Simpler cleanup**: a single `removeEventListener`.

### How to match the right element
- `event.target.matches("li.item")` - when the target is exactly the element.
- `event.target.closest("li")` - when the clicked element can be a child (an icon inside a button). Prefer `closest`.
- Use `data-action="delete"` attributes and branch on `target.dataset.action` for menus and toolbars.

### Limits
- Only works for events that **bubble** (not `focus`, `blur`; use `focusin`/`focusout`).
- If a child calls `stopPropagation`, the parent never hears about it.
- Very high-frequency events (`mousemove`) still need throttling.

### Typical uses
Todo lists, tables with row buttons, dropdown menus, grids of cards or tiles, comment threads.

interview.a: A pattern where a single event listener is attached to a parent element to handle events of its children, using bubbling and event.target to identify the source.

interview.q: What are the benefits of event delegation?

topics.title: Forms and Form Events
topics.summary: Handle form submission, read input values, validate and prevent the default page reload.
topics.description:
Forms collect user input. JavaScript lets you intercept submission, validate and send data without reloading the page.

### Submit handling
```js
form.addEventListener("submit", (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();                 // stop page reload
  const data = Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form));
});
```
Listen to **`submit` on the form**, not `click` on the button - it also fires when the user presses Enter.

### Reading values
- `input.value` (always a **string**; convert numbers with `Number()`).
- `checkbox.checked`, `radio` (`form.elements.gender.value`), `select.value`, `textarea.value`.
- `new FormData(form)` collects everything with a `name`.

### Events
| Event | Fires |
|---|---|
| `input` | on every change while typing |
| `change` | when value is committed (blur / select) |
| `focus`, `blur` | gaining / losing focus |
| `reset` | form reset |

### Validation
- HTML attributes: `required`, `minlength`, `pattern`, `type="email"`.
- Constraint API: `form.checkValidity()`, `input.validity.valueMissing`, `input.setCustomValidity("msg")`, `form.reportValidity()`.
- Always **re-validate on the server** - client checks can be bypassed.

### Good practice
- Disable the submit button while sending.
- Show errors next to the field with `aria-live` or `role="alert"`.
- Clear the form with `form.reset()`.

topics.title: Mini Project: Todo List
topics.summary: Combine DOM creation, events, delegation and localStorage into a working todo app.
topics.description:
A todo app is the classic first DOM project because it uses everything in this section.

### Features
- Add a task from an input (button or Enter key).
- Mark a task complete by clicking it (toggle a class).
- Delete a task with a button.
- Save tasks to `localStorage` so they survive a refresh.

### Design
1. **State** - keep an array of objects `{ id, text, done }` as the single source of truth.
2. **render()** - rebuild the list from the state.
3. **Events** - a form `submit` handler adds a task; a **delegated** click handler on the `<ul>` handles toggle and delete using `data-action` attributes.
4. **Persistence** - `save()` after every change with `JSON.stringify`, and load with `JSON.parse` on startup.

### Why this structure
Updating the **state first**, then rendering, avoids bugs where the DOM and data drift apart. This is the same idea that React and other frameworks automate.

### Extensions
Filter (all/active/done), edit in place, drag and drop ordering, counters, and keyboard shortcuts.

### Escaping
Use `textContent` for task text so a user cannot inject HTML.

topics.summary: The BOM exposes the browser itself: window size, URL, user agent, screen and dialogs.
topics.description:
The **Browser Object Model (BOM)** is the set of objects the browser gives JavaScript to talk to the **browser window**, not the document. There is no official standard for the BOM as a whole, but all browsers support the common objects.

### window
The global object in browsers. Global variables and functions become its properties.
- `innerWidth` / `innerHeight` - viewport size (without toolbars).
- `outerWidth` / `outerHeight` - whole browser window.
- `scrollX` / `scrollY`, `scrollTo()`, `scrollBy()`.
- `open(url)`, `close()`, `alert()`, `confirm()`, `prompt()`.
- `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, `console`, `document`.

### location
Information about the **current URL** and navigation.
| Property / method | Example |
|---|---|
| `href` | full URL |
| `origin`, `protocol`, `host`, `hostname` | `https://site.com` |
| `pathname` | `/courses/js` |
| `search` | `?name=John&age=25` |
| `hash` | `#intro` |
| `assign(url)` | navigate, keeps history |
| `replace(url)` | navigate, no back button entry |
| `reload()` | refresh page |

### navigator
`userAgent`, `language`, `languages`, `onLine`, `cookieEnabled`, `platform`, `hardwareConcurrency`, plus APIs such as `clipboard`, `geolocation`, `serviceWorker`, `share()`.

### screen
`width`, `height`, `availWidth`, `availHeight`, `colorDepth`, `orientation`.

### Useful events
`resize`, `scroll`, `online` / `offline`, `beforeunload`, `visibilitychange`.

### Reminder
Dialogs (`alert`, `confirm`, `prompt`) block the page and are poor UX; prefer in-page modals.
keyPoints: window is the global object in the browser
location reads/changes the URL; replace skips history
navigator gives browser and device information
screen describes the display
innerWidth is the viewport, outerWidth is the whole window
pitfalls: Detecting browsers with userAgent is unreliable; use feature detection
alert/prompt block the main thread
location.href assignment adds a history entry; replace does not

examples.title: Reading BOM info
examples.html: Browser information

interview.q: What is the difference between BOM and DOM?
interview.a: The DOM represents the HTML document (elements, text); the BOM represents the browser environment (window, location, navigator, history, screen).

interview.q: Difference between location.assign and location.replace?
interview.a: assign loads the new URL and keeps the current page in history; replace loads it and removes the current page from history so back does not return to it.

interview.q: What is window in a browser?
interview.a: The global object that represents the browser window/tab and holds global variables, the document, timers, storage and the other BOM objects.

topics.title: History API and URL Handling
topics.summary: Change the address bar without reloading using pushState, and parse URLs with URL and URLSearchParams.
topics.description:
### history object
```js
history.back();      // like the back button
history.forward();
history.go(-2);      // relative jump
history.length;      // entries in the session
```

### pushState and replaceState
These change the URL **without reloading** the page. They are how single-page apps (React Router, Vue Router) work.
```js
history.pushState({ page: 2 }, "", "/products?page=2");   // adds an entry
history.replaceState({ page: 3 }, "", "/products?page=3"); // replaces current
```
- The first argument is a **state object** (retrievable via `history.state`).
- The URL must be the **same origin**.
- Nothing happens on the page automatically; you must update the UI yourself.
- When the user clicks back/forward, the **`popstate`** event fires with `event.state`.

### URL and URLSearchParams
```js
const url = new URL("https://shop.com/items?cat=shoes&page=2#top");
url.searchParams.get("cat");        // "shoes"
url.searchParams.set("page", 3);
url.searchParams.append("tag", "sale");
url.toString();
[...url.searchParams.entries()];
```
Use `URLSearchParams` instead of manual string splitting, and `encodeURIComponent()` for values.

### Hash routing
`location.hash` and the `hashchange` event give a simple router that needs no server configuration.

### Notes
Direct visits to a pushed URL need server configuration (fallback to `index.html`) for SPAs.
keyPoints: history.back/forward/go navigate the session
pushState and replaceState change the URL without reload
popstate fires on back and forward
URL and URLSearchParams parse and build URLs safely
SPA routers are built on the History API
pitfalls: pushState does not trigger popstate by itself
Different origins throw a SecurityError
Building query strings by hand without encoding

examples.title: URL parsing and state
Router with pushState (web)
examples.explanation: pushState updates the displayed path inside the preview without a reload; popstate restores the page on back/forward.
examples.html: Current state:

interview.q: How do SPAs change the URL without a page reload?
interview.a: They use history.pushState/replaceState to update the address bar and listen to the popstate event to render the right view on back/forward.

interview.q: Does pushState trigger the popstate event?
interview.a: No. popstate fires only when the user navigates through history (back, forward, history.go).

interview.q: How do you read query string parameters?
interview.a: new URL(location.href).searchParams.get("name") or new URLSearchParams(location.search).

topics.title: localStorage, sessionStorage and Cookies
topics.summary: Store small amounts of data in the browser with localStorage, sessionStorage or cookies.
topics.description:
Browsers offer several places to keep data on the client.

### localStorage
- Key-value pairs of **strings**, stays **until cleared** (survives restart).
- About 5 MB per origin, **synchronous**, shared between tabs of the same origin.
```js
localStorage.setItem("theme", "dark");
localStorage.getItem("theme");     // "dark" (null if missing)
localStorage.removeItem("theme");
localStorage.clear();
```

### sessionStorage
Same API, but data is cleared when the **tab** closes and is not shared between tabs.

### Storing objects
Only strings are stored, so serialise:
```js
localStorage.setItem("user", JSON.stringify({ name: "Vinod", age: 30 }));
const user = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("user"));
```

### Cookies
Small (4 KB) strings **sent to the server on every request** - used for sessions and authentication. Set via `document.cookie` or the `Set-Cookie` header. Important flags: `HttpOnly` (JS cannot read it), `Secure`, `SameSite`, `Max-Age`.

### Comparison
| | localStorage | sessionStorage | cookie | IndexedDB |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lifetime | forever | tab | configurable | forever |
| Size | ~5 MB | ~5 MB | ~4 KB | large |
| Sent to server | no | no | yes | no |
| API | sync | sync | string | async |

### Rules
- Never store passwords, tokens or sensitive data in localStorage - any XSS script can read it.
- Wrap access in `try/catch` (private mode, blocked storage, quota exceeded).
- Listen to the `storage` event to sync tabs.
keyPoints: localStorage persists, sessionStorage lasts for the tab
Values are strings: use JSON.stringify and JSON.parse
Synchronous and about 5 MB
Cookies are sent to the server with every request
Never keep secrets in web storage
pitfalls: Storing objects directly saves "[object Object]"
Reading a missing key returns null, not undefined
Storage may be disabled or full - handle errors

examples.title: Persist a visit counter and an object
examples.html: Visits: 0

interview.q: Difference between localStorage and sessionStorage?
interview.a: localStorage data persists until it is removed; sessionStorage data is limited to the tab/session and is deleted when the tab closes.

interview.q: Can localStorage store objects?
interview.a: Only strings. Convert objects with JSON.stringify and back with JSON.parse.

interview.q: When would you choose cookies instead of localStorage?
interview.a: When the server needs the data on every request (sessions), or when you need HttpOnly/Secure protection and expiry control.

topics.title: Clipboard API
topics.summary: Copy and paste text programmatically with navigator.clipboard, which requires a secure context and permission.
topics.description:
The **Async Clipboard API** (`navigator.clipboard`) lets pages read and write the system clipboard using promises.

```js
await navigator.clipboard.writeText("Copied!");
const text = await navigator.clipboard.readText();
```

### Requirements
- Works only in a **secure context** (HTTPS or localhost).
- `writeText` normally needs a **user gesture** (a click handler).
- `readText` triggers a **permission prompt** and may be denied.
- In iframes the `clipboard-write` permission policy must be allowed.
- Both methods return promises, so handle rejections.

### Rich content
`navigator.clipboard.write([new ClipboardItem({ "text/html": blob })])` copies images or HTML.

### Fallback
The old `document.execCommand("copy")` still exists but is **deprecated**. For legacy support select the text in a hidden `<textarea>` and call it inside try/catch.

### Clipboard events
`copy`, `cut` and `paste` events let you intercept the action: `event.clipboardData.getData("text")` and `event.preventDefault()`.

### UX tips
- Give feedback ("Copied!") and revert after a short time.
- Do not overwrite the clipboard silently - users find it hostile.
- Never read the clipboard without a clear reason.
keyPoints: navigator.clipboard.writeText / readText return promises
Needs HTTPS and usually a user gesture
readText asks for permission
Handle errors and provide a fallback
Show feedback when the copy succeeds
pitfalls: Calling writeText outside a user gesture can fail
Not handling the rejected promise in iframes or insecure pages
Using deprecated execCommand as the only approach

examples.title: Copy button with feedback

interview.q: How do you copy text to the clipboard in modern JavaScript?
interview.a: await navigator.clipboard.writeText(text) from a user-initiated event handler on a secure origin.

interview.q: Why might navigator.clipboard be undefined?
interview.a: It is only exposed in secure contexts (HTTPS, localhost), so on plain HTTP pages it is undefined.

interview.q: Is document.execCommand("copy") recommended?
interview.a: No. It is deprecated; use the async Clipboard API and keep execCommand only as a legacy fallback.

topics.title: Geolocation API
topics.summary: Ask the user for their position with navigator.geolocation and handle permission errors.
topics.description:
The **Geolocation API** gives the device's position with the user's explicit permission.

```js
navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(success, error, options);
const watchId = navigator.geolocation.watchPosition(success, error);
navigator.geolocation.clearWatch(watchId);
```

### Success callback
Receives a `position` object:
- `position.coords.latitude`, `longitude`
- `position.coords.accuracy` (metres)
- `altitude`, `speed`, `heading` (may be `null`)
- `position.timestamp`

### Error callback
`error.code`:
| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `1` PERMISSION_DENIED | user said no |
| `2` POSITION_UNAVAILABLE | device cannot find location |
| `3` TIMEOUT | took longer than `timeout` |

### Options
`{ enableHighAccuracy: true, timeout: 10000, maximumAge: 0 }`. High accuracy uses GPS and drains battery.

### Requirements and privacy
- **Secure context** (HTTPS) and user permission prompt.
- Explain why you need location before asking; ask on user action, not on page load.
- Handle denial gracefully with a manual city search fallback.
- Never send precise location without consent.

### Promise wrapper
```js
const getPosition = (opts) =>
  new Promise((res, rej) => navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(res, rej, opts));
```
Use with `await` and combine with a weather API for local forecasts.
keyPoints: getCurrentPosition for one reading, watchPosition for updates
Requires HTTPS and user permission
coords.latitude and coords.longitude hold the position
Handle error codes: denied, unavailable, timeout
Wrap callbacks in a promise for async/await
pitfalls: Requesting location on page load without context
No fallback when permission is denied
Leaving watchPosition running (battery drain)

examples.title: Get my position (permission required)
examples.html: Press the button. The browser will ask for permission.

interview.q: What permissions does the Geolocation API need?
interview.a: The user must grant permission through the browser prompt, and the page must be served from a secure context (HTTPS or localhost).

interview.q: Difference between getCurrentPosition and watchPosition?
interview.a: getCurrentPosition returns the position once; watchPosition calls the callback every time the position changes and returns an id for clearWatch.

interview.q: How do you handle the user denying permission?
interview.a: Use the error callback (code 1), show a clear message and offer an alternative such as typing a city or postcode.

topics.title: Proxy and Reflect
topics.summary: A Proxy intercepts operations on an object (get, set, delete...) and Reflect performs the default behaviour.
topics.description:
A **Proxy** wraps an object (the target) and lets you define **traps** that intercept fundamental operations. It is the basis of reactivity in Vue 3, validation layers, logging and mocking.

```js
const proxy = new Proxy(target, {
  get(target, prop, receiver) { return Reflect.get(target, prop, receiver); },
  set(target, prop, value, receiver) { return Reflect.set(target, prop, value, receiver); },
});
```

### Common traps
| Trap | Intercepts |
|---|---|
| `get` | reading a property |
| `set` | assigning a property |
| `has` | the `in` operator |
| `deleteProperty` | `delete obj.x` |
| `ownKeys` | `Object.keys`, `for...in` |
| `apply` | calling a function |
| `construct` | `new` on a function |

The `set` trap must return `true` for success (in strict mode returning `false` throws).

### Reflect
A built-in object whose methods mirror the proxy traps (`Reflect.get`, `set`, `has`, `ownKeys`, `apply`...). Use it inside traps to perform the **default operation** with correct `this` handling and a boolean result instead of exceptions.

### Use cases
- **Validation** - reject wrong types in `set`.
- **Default values** - return a fallback in `get` for missing keys.
- **Observable state** - run effects when data changes.
- **Logging / profiling** API calls.
- **Negative array indexes** or read-only views.

### Caveats
- Proxies add overhead; do not use them in hot loops.
- Private class fields (`#x`) do not work through a proxy.
- `proxy !== target`; identity checks can surprise.
keyPoints: Proxy wraps a target and intercepts operations via traps
Reflect provides the default behaviour inside traps
set trap must return true
Used for validation, reactivity, defaults and logging
Slower than direct access
pitfalls: Forgetting to return true from the set trap
Infinite recursion by touching the proxy inside its own trap
Private fields and built-ins like Map can break through proxies

examples.title: Validation and default values

interview.q: What is a Proxy?
interview.a: An object that wraps another object and intercepts operations like get, set and delete through handler traps, allowing custom behaviour.

interview.q: Why use Reflect inside proxy traps?
interview.a: Reflect methods perform the default operation with the correct receiver and return booleans, keeping the proxy behaving like the original.

interview.q: Name a framework that uses Proxy.
interview.a: Vue 3 uses Proxy for its reactivity system to track property reads and writes.

topics.title: Memory Management and Garbage Collection
topics.summary: JavaScript frees memory automatically when objects become unreachable; leaks happen when you keep references.
topics.description:
JavaScript manages memory for you. You create objects; the **garbage collector (GC)** frees them when they are no longer **reachable**.

### Life cycle
1. **Allocate** - creating objects, arrays, closures, strings.
2. **Use** - read and write.
3. **Release** - the GC frees unreachable memory.

### Reachability and mark-and-sweep
Starting from **roots** (global object, current stack, active closures), the GC **marks** everything reachable and **sweeps** (frees) the rest. Circular references are fine - if nothing reachable points to the cycle, it is collected. The old reference counting approach could not do this.

### Common memory leaks
1. **Accidental globals** (`leak = [];`).
2. **Forgotten timers**: `setInterval` callbacks keep their scope alive.
3. **Event listeners** never removed from DOM nodes that are discarded.
4. **Detached DOM nodes** still referenced from a variable or array.
5. **Closures** capturing large objects unnecessarily.
6. **Unbounded caches** (a `Map` that only grows).

### Prevent and detect
- Clear timers; remove listeners (or use `{ signal }` with AbortController).
- Use **WeakMap / WeakSet / WeakRef** for caches keyed by objects.
- Set references to `null` when finished with big data.
- Use browser DevTools: **Memory** tab, heap snapshots and the allocation timeline. A steadily rising line after repeated GC means a leak.

### Stack vs heap
Primitives and references live on the stack; objects live on the heap and are managed by the GC.
keyPoints: GC frees objects that are no longer reachable
Mark-and-sweep starts from roots
Leaks: globals, timers, listeners, detached DOM, large closures
Weak collections do not prevent collection
Use DevTools heap snapshots to find leaks
pitfalls: Assuming setting a variable to null always frees the memory immediately
Forgetting clearInterval in components
Caches that never evict

examples.title: Cache with WeakMap vs Map

interview.q: How does garbage collection work in JavaScript?
interview.a: Engines use mark-and-sweep: they mark all objects reachable from roots (globals, stack) and free everything unmarked.

interview.q: Name common causes of memory leaks in JavaScript.
interview.a: Accidental globals, uncleared timers, undeleted event listeners, references to detached DOM nodes, closures holding large data and ever-growing caches.

interview.q: What is the benefit of WeakMap?
interview.a: Its keys are held weakly, so cached or associated data is automatically released when the key object is no longer referenced elsewhere.

topics.title: Debounce, Throttle and Memoization
topics.summary: Limit how often a function runs (debounce/throttle) or cache its results (memoize).
keyPoints: Debounce waits for a pause, then runs once
Throttle runs at most once per interval
Both are closures around a timer or flag
Memoize caches results of pure functions
Clear timers and limit cache size
pitfalls: Using debounce when you need regular updates (use throttle)
Losing this and arguments when wrapping functions
Unbounded memoization caches
