topics.title: Short-circuit, Truthiness and Optional Chaining Tricks
topics.summary: Idioms that use && || ?? ?. and truthiness to write less code, and when they hurt readability.
topics.description:
Logical operators return one of their **operands**, not a boolean. That enables compact idioms.

| Idiom | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `a \|\| b` | `a` if truthy, else `b` (default) |
| `a ?? b` | `a` unless `null`/`undefined` |
| `a && b` | `b` if `a` truthy, else `a` (guard) |
| `cond && doIt()` | call only when `cond` truthy |
| `!!x` or `Boolean(x)` | convert to boolean |
| `+x` | convert to number (`+'42'` is 42, `+''` is 0) |
| `` `${x}` `` / `x + ''` | convert to string |
| `~~x` / `x \| 0` | truncate to int32 |
| `x ?.y ?.[0] ?? 'dflt'` | safe deep read with default |
| `arr?.length > 0` | false when arr missing (comparison with undefined is false) |
| `typeof x === 'function' && x()` | call if function |
| `fn?.()` | call if defined |
| `a ||= b`, `a &&= b`, `a ??= b` | conditional assignment |
| `const { a = 1 } = obj ?? {}` | destructure possibly null object |
| `void 0` | reliable `undefined` |
| `if (!(key in obj))` | existence check including inherited keys |

### The eight falsy values
`false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `''`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN` (plus the legacy `document.all` in browsers). Everything else is truthy, including `'0'`, `'false'`, `[]` and `{}`.

### React-style conditional pitfall
`count && <Item />` renders `0` when `count` is `0`. Use `count > 0 && ...` or a ternary.

### When not to
Chained short-circuit expressions hurt readability when they contain side effects. Prefer `if` for statements; use the idioms for values.
keyPoints: && and || return operands, not booleans.
Use ?? instead of || when 0, '' and false are valid.
Unary + is the shortest string-to-number conversion.
The falsy values are false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN.
Optional chaining plus ?? gives safe reads with defaults.
pitfalls: cond && value yields 0 or '' when cond is a falsy number or string.
~~x and x | 0 break for values beyond 32-bit range.

examples.title: Idioms in action
examples.explanation: Printing the results of each trick.

interview.q: What does 0 || 'x' return and how would you keep the 0?
interview.a: 'x'. Use the nullish operator: 0 ?? 'x' returns 0.

interview.q: Name the falsy values.
interview.a: false, 0, -0, 0n, empty string, null, undefined and NaN.

topics.title: Bitwise Tricks and Flags
topics.summary: Use bitwise operators for integer truncation, parity, powers of two, flags/permissions and tiny hash functions.
topics.description:
JavaScript bitwise operators convert operands to **32-bit signed integers**, operate, and return a signed 32-bit result (except `>>>` which returns unsigned).

| Operator | Meaning | Trick |
|---|---|---|
| `a & b` | AND | test a bit: `n & 1` is odd |
| `a \| b` | OR | set a bit: `flags \| FLAG` |
| `a ^ b` | XOR | toggle: `flags ^ FLAG`; swap without temp |
| `~a` | NOT | `~indexOf(x)` is falsy only for `-1` |
| `a << n` | shift left | `1 << n` is 2 to the power n (within 31) |
| `a >> n` | arithmetic shift right | divide by 2^n, keeps sign |
| `a >>> n` | unsigned shift right | `x >>> 0` converts to uint32 |

### Common tricks
- Parity: `n & 1` (1 for odd). Works for negative integers too.
- Truncate: `x | 0` or `~~x` (only within +-2^31).
- Power of two check: `n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) === 0`.
- Clear lowest set bit: `n & (n - 1)`; isolate it: `n & -n`.
- Count set bits: loop `n &= n - 1`.
- Swap: `a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b` (clearer with destructuring).
- Midpoint: `(lo + hi) >>> 1` is safe from overflow in typed code.

### Flags pattern
Give each permission one bit (`READ = 1, WRITE = 2, EXEC = 4`). Combine with `|`, check with `(perm & WRITE) !== 0`, remove with `perm & ~WRITE`. Toggle with `^`.

### Hash example
`h = (h * 31 + code) | 0` keeps the hash inside int32 (use `Math.imul` for exact 32-bit multiplication).

### Limits
Numbers above 2^31 wrap around. Use `BigInt` (`&`, `|`, `<<`, `>>` work on BigInt too, but `>>>` does not) for wide values.
keyPoints: Bitwise operators work on 32-bit signed integers.
n & 1 tests odd/even; n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit.
Use bit flags to pack many booleans into one number.
x >>> 0 converts to an unsigned 32-bit integer.
Math.imul does correct 32-bit multiplication.
pitfalls: ~~x and x | 0 return wrong results for numbers outside int32 range.
Precedence: n & 1 === 0 means n & (1 === 0); always use parentheses.

examples.explanation: Permissions, parity, power of two, hash.

interview.q: How do you check whether a number is a power of two?
interview.a: n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) === 0, because powers of two have exactly one set bit.

interview.q: What does >>> 0 do?
interview.a: It converts the value to an unsigned 32-bit integer.

topics.title: Formatting Numbers and Dates with Intl
topics.summary: Replace hand-rolled formatting with Intl: currency, compact numbers, percent, units, relative time, dates and lists.
topics.description:
Hand-written formatting breaks for other locales. `Intl` (built into every modern runtime) does it correctly, and it is fast when you reuse the formatter object.

| Need | Code |
|---|---|
| Thousands separators | `n.toLocaleString('en-US')` |
| Currency | `new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { style: 'currency', currency: 'USD' }).format(n)` |
| Indian grouping | `n.toLocaleString('en-IN')` gives 12,34,567 |
| Percent | `{ style: 'percent', maximumFractionDigits: 1 }` |
| Compact | `{ notation: 'compact' }` gives 1.2K |
| Units | `{ style: 'unit', unit: 'kilometer-per-hour' }` |
| Fixed decimals | `n.toFixed(2)` (returns a string, rounds the binary value) |
| Pad number | `String(n).padStart(2, '0')` |
| Date | `new Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-GB', { dateStyle: 'medium' }).format(d)` |
| Relative time | `new Intl.RelativeTimeFormat('en', { numeric: 'auto' }).format(-1, 'day')` gives yesterday |
| List | `new Intl.ListFormat('en', { type: 'conjunction' }).format(arr)` |
| Plural | `new Intl.PluralRules('en').select(n)` |
| Time zone | `{ timeZone: 'Asia/Kolkata' }` option |

### Date tricks
- ISO string: `d.toISOString()`; date only: `.slice(0, 10)`.
- Add days: `d.setDate(d.getDate() + n)` (handles month rollover).
- Days between: `Math.round((b - a) / 864e5)` (DST can shift an hour).
- Last day of month: `new Date(y, m + 1, 0).getDate()`.
- Timestamp: `Date.now()`; end of day: `d.setHours(23, 59, 59, 999)`.
- `new Date('2024-01-05')` parses as **UTC**, while `new Date(2024, 0, 5)` is **local**.

### Tips
Pass `'en-US'` (a fixed locale) in tests so output is deterministic, and reuse formatters in loops.
keyPoints: Intl formatters handle grouping, currency, units and plurals for every locale.
toFixed returns a string and can look wrong due to binary floating point.
Date-only ISO strings parse as UTC, while component constructors use local time.
Reuse Intl objects instead of calling toLocaleString in hot loops.
Fix the locale in tests for stable output.
pitfalls: (1.005).toFixed(2) is '1.00' because 1.005 is stored slightly lower.
Month index is zero-based in new Date(y, m, d).
Subtracting dates across DST gives days that are not exactly 24 hours.

interview.q: Why use Intl.NumberFormat instead of regex-based comma insertion?
interview.a: Intl handles locale rules such as different separators and grouping (for example 12,34,567 in en-IN) and currencies correctly.

interview.q: What is the date parsing gotcha with ISO strings?
interview.a: Date-only ISO strings like '2024-01-05' are treated as UTC, whereas new Date(2024, 0, 5) uses local time, which can shift the displayed day.

topics.title: String Recipes: slugify, case, truncate, mask, count, reverse
topics.summary: Handy string helpers: slugify, title case, truncate with ellipsis, mask card numbers, count words, safe reversal and escaping regex input.
topics.description:
Most text helpers combine `replace`, `split`, `map`, `join` and regex. Here are the ones you will actually reuse.

| Task | Recipe |
|---|---|
| Capitalize | `s[0].toUpperCase() + s.slice(1)` |
| Title case | `s.replace(/\b\w/g, c => c.toUpperCase())` |
| camelCase from kebab | `s.replace(/-(\w)/g, (_, c) => c.toUpperCase())` |
| kebab from camel | `s.replace(/([a-z])([A-Z])/g, '$1-$2').toLowerCase()` |
| Slugify | normalize, strip diacritics, lowercase, replace non-alphanumerics with `-` |
| Truncate | `s.length > n ? s.slice(0, n - 1) + '...' : s` |
| Mask | `s.slice(-4).padStart(s.length, '*')` |
| Reverse | `[...s].reverse().join('')` (handles surrogate pairs) |
| Palindrome | clean the string, compare with its reverse |
| Count words | `s.trim().split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean).length` |
| Repeat | `'ab'.repeat(3)` |
| Pad | `padStart`, `padEnd` |
| Replace all | `s.replaceAll('a', 'b')` |
| Escape for regex | `s.replace(/[.*+?^${}()\|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&')` |
| Template without code | `tpl.replace(/\{(\w+)\}/g, (_, k) => data[k] ?? '')` |
| Char frequency | `[...s].reduce((m, c) => m.set(c, (m.get(c) ?? 0) + 1), new Map())` |

### Slugify details
`s.normalize('NFD').replace(/[̀-ͯ]/g, '')` strips accent marks. Then lowercase, replace runs of non-alphanumerics with a single hyphen and trim hyphens from the ends.

### Unicode cautions
`.length` counts UTF-16 code units; emoji take 2. Spread (`[...s]`) iterates by code point, but even that does not group combined characters. Use `Intl.Segmenter` for user-visible characters (grapheme clusters).
keyPoints: split/map/join and replace with a callback solve most text tasks.
normalize('NFD') plus a combining-mark regex removes accents.
[...str] respects code points; Intl.Segmenter respects visible characters.
replaceAll avoids the need for a global regex for literal replacements.
Escape user input before building a RegExp from it.
pitfalls: s.split('').reverse() breaks emoji and other surrogate pairs.
String length counts UTF-16 units, so emoji count as 2.

interview.a: split('') splits UTF-16 code units, so emoji and other surrogate pairs get broken; spread or Array.from keeps code points together.

interview.q: How do you remove accents from a string?
interview.a: Normalize to NFD and strip the combining marks range with a regex such as /[̀-ͯ]/g.

topics.title: DOM and URL Helpers: delegation, qs, URLSearchParams
topics.summary: Small DOM helpers and URL/URLSearchParams tricks, with a runnable event-delegation demo.
topics.description:
### Handy DOM helpers
```js
const $  = (sel, root = document) => root.querySelector(sel);
const $$ = (sel, root = document) => [...root.querySelectorAll(sel)];
const on = (el, ev, fn, opts) => (el.addEventListener(ev, fn, opts), () => el.removeEventListener(ev, fn, opts));
```
- `on` returns an unsubscribe function, which keeps cleanup tidy.
- Create elements: `Object.assign(document.createElement('li'), { textContent: 'x', className: 'item' })`.
- Build many nodes at once with `el.append(...nodes)` or `replaceChildren(...nodes)`.
- `el.closest('.card')` finds the nearest ancestor (or itself) matching a selector.
- `el.classList.toggle('on', condition)` sets a class by boolean.
- `el.dataset.userId` reads `data-user-id`.
- `document.createDocumentFragment()` batches insertions.
- `{ once: true }` auto-removes a listener; `{ passive: true }` speeds scrolling.

### Event delegation
Attach one listener to a parent and use `event.target.closest(selector)` to find the real item. It works for items added later and scales to thousands of elements.

### URL tricks
| Task | Code |
|---|---|
| Parse | `const u = new URL('https://x.com/a?b=1#h')` |
| Read query | `u.searchParams.get('b')` |
| Build query | `new URLSearchParams({ q: 'a b', page: 2 }).toString()` gives `q=a+b&page=2` |
| Query to object | `Object.fromEntries(new URL(location).searchParams)` |
| Resolve relative | `new URL('../x', base).href` |
| Multiple values | `params.getAll('tag')`, `params.append('tag', 'x')` |
| Encode | `encodeURIComponent(value)` for single components |

Never build URLs by string concatenation with user input.
keyPoints: Event delegation uses one parent listener plus event.target.closest().
URLSearchParams safely encodes and parses query strings.
on() helpers that return an unsubscribe function simplify cleanup.
classList.toggle accepts a second boolean argument.
Use fragments or replaceChildren to batch DOM updates.
pitfalls: event.target may be a child element of the item; use closest() instead of comparing directly.
URLSearchParams encodes spaces as + while encodeURIComponent uses %20.

examples.explanation: Works in browsers and Node.

interview.q: Why use event delegation?
interview.a: One listener on a parent handles all current and future children, saving memory and handling dynamically added elements.

interview.q: Why use URLSearchParams instead of string concatenation?
interview.a: It encodes keys and values correctly and avoids injection and malformed-URL bugs.

topics.title: Proxy Tricks, WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry
topics.summary: Practical Proxy patterns (defaults, validation, negative indices, observable) and the rarely-needed WeakRef/FinalizationRegistry.
topics.description:
### Proxy tricks
A `Proxy` wraps an object and intercepts operations (`get`, `set`, `has`, `deleteProperty`, `apply`, ...). Always forward with `Reflect` so default behaviour stays correct.

| Trick | Trap |
|---|---|
| Default values for missing keys | `get` returns `0` or `[]` when missing |
| Validation | `set` throws on bad data |
| Negative array indices | `get` converts `-1` to `length - 1` |
| Read-only view | `set` and `deleteProperty` return `false` or throw |
| Hide private-looking keys | `has`, `ownKeys`, `get` filter `_x` |
| Logging / tracing | log inside every trap |
| Observable / reactive | `set` notifies subscribers (the idea behind Vue 3) |
| Auto-vivification | `get` creates nested objects on demand |
| Function wrapping | `apply` trap for timing or memoization |

### WeakRef
`new WeakRef(obj)` holds an object **without preventing garbage collection**. `ref.deref()` returns the object or `undefined` if it was collected. Useful for caches of large derived data. The language gives **no guarantee** when (or if) collection happens, so never depend on it for correctness.

### FinalizationRegistry
`registry.register(target, heldValue)` asks for a callback after `target` is collected. Callbacks may run late or never (also not at process exit), so use them only for optional cleanup such as freeing external caches. Use `try/finally`, `using` or explicit `close()` for real resources.

### Related weak structures
`WeakMap` and `WeakSet` hold keys weakly and are the better tool for per-object metadata (private data, memoisation keyed by object).
keyPoints: Always forward unhandled operations to Reflect inside Proxy traps.
Proxies enable defaults, validation, negative indices and reactivity.
WeakRef.deref() may return undefined at any time after the target is unreachable.
FinalizationRegistry callbacks are best-effort and not guaranteed to run.
Prefer WeakMap for per-object data.
pitfalls: A proxy is not equal (===) to its target, which can confuse identity checks.
Built-ins with internal slots (Map, Date) break if you call methods through a proxy without binding to the target.
Never rely on garbage collection timing for program logic.

examples.title: Practical Proxy patterns
examples.explanation: Defaults, validation, negative index, observable.

interview.q: Why use Reflect inside Proxy traps?
interview.a: Reflect performs the default operation with correct receiver semantics, so the proxy changes only what you intend.

interview.q: Can you rely on FinalizationRegistry callbacks?
interview.a: No. They are not guaranteed to run and may be delayed, so use them only for optional cleanup.

topics.title: Console and Debugging Tricks
topics.summary: Go beyond console.log with table, group, time, assert, dir, count, trace, styling and debugger, plus monkey-patching for tracing.
topics.description:
The console has far more than `log`.

| Method | Use |
|---|---|
| `console.table(arrayOrObject, [cols])` | print rows as a table |
| `console.group(label)` / `groupEnd()` | indent related logs; `groupCollapsed` hides them |
| `console.time(label)` / `timeEnd` / `timeLog` | measure elapsed time |
| `console.count(label)` / `countReset` | count how many times a line runs |
| `console.assert(cond, ...msg)` | log only when `cond` is false |
| `console.dir(obj, { depth: null })` | inspect deeply (Node) or browse properties (browser) |
| `console.trace()` | print the call stack |
| `console.error` / `warn` / `info` | levels, `error` goes to stderr in Node |
| `console.log('%c styled', 'color:red')` | CSS styling in browsers |
| `console.log('%s is %d', 'x', 5)` | printf-style substitution (`%o %O %j %i %f`) |
| `console.log({ a, b })` | shorthand to print variable **names** with values |

### Debugging tricks
- `debugger;` pauses execution when DevTools is open.
- Conditional breakpoints and logpoints in DevTools avoid editing code.
- `console.log(JSON.stringify(x, null, 2))` pretty-prints; `structuredClone(x)` logs a snapshot before later mutation.
- **Monkey-patch** to trace: wrap a function and log calls, then restore it:

```js
const orig = obj.method;
obj.method = function (...args) { console.log('call', args); return orig.apply(this, args); };
```
- Wrap `fetch` or `Array.prototype.push` temporarily to find who calls it (add `console.trace()`).
- `new Error().stack` gives a stack string anywhere.
- Node: `node --inspect-brk`, `node --watch`, `node --trace-warnings`.
- Browser: `copy(obj)` in DevTools console copies a value, `$0` is the selected element, `monitorEvents(el)` logs events.
keyPoints: console.table, group, time, count and assert make logs structured and quicker to scan.
console.log({ x }) prints the variable name with its value.
debugger statements and DevTools logpoints replace noisy log lines.
Monkey-patch a method to trace callers, then restore the original.
Log a cloned snapshot when objects mutate later.
pitfalls: Logging a live object in the browser shows its current state when expanded, not the state at log time.
Leaving debugger statements or heavy logging in production hurts performance and leaks data.

examples.title: console toolbox
examples.explanation: Runs in Node and browsers.

interview.q: How can you log a variable together with its name?
interview.a: Wrap it in an object literal shorthand: console.log({ myVar }).

interview.q: How do you trace who calls a function without editing it?
interview.a: Monkey-patch the function to call console.trace() or log arguments, then delegate to the original.

topics.title: WAT Quirks I: Numbers, NaN, typeof and parseInt
topics.summary: Why 0.1 + 0.2 isn't 0.3, NaN !== NaN, typeof null is object, parseInt('08') and other number oddities, explained.
topics.description:
These "wat" moments are not bugs; each follows a clear rule.

| Expression | Result | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `0.1 + 0.2` | `0.30000000000000004` | IEEE 754 binary floating point cannot store 0.1 exactly |
| `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` | `false` | compare with `Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON` |
| `NaN === NaN` | `false` | NaN is not equal to anything; use `Number.isNaN` or `Object.is` |
| `typeof NaN` | `'number'` | NaN is a number value meaning "invalid" |
| `typeof null` | `'object'` | a first-version bug kept for compatibility |
| `typeof undeclared` | `'undefined'` | `typeof` never throws for undeclared names |
| `typeof class {}` | `'function'` | classes are functions |
| `parseInt('08')` | `8` | modern engines use base 10 (old ones treated 0-prefix as octal) |
| `parseInt('0x1f')` | `31` | prefix 0x switches to hex |
| `['1','2','3'].map(parseInt)` | `[1, NaN, NaN]` | map passes the index as the radix |
| `parseInt(0.0000005)` | `5` | number is converted to string `'5e-7'` first |
| `9007199254740993` | `9007199254740992` | integers above 2^53 lose precision (use BigInt) |
| `-0 === 0` | `true` | but `Object.is(-0, 0)` is `false`; `1 / -0` is `-Infinity` |
| `Math.max()` | `-Infinity` | identity element for max |
| `Math.min() > Math.max()` | `true` | follows from the line above |
| `[10, 9, 1].sort()` | `[1, 10, 9]` | default sort compares strings |
| `0 === -0`, `Number.MIN_VALUE > 0` | both `true` | MIN_VALUE is the smallest **positive** value |

### How to cope
- Money: store integer cents or use a decimal library.
- Floats: round for display (`toFixed`, `Intl`) and compare with an epsilon.
- Always pass the radix: `parseInt(s, 10)`, or use `Number(s)` / `parseFloat`.
- Sort numbers with `(a, b) => a - b`.
keyPoints: 0.1 + 0.2 differs from 0.3 because of binary floating point representation.
NaN is the only value not equal to itself; use Number.isNaN.
typeof null is the historic 'object'.
map(parseInt) fails because the index becomes the radix argument.
Default sort() converts items to strings.
pitfalls: Global isNaN('abc') coerces and returns true; Number.isNaN does not coerce.
Number.EPSILON comparisons need scaling for large magnitudes.

examples.title: Number oddities
examples.explanation: Predict, then run.

interview.q: Why is 0.1 + 0.2 not 0.3?
interview.a: Numbers are binary IEEE 754 doubles; 0.1 and 0.2 cannot be represented exactly, so the sum has a tiny error. Compare with an epsilon or use integers.

interview.q: Why does ['1','2','3'].map(parseInt) return [1, NaN, NaN]?
interview.a: map passes (value, index) and parseInt treats the index as the radix, so '2' is parsed in base 1 and '3' in base 2, both invalid.

topics.title: WAT Quirks II: Coercion, == Table and Plus Operator
topics.summary: Explains [] + {}, [1,2,3] + [4], '5' - 2, the loose equality table and the conversion algorithm behind them.
topics.description:
Most JavaScript "wat" results come from two rules: **`+` concatenates if either side becomes a string**, and **objects convert to primitives** through `valueOf()` then `toString()` (or `Symbol.toPrimitive`).

### The conversion steps
1. For `+`, both operands become primitives first.
2. Arrays become strings via `join(',')`: `[]` is `''`, `[1,2,3]` is `'1,2,3'`.
3. Plain objects become `'[object Object]'`.
4. If either primitive is a string, concatenate; otherwise add as numbers.
5. Other arithmetic operators (`- * /`) always convert to numbers.

| Expression | Result |
|---|---|
| `[] + []` | `''` |
| `[] + {}` | `'[object Object]'` |
| `{} + []` | `0` as a statement in a console (block + unary plus), `'[object Object]'` as an expression |
| `[1,2,3] + [4]` | `'1,2,34'` |
| `'5' + 3` / `'5' - 3` | `'53'` / `2` |
| `true + true` | `2` |
| `[] == false` | `true` (`[]` to `''` to `0`, `false` to `0`) |
| `null == 0` | `false` (null only equals undefined) |
| `null >= 0` | `true` (relational comparison converts null to 0) |
| `undefined == null` | `true` |
| `'' == 0`, `'0' == 0` | `true`, `true` |
| `'' == '0'` | `false` (both strings, compared as text) |
| `[0] == false` | `true` |
| `NaN == NaN` | `false` |
| `!!'false'` | `true` |

### Loose equality `==` algorithm (short)
- Same type: behaves like `===`.
- `null`/`undefined`: equal only to each other.
- Number vs string: string becomes number. Boolean: becomes number first.
- Object vs primitive: object converts to primitive.

### Advice
Use `===` everywhere, with the one accepted exception `x == null` to test for both null and undefined.
keyPoints: + concatenates when either primitive operand is a string; - * / always use numbers.
Arrays convert via join, plain objects become [object Object].
== coerces; null == undefined but neither equals 0 or ''.
Relational operators (>=) coerce null to 0, so null >= 0 is true.
Prefer === except for the x == null idiom.
pitfalls: {} + [] at the start of a statement is parsed as an empty block, giving different results than inside an expression.
[] == ![] is true even though it looks contradictory.

examples.title: Coercion table
examples.explanation: Everything evaluated as expressions.

interview.q: Why is [] + {} equal to '[object Object]'?
interview.a: Both operands convert to strings: [] becomes '' and {} becomes '[object Object]', and + concatenates them.

interview.q: Why is null >= 0 true but null == 0 false?
interview.a: Relational operators convert null to 0, while == has a special rule that null only equals undefined.

topics.title: Array Methods Cheat Sheet
topics.summary: Every Array static and instance method with what it returns, whether it mutates, and the ES version.
topics.description:
Know first whether a method **mutates** the array: mutating methods (`push`, `sort`, `splice`...) change it in place, while the rest return new values. ES2023 added non-mutating twins (`toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced`, `with`).

### Mutating methods
| Method | Returns | Mutates | ES |
|---|---|---|---|
| `push(...x)` / `unshift(...x)` | new length | yes | 3 |
| `pop()` / `shift()` | removed item | yes | 3 |
| `splice(i, del, ...add)` | array of removed | yes | 3 |
| `sort(cmp)` | same array | yes | 3 |
| `reverse()` | same array | yes | 3 |
| `fill(v, s, e)` | same array | yes | 6 |
| `copyWithin(t, s, e)` | same array | yes | 6 |

### Non-mutating methods
| Method | Returns | ES |
|---|---|---|
| `slice(s, e)` | shallow copy of range | 3 |
| `concat(...a)` | new merged array | 3 |
| `join(sep)` | string | 3 |
| `indexOf(x)` / `lastIndexOf(x)` | index or -1 | 5 |
| `includes(x)` | boolean (finds NaN) | 2016 |
| `at(i)` | item (negative allowed) | 2022 |
| `flat(depth)` / `flatMap(fn)` | new flattened array | 2019 |
| `toSorted(cmp)` / `toReversed()` | sorted / reversed copy | 2023 |
| `toSpliced(i, d, ...a)` / `with(i, v)` | modified copy | 2023 |
| `keys()` / `values()` / `entries()` | iterator | 6 |
| `toString()` | comma string | 1 |

### Iteration and search
| Method | Returns | ES |
|---|---|---|
| `forEach(fn)` | `undefined` | 5 |
| `map(fn)` | new array, same length | 5 |
| `filter(fn)` | new array of passing items | 5 |
| `reduce(fn, init)` / `reduceRight` | accumulated value | 5 |
| `some(fn)` / `every(fn)` | boolean | 5 |
| `find(fn)` / `findIndex(fn)` | item / index (-1) | 6 |
| `findLast(fn)` / `findLastIndex(fn)` | from the end | 2023 |

### Statics
| Method | Returns | ES |
|---|---|---|
| `Array.isArray(x)` | boolean | 5 |
| `Array.of(...x)` | array from args | 6 |
| `Array.from(iter, mapFn)` | array from iterable/array-like | 6 |
| `Array.fromAsync(iter)` | Promise of array | 2023+ (engines; Node 22+) |

Callbacks receive `(item, index, array)`. Holes are skipped by most iteration methods.
keyPoints: Mutating: push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, sort, reverse, fill, copyWithin.
ES2023 added toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced and with as non-mutating versions.
map/filter/reduce return new values; forEach returns undefined.
includes finds NaN, indexOf does not.
Array.from converts iterables and array-likes and can map in one step.
pitfalls: sort() without a comparator sorts as strings, so [10, 9, 1] becomes [1, 10, 9].
Array.prototype.fill with an object shares one reference across slots.

examples.title: One tiny example per group
examples.explanation: Mutating vs non-mutating results.

interview.q: Which array methods mutate the original array?
interview.a: push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, sort, reverse, fill and copyWithin.

interview.q: What is the difference between find and filter?
interview.a: find returns the first matching item (or undefined) and stops; filter returns an array of all matches.

topics.title: String Methods Cheat Sheet
topics.summary: All common String methods with return types and ES versions; strings are immutable so every method returns a new value.
topics.description:
Strings are **immutable**: no method changes the original, they all return a new string (or another type). Indexes are UTF-16 code units.

### Inspect and search
| Method | Returns | ES |
|---|---|---|
| `length` | number of UTF-16 units | 1 |
| `charAt(i)` / `s[i]` / `at(i)` | one character (`at` allows negatives) | 1 / 5 / 2022 |
| `charCodeAt(i)` / `codePointAt(i)` | UTF-16 unit / full code point number | 1 / 6 |
| `indexOf(x, from)` / `lastIndexOf(x)` | index or -1 | 1 |
| `includes(x)` | boolean | 6 |
| `startsWith(x)` / `endsWith(x)` | boolean | 6 |
| `search(re)` | index or -1 | 3 |
| `match(re)` | array / null (all matches with `g`) | 3 |
| `matchAll(re)` | iterator of match arrays (needs `g`) | 2020 |
| `localeCompare(b)` | -1, 0, 1 | 3 |

### Transform
| Method | Returns | ES |
|---|---|---|
| `slice(s, e)` | substring (negative indexes ok) | 3 |
| `substring(s, e)` | substring (swaps args, no negatives) | 1 |
| `substr(s, len)` | deprecated, avoid | legacy |
| `toUpperCase()` / `toLowerCase()` | new string | 1 |
| `trim()` / `trimStart()` / `trimEnd()` | new string | 5 / 2019 |
| `padStart(n, ch)` / `padEnd(n, ch)` | padded string | 2017 |
| `repeat(n)` | repeated string | 6 |
| `replace(x, y)` / `replaceAll(x, y)` | replace first / all | 3 / 2021 |
| `split(sep, limit)` | array | 3 |
| `concat(...s)` | joined string | 1 |
| `normalize(form)` | Unicode normalised string | 6 |
| `isWellFormed()` / `toWellFormed()` | boolean / fixed string | 2024 |

### Statics
| Method | Returns |
|---|---|
| `String.fromCharCode(...n)` | string from UTF-16 units |
| `String.fromCodePoint(...n)` | string from code points |
| `String.raw` (as a template tag) | raw template text |

`replace` callbacks receive `(match, ...groups, offset, string)`; replacement strings support `$1`, `$&`, `$<name>`.
keyPoints: Strings are immutable; every method returns a new value.
slice supports negative indexes; substring does not.
replaceAll and matchAll are ES2021 and ES2020 respectively.
padStart is perfect for zero-padding numbers.
split('') splits UTF-16 units; use [...str] for code points.
pitfalls: replace with a string pattern replaces only the first occurrence.
match without the g flag returns match details, with g it returns plain matched strings.
indexOf returns 0 for a match at the start, so check !== -1 not truthiness.

examples.title: String method tour
examples.explanation: Common methods on one sentence.

interview.q: Difference between slice, substring and substr?
interview.a: slice and substring take start and end; slice accepts negatives while substring treats them as 0 and swaps arguments if needed. substr takes a length and is deprecated.

interview.q: How do you replace all occurrences of a substring?
interview.a: Use replaceAll, or replace with a global regex.

topics.title: Object Static Methods Cheat Sheet
topics.summary: Object.* methods for keys, entries, copying, freezing, prototypes and property descriptors with mutation notes.
topics.description:
`Object` statics are the toolkit for inspecting and building objects. "Own" means directly on the object, not inherited.

### Inspect
| Method | Returns | ES |
|---|---|---|
| `Object.keys(o)` | own enumerable string keys | 5 |
| `Object.values(o)` | own enumerable values | 2017 |
| `Object.entries(o)` | `[key, value]` pairs | 2017 |
| `Object.getOwnPropertyNames(o)` | own string keys incl. non-enumerable | 5 |
| `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols(o)` | own symbol keys | 6 |
| `Reflect.ownKeys(o)` | all own keys | 6 |
| `Object.hasOwn(o, k)` | boolean (replaces hasOwnProperty) | 2022 |
| `Object.is(a, b)` | boolean `SameValue` | 6 |
| `Object.getPrototypeOf(o)` | prototype | 5 |
| `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(s)` | descriptor(s) | 5 / 2017 |

### Create and copy
| Method | Returns | Mutates | ES |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Object.assign(target, ...src)` | target | **target** | 6 |
| `Object.create(proto, descs)` | new object | no | 5 |
| `Object.fromEntries(iter)` | object from pairs | no | 2019 |
| `Object.groupBy(items, fn)` | null-prototype object of arrays | no | 2024 |
| `{ ...o }` (syntax) | shallow copy | no | 2018 |
| `structuredClone(o)` (global) | deep copy | no | web/Node 17 |

### Define and restrict
| Method | Effect | Mutates |
|---|---|---|
| `Object.defineProperty(o, k, d)` / `defineProperties` | add/change one property | yes |
| `Object.setPrototypeOf(o, p)` | change prototype (slow) | yes |
| `Object.preventExtensions(o)` | no new props | yes |
| `Object.seal(o)` | no add/delete, values editable | yes |
| `Object.freeze(o)` | read-only (shallow) | yes |
| `Object.isExtensible / isSealed / isFrozen` | boolean | no |

Instance methods: `hasOwnProperty`, `isPrototypeOf`, `propertyIsEnumerable`, `toString`, `toLocaleString`, `valueOf`.
keyPoints: keys/values/entries return only own enumerable string-keyed data.
Object.assign and defineProperty mutate their target; fromEntries and spread create new objects.
freeze is shallow; sealed objects still allow value changes.
Use Object.hasOwn instead of obj.hasOwnProperty.
Object.groupBy returns a null-prototype object.
pitfalls: Object.assign({}, obj) skips nothing but copies getters as values and is shallow.
Frozen objects silently ignore writes in sloppy mode but throw in strict mode.

examples.title: Inspect, copy, restrict
examples.explanation: Shows several statics at work.

interview.q: Difference between Object.freeze and Object.seal?
interview.a: freeze makes properties read-only and non-configurable; seal prevents adding or deleting properties but still allows changing values.

interview.q: Does Object.keys include inherited or symbol keys?
interview.a: No, only own enumerable string keys.

topics.title: Number and Math Cheat Sheet
topics.summary: Number statics and instance methods plus every Math function, with returns and gotchas.
topics.description:
### Number
| Member | Returns / meaning | ES |
|---|---|---|
| `Number.isInteger(x)` | true for integers (no coercion) | 6 |
| `Number.isSafeInteger(x)` | within +-(2^53 - 1) | 6 |
| `Number.isFinite(x)` / `Number.isNaN(x)` | strict checks, no coercion | 6 |
| `Number.parseFloat` / `parseInt` | same as globals | 6 |
| `Number.EPSILON` | smallest difference near 1 | 6 |
| `MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, `MIN_SAFE_INTEGER` | +-9007199254740991 | 6 |
| `MAX_VALUE`, `MIN_VALUE` | largest / smallest positive | 1 |
| `n.toFixed(d)` | string with d decimals | 3 |
| `n.toPrecision(p)` | string with p significant digits | 3 |
| `n.toString(radix)` | string in base 2-36 | 1 |
| `n.toExponential(d)` | exponent string | 3 |
| `n.toLocaleString(loc, opts)` | locale string | 3 |

### Math (all static, never `new Math`)
| Group | Functions |
|---|---|
| Rounding | `round` (half up), `floor`, `ceil`, `trunc`, `fround`, `sign` |
| Power/roots | `pow(x, y)`, `sqrt`, `cbrt`, `hypot`, `exp`, `expm1` |
| Logs | `log` (natural), `log2`, `log10`, `log1p` |
| Trig | `sin cos tan asin acos atan atan2 sinh cosh tanh` and inverses |
| Min/max | `min(...n)` (empty gives Infinity), `max(...n)` (empty gives -Infinity) |
| Other | `abs`, `random()` in [0, 1), `clz32`, `imul` |
| Constants | `PI`, `E`, `LN2`, `LN10`, `LOG2E`, `LOG10E`, `SQRT2`, `SQRT1_2` |

### Recipes
- Random int in [min, max]: `Math.floor(Math.random() * (max - min + 1)) + min`.
- Clamp: `Math.min(max, Math.max(min, n))`.
- Round to 2 decimals: `Math.round(n * 100) / 100` (or `Intl`).
- Math methods coerce arguments; `Number.isX` methods do not.

`Math.round(-2.5)` is `-2` (rounds toward +Infinity at .5), while `Math.trunc` cuts decimals.
keyPoints: Number.isX functions do not coerce; global isNaN and isFinite do.
toFixed returns a string and may misround due to binary storage.
Math.round rounds .5 up toward +Infinity, so -2.5 becomes -2.
Math.random() returns [0, 1) and is not cryptographically secure.
Safe integers end at 2^53 - 1; use BigInt beyond that.
pitfalls: Math.max([1,2,3]) is NaN; spread the array or use apply.
Number('') is 0 and Number(null) is 0, which surprises validation code.

examples.title: Numbers and Math
examples.explanation: Rounding, clamping, random range, formatting.

interview.q: Why does (1.005).toFixed(2) give '1.00'?
interview.a: 1.005 is stored as a binary value slightly below 1.005, so rounding to two decimals goes down.

interview.q: What is the difference between Number.isNaN and isNaN?
interview.a: isNaN coerces its argument first (isNaN('abc') is true); Number.isNaN is true only for the actual NaN value.

topics.title: Date Cheat Sheet
topics.summary: Date construction, getters/setters, formatting and parsing with local vs UTC variants and common traps.
topics.description:
A `Date` stores milliseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z. Most methods come in **local** and **UTC** pairs.

### Creating
| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `new Date()` / `Date.now()` | now (object / ms number) |
| `new Date(ms)` | from timestamp |
| `new Date('2024-05-06T10:00:00Z')` | parse ISO string |
| `new Date(2024, 4, 6, 10, 0)` | local components, **month is 0-11** |
| `Date.UTC(y, m, d, ...)` | timestamp from UTC components |
| `Date.parse(str)` | timestamp or NaN |

### Getters (setters use `set` instead of `get`)
| Local | UTC | Range |
|---|---|---|
| `getFullYear()` | `getUTCFullYear()` | year |
| `getMonth()` | `getUTCMonth()` | 0-11 |
| `getDate()` | `getUTCDate()` | 1-31 |
| `getDay()` | `getUTCDay()` | 0 (Sun) - 6 |
| `getHours()` | `getUTCHours()` | 0-23 |
| `getMinutes()` / `getSeconds()` / `getMilliseconds()` | UTC versions | |
| `getTime()` / `valueOf()` | - | ms since epoch |
| `getTimezoneOffset()` | - | minutes behind UTC |

### Output
| Method | Example output |
|---|---|
| `toISOString()` | `2024-05-06T10:00:00.000Z` (always UTC) |
| `toJSON()` | same as ISO |
| `toString()` | long local string |
| `toDateString()` / `toTimeString()` | parts |
| `toUTCString()` | `Mon, 06 May 2024 10:00:00 GMT` |
| `toLocaleDateString(loc, opts)` / `toLocaleTimeString` / `toLocaleString` | localised |

### Behaviour to remember
- Setters mutate the date and **overflow rolls over**: `d.setDate(32)` moves to next month.
- Date minus Date gives milliseconds; Date plus anything concatenates strings.
- Invalid dates have `getTime()` of `NaN` and print "Invalid Date".
- ISO date-only strings parse as UTC; date-time strings without `Z` parse as local.
- Temporal (a new API) is the long-term replacement; see the latest-features section.
keyPoints: Months are zero-based; days of month start at 1.
ISO date-only strings are UTC, other forms are local.
Setters mutate and overflow carries into the next unit.
Subtract Dates to get milliseconds; use Intl for display.
toISOString always outputs UTC and throws on invalid dates.
pitfalls: Looping 24 * 3600 * 1000 ms steps drifts across DST changes.
new Date('2024-02-30') is Invalid Date in most engines, but new Date(2024, 1, 30) rolls to March 1.

examples.title: Date operations
examples.explanation: UTC based so output is stable anywhere.

interview.q: Why do dates show the previous day sometimes?
interview.a: A date-only ISO string is parsed as UTC midnight but displayed in local time, which is behind UTC in many zones.

interview.q: How do you get the number of days between two dates?
interview.a: Subtract the timestamps and divide by 86,400,000, rounding because of DST.

topics.title: Map, Set, WeakMap, WeakSet Cheat Sheet
topics.summary: Complete member tables for Map, Set, WeakMap and WeakSet including the ES2025 set algebra methods.
topics.description:
### Map (key-value, any key type, insertion order)
| Member | Returns | Mutates |
|---|---|---|
| `new Map(iterable)` | map from `[k, v]` pairs | - |
| `set(k, v)` | the map (chainable) | yes |
| `get(k)` | value or `undefined` | no |
| `has(k)` | boolean | no |
| `delete(k)` | boolean | yes |
| `clear()` | undefined | yes |
| `size` | number | - |
| `keys()` / `values()` / `entries()` | iterators | no |
| `forEach((v, k, m) => ...)` | undefined | no |
| `Map.groupBy(items, fn)` | map of arrays (ES2024) | - |

Keys compare with `SameValueZero` (NaN works as a key, `0` and `-0` are the same). Map is directly iterable.

### Set (unique values)
| Member | Returns |
|---|---|
| `new Set(iterable)` | set of unique values |
| `add(v)` (chainable), `has(v)`, `delete(v)`, `clear()`, `size` | as expected |
| `values()` / `keys()` / `entries()` / `forEach` | iteration |
| `union(o)`, `intersection(o)`, `difference(o)`, `symmetricDifference(o)` | new Set (ES2025) |
| `isSubsetOf(o)`, `isSupersetOf(o)`, `isDisjointFrom(o)` | boolean (ES2025) |

### WeakMap and WeakSet
| | WeakMap | WeakSet |
|---|---|---|
| Keys/values | object (or non-registered symbol) keys only | objects only |
| Methods | `get set has delete` | `add has delete` |
| Iterable / size | **no** | **no** |
| Purpose | private data, caches tied to object lifetime | tagging objects |

### Map vs Object
Map keeps insertion order for all keys, accepts any key type, has `size`, and is faster for frequent add/delete. Objects are better for fixed-shape records and JSON.
keyPoints: Map and Set preserve insertion order and use SameValueZero equality.
set and add return the collection, so calls can be chained.
Set algebra methods (union, intersection ...) are standard in modern engines (ES2025).
WeakMap/WeakSet keys are weakly held, are not iterable and have no size.
Convert with [...map], Object.fromEntries(map) and new Map(Object.entries(o)).
pitfalls: Map keys that are objects are compared by reference, not by value.
JSON.stringify(map) gives {}; convert to entries first.

examples.title: Collections in action
examples.explanation: Map, Set, set algebra, WeakMap privacy.

interview.q: When should you pick Map over a plain object?
interview.a: When keys are not plain strings, when insertion order and size matter, or when entries are added and removed frequently.

interview.q: Why can't you iterate a WeakMap?
interview.a: Keys are held weakly and may be collected at any time, so the engine does not expose enumeration or size.

topics.title: Promise and JSON Cheat Sheet
topics.summary: Promise statics and instance methods (all, allSettled, race, any, withResolvers) and JSON.parse/stringify options.
topics.description:
### Promise
| Method | Resolves with | Rejects when | ES |
|---|---|---|---|
| `new Promise((res, rej) => {})` | value passed to `res` | `rej` or throw | 6 |
| `Promise.resolve(v)` / `reject(e)` | already settled promise | - | 6 |
| `Promise.all(list)` | array of all values | **first** rejection | 6 |
| `Promise.allSettled(list)` | array of `{status, value/reason}` | never | 2020 |
| `Promise.race(list)` | first to settle | first to settle (if rejected) | 6 |
| `Promise.any(list)` | first **fulfilled** value | all reject (`AggregateError`) | 2021 |
| `Promise.withResolvers()` | `{ promise, resolve, reject }` | - | 2024 |
| `Promise.try(fn)` | result of sync or async fn | fn throws | 2025 |
| `p.then(onOk, onErr)` | new promise | - | 6 |
| `p.catch(fn)` | new promise | - | 6 |
| `p.finally(fn)` | same value, runs always | - | 2018 |

Handlers run as **microtasks**. A thrown error inside `then` rejects the returned promise. An unhandled rejection crashes Node (default since v15).

### JSON
| Call | Notes |
|---|---|
| `JSON.stringify(v, replacer, space)` | `space` (2 or '\t') pretty prints; replacer is a function or key whitelist array |
| `JSON.parse(text, reviver)` | reviver `(key, value)` transforms values bottom-up |
| `toJSON()` method | object controls its own serialisation (`Date` has one) |
| Skipped | `undefined`, functions, symbols are omitted in objects and become `null` in arrays |
| `NaN`, `Infinity` | become `null` |
| `BigInt` | throws TypeError |
| Cycles | throw TypeError |
| `Map`, `Set` | become `{}` |
| `JSON.rawJSON(text)` / `isRawJSON` | embed exact number text (new) |

Invalid JSON (single quotes, trailing commas, comments) throws `SyntaxError`.
keyPoints: Promise.all fails fast, allSettled waits for all, any picks the first success, race the first settlement.
Promise.withResolvers gives resolve/reject outside the executor.
finally passes the original value or error through.
JSON.stringify drops undefined, functions and symbols; Dates become ISO strings.
JSON.parse needs double-quoted strict JSON.
pitfalls: Forgetting to return a promise inside then breaks the chain order.
JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) changes types (Dates become strings).

examples.title: Promise combinators and JSON options
examples.explanation: Deterministic results via Promise.resolve.

interview.q: What is the difference between Promise.all and Promise.allSettled?
interview.a: all rejects as soon as one promise rejects; allSettled waits for every promise and reports each outcome.

interview.q: What does JSON.stringify do with undefined and functions?
interview.a: They are omitted from objects and replaced with null inside arrays.

topics.title: Reflect and Proxy Traps Cheat Sheet
topics.summary: All 13 Proxy traps paired with their Reflect methods, trigger operations and invariants.
topics.description:
`Reflect` has a static method for each Proxy trap, with identical signature. Inside a trap, call the matching `Reflect` method to perform the default action.

| Trap (handler method) | Triggered by | Reflect equivalent | Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| `get(t, k, receiver)` | `obj.k`, `obj[k]` | `Reflect.get` | value |
| `set(t, k, v, receiver)` | `obj.k = v` | `Reflect.set` | boolean (success) |
| `has(t, k)` | `k in obj` | `Reflect.has` | boolean |
| `deleteProperty(t, k)` | `delete obj.k` | `Reflect.deleteProperty` | boolean |
| `ownKeys(t)` | `Object.keys`, `for...in`, `Reflect.ownKeys` | `Reflect.ownKeys` | array of keys |
| `getOwnPropertyDescriptor(t, k)` | `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor`, `keys` filtering | same name | descriptor/undefined |
| `defineProperty(t, k, d)` | `Object.defineProperty` | same name | boolean |
| `getPrototypeOf(t)` | `instanceof`, `Object.getPrototypeOf` | same name | object/null |
| `setPrototypeOf(t, p)` | `Object.setPrototypeOf` | same name | boolean |
| `isExtensible(t)` | `Object.isExtensible` | same name | boolean |
| `preventExtensions(t)` | `Object.preventExtensions` | same name | boolean |
| `apply(t, thisArg, args)` | `proxy(...)` (target must be callable) | `Reflect.apply` | any |
| `construct(t, args, newTarget)` | `new proxy(...)` | `Reflect.construct` | object |

### Extras
- `Proxy.revocable(target, handler)` returns `{ proxy, revoke }`; after `revoke()` every operation throws.
- `Reflect.apply(fn, thisArg, args)` is a safe replacement for `Function.prototype.apply.call`.
- Reflect returns booleans (instead of throwing) for `defineProperty`, `set`, `deleteProperty`.

### Invariants
A trap cannot lie about non-configurable, non-writable target properties: reporting a different value for a frozen property throws a `TypeError`. A `set` trap that returns `false` throws in strict mode.
keyPoints: Each of the 13 traps has a Reflect method with the same name and parameters.
A set trap must return true to indicate success, otherwise strict mode throws.
Proxy.revocable provides a kill switch for access.
Traps must respect invariants of non-configurable target properties.
apply and construct traps require a callable target.
pitfalls: Forgetting to return true from the set trap causes TypeErrors in modules and classes.
Proxies do not forward internal slots, so wrapping a Map without binding methods fails.

examples.title: Logging proxy with Reflect
examples.explanation: A single handler printing every operation.

interview.q: Why use Reflect in a Proxy handler?
interview.a: It runs the default operation with correct receiver semantics and returns the proper boolean or value so invariants are preserved.

interview.q: How many Proxy traps exist?
interview.a: Thirteen: get, set, has, deleteProperty, ownKeys, getOwnPropertyDescriptor, defineProperty, getPrototypeOf, setPrototypeOf, isExtensible, preventExtensions, apply and construct.

topics.title: RegExp Syntax, Flags, Lookarounds and Named Groups
topics.summary: Complete regex syntax table plus flags, lookahead/lookbehind, named groups, and RegExp/String method behaviours.
topics.description:
### Syntax
| Token | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `.` | any char except line break (`s` flag includes it) |
| `\d \w \s` / `\D \W \S` | digit, word char, whitespace / negations |
| `\b` / `\B` | word boundary / not boundary |
| `^` `$` | start / end (per line with `m`) |
| `[abc]` `[^abc]` `[a-z]` | class, negated class, range |
| `a\|b` | alternation |
| `(x)` / `(?:x)` | capturing / non-capturing group |
| `(?<name>x)` / `\k<name>` | named group / back-reference |
| `\1` | numbered back-reference |
| `* + ? {n} {n,} {n,m}` | quantifiers (greedy) |
| `*? +? ??` | lazy quantifiers |
| `x(?=y)` / `x(?!y)` | lookahead positive / negative |
| `(?<=y)x` / `(?<!y)x` | **lookbehind** positive / negative |
| `\p{L}` `\p{Script=Greek}` `\P{...}` | Unicode property escapes (needs `u` or `v`) |
| `\u{1F600}` | code point (needs `u`) |
| `(?i:x)` | inline flag modifiers (ES2025) |

### Flags
| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `g` | global, all matches (stateful `lastIndex`) |
| `i` | ignore case |
| `m` | multiline anchors |
| `s` | dotAll |
| `u` | Unicode mode |
| `v` | unicodeSets (set operations, string properties) |
| `y` | sticky, match only at `lastIndex` |
| `d` | indices, adds `match.indices` |

### Methods
| Method | Returns |
|---|---|
| `re.test(s)` | boolean |
| `re.exec(s)` | match array (with `index`, `groups`) or null |
| `s.match(re)` | first match, or all strings with `g` |
| `s.matchAll(re)` | iterator of full matches (needs `g`) |
| `s.replace / replaceAll(re, fn or $-string)` | new string; `$<name>`, `$1`, `$&` |
| `s.split(re)` | array (captures are included) |
| `s.search(re)` | index |
| `RegExp.escape(str)` | escaped literal text (ES2025) |

Regex literals with the `g` or `y` flag keep `lastIndex` state: `re.test()` twice on the same string can differ.
keyPoints: Named groups (?<year>\d{4}) are read from match.groups.
Lookbehind (?<=...) and (?<!...) match without consuming text.
The g flag makes test/exec stateful through lastIndex.
Use u (or v) for Unicode property escapes like \p{L}.
Lazy quantifiers (*?) match as little as possible.
pitfalls: Reusing a global regex with test() alternates true/false because of lastIndex.
Greedy .* can cause catastrophic backtracking on adversarial input.

examples.title: Named groups, lookarounds, flags
examples.explanation: Practical regex snippets.

interview.q: What is the difference between greedy and lazy quantifiers?
interview.a: Greedy ones (*, +) match as much as possible and backtrack; lazy ones (*?, +?) match as little as possible.

interview.q: Why does a global regex's test() alternate results on the same string?
interview.a: The g flag stores lastIndex; each successful test continues from there, and after a failure lastIndex resets to 0.

topics.title: Intl API Cheat Sheet
topics.summary: Every Intl formatter with its options, typical output and when to use it.
topics.description:
`Intl` is the built-in internationalisation API. Create a formatter once with a locale and options, then call its method repeatedly.

| Constructor | Main method | Common options | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Intl.NumberFormat` | `format(n)` | `style` (decimal, currency, percent, unit), `currency`, `unit`, `notation` (compact, scientific), `minimumFractionDigits`, `maximumFractionDigits`, `signDisplay`, `compactDisplay` | `1,234.50` or `$1,234.50` |
| `Intl.DateTimeFormat` | `format(d)`, `formatToParts` | `dateStyle`, `timeStyle`, `year`, `month`, `day`, `weekday`, `hour`, `hour12`, `timeZone`, `timeZoneName` | `6 May 2024` |
| `Intl.RelativeTimeFormat` | `format(n, unit)` | `numeric: 'auto'`, `style` | `yesterday`, `in 3 days` |
| `Intl.ListFormat` | `format(arr)` | `type` (conjunction, disjunction, unit), `style` | `a, b, and c` |
| `Intl.PluralRules` | `select(n)` | `type: 'ordinal'` | `one`, `other`, `few` |
| `Intl.Collator` | `compare(a, b)` | `numeric`, `sensitivity`, `caseFirst` | natural sort |
| `Intl.Segmenter` | `segment(str)` | `granularity` (grapheme, word, sentence) | split visible characters |
| `Intl.DisplayNames` | `of(code)` | `type` (region, language, currency) | `India` from `IN` |
| `Intl.Locale` | properties | language, region, maximize() | parse `en-US` |
| `Intl.DurationFormat` | `format(obj)` | newer, check support | `1 hr, 30 min` |

### Shortcuts
`n.toLocaleString(loc, opts)`, `d.toLocaleDateString`, `arr.toLocaleString`, and `a.localeCompare(b, loc, { numeric: true })` call Intl internally. For sorting use `arr.sort(new Intl.Collator('en', { numeric: true }).compare)`.

### Notes
- Pass `undefined` as locale to use the user's default; hard-code a locale in tests.
- `formatToParts` returns typed parts (integer, group, currency) for custom rendering.
- `Intl.supportedValuesOf('timeZone')` lists available names.
- Currency has no default; you must pass `currency`.
keyPoints: Create a formatter once and reuse it for performance.
Collator with numeric: true gives natural sort (file2 before file10).
RelativeTimeFormat with numeric: 'auto' prints yesterday/tomorrow.
Intl.Segmenter splits text by grapheme, word or sentence correctly.
Tests should pass an explicit locale for stable output.
pitfalls: Locale default differs between environments, so unpinned output varies.
Intl.NumberFormat with style currency throws if currency is missing.

examples.title: Several Intl formatters
examples.explanation: Pinned locales for deterministic output.

interview.q: How do you sort strings with numbers naturally?
interview.a: Use Intl.Collator with numeric: true, or localeCompare(b, undefined, { numeric: true }).

interview.q: Why create Intl formatters outside loops?
interview.a: Constructing them is relatively expensive; reuse one instance and call format repeatedly.

topics.title: Console API Cheat Sheet
topics.summary: Every console method, format specifier and its effect in Node and browsers.
topics.description:
| Method | Purpose | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `log` / `info` / `debug` | general output | `debug` hidden by default in browsers |
| `warn` | warning (yellow) | goes to stderr in Node |
| `error` | error (red) | stderr; includes stack in browsers |
| `table(data, cols?)` | tabular view | arrays of objects or arrays |
| `dir(obj, opts)` | object inspector | `depth: null` for full depth (Node) |
| `dirxml(el)` | DOM tree view | browsers |
| `group(label)` / `groupCollapsed` / `groupEnd` | indent output | nest freely |
| `time(l)` / `timeLog(l)` / `timeEnd(l)` | timers | label based |
| `count(l)` / `countReset(l)` | counters | default label `default` |
| `assert(cond, ...msg)` | logs if false | does not throw |
| `trace()` | stack trace | prints call stack |
| `clear()` | clear console | no-op in some environments |
| `profile()` / `timeStamp()` | profiler marker | browsers/devtools |

### Format specifiers (first argument)
| Spec | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `%s` | string |
| `%d` / `%i` | number / integer |
| `%f` | float |
| `%o` / `%O` | object (expandable / plain) |
| `%j` | JSON (Node) |
| `%c` | CSS styles (browsers) |
| `%%` | literal percent |

### Tips
- `console.log({ a, b })` prints names and values.
- Template: `console.log('%c Title', 'font-size:20px;color:teal')` in browsers.
- Arrays of objects with `console.table(rows, ['id'])` filter columns.
- `console.log(JSON.stringify(x, null, 2))` prints a stable snapshot.
- In Node, `util.inspect` and `console.dir` accept `colors`, `depth`, `compact`, `breakLength`.
- Replace console methods to build a logger: `console.log = (...a) => orig('[app]', ...a)`.
- Browser console utilities (not on `console`): `$0`, `$_`, `copy()`, `monitorEvents()`, `getEventListeners()`.
keyPoints: table, group, time, count and assert are the underused console methods.
%s %d %i %f %o %O %j and %c format specifiers work in the first argument.
error and warn write to stderr in Node, log writes to stdout.
console.assert logs but never throws.
console.log({ x }) is a handy way to label values.
pitfalls: Logging huge objects in loops slows the app and DevTools.
Browser consoles evaluate live objects lazily, so expanded output may show later state.

examples.title: Console API tour
examples.explanation: Every group once.

interview.q: What is the difference between console.log and console.dir?
interview.a: log prints a formatted representation, while dir prints the object as an inspectable structure with options such as depth in Node.

interview.q: Does console.assert throw?
interview.a: No; it only logs a message when the condition is false.

topics.title: DOM API Quick List
topics.summary: Quick reference of selecting, creating, modifying, styling, traversing and event APIs in the DOM.
topics.description:
### Select
| API | Returns |
|---|---|
| `document.getElementById(id)` | element or null |
| `querySelector(sel)` / `querySelectorAll(sel)` | first element / **static** NodeList |
| `getElementsByClassName / TagName` | **live** HTMLCollection |
| `el.closest(sel)` | nearest matching ancestor (or itself) |
| `el.matches(sel)` | boolean |
| `document.forms`, `document.body`, `document.documentElement` | shortcuts |

### Create and change
| API | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `document.createElement(tag)` / `createTextNode` / `createDocumentFragment` | make nodes |
| `parent.append(...)` / `prepend` / `before` / `after` | insert nodes or text |
| `appendChild`, `insertBefore`, `replaceChild`, `removeChild` | classic insertion |
| `el.remove()` / `replaceWith()` / `replaceChildren()` | remove/replace |
| `el.cloneNode(deep)` | copy |
| `el.insertAdjacentHTML(pos, html)` | `beforebegin afterbegin beforeend afterend` |
| `textContent` | text (safe) |
| `innerHTML` / `outerHTML` | parse HTML (XSS risk with user data) |

### Attributes, classes, styles
| API | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `getAttribute / setAttribute / removeAttribute / hasAttribute / toggleAttribute` | attributes |
| `el.dataset.fooBar` | `data-foo-bar` |
| `el.classList.add / remove / toggle / contains / replace` | classes |
| `el.style.prop = v`, `style.setProperty('--x', v)` | inline style |
| `getComputedStyle(el)` | resolved styles |
| `el.hidden`, `el.value`, `el.checked`, `el.disabled` | properties |

### Traversal
`parentElement`, `children`, `firstElementChild`, `lastElementChild`, `nextElementSibling`, `previousElementSibling`, `childNodes` (includes text nodes), `contains(node)`.

### Geometry
`getBoundingClientRect()`, `offsetWidth/Height`, `scrollTop`, `scrollIntoView()`, `window.innerWidth`.

### Events
`addEventListener(type, fn, { once, passive, capture, signal })`, `removeEventListener`, `dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent(name, { detail }))`, `event.preventDefault()`, `stopPropagation()`, `target`, `currentTarget`.
keyPoints: querySelectorAll returns a static list; getElementsBy* returns a live collection.
textContent is safe; innerHTML parses HTML and is an XSS risk.
classList and dataset are the clean ways to handle classes and data attributes.
append/prepend/before/after accept strings and multiple nodes.
addEventListener accepts options including once, passive and an AbortSignal.
pitfalls: children excludes text nodes but childNodes includes them (including whitespace).
Reading layout properties after writes forces reflow; batch reads and writes.

examples.title: Build and modify DOM
examples.explanation: Create, class toggle, dataset, closest.

interview.q: What is the difference between querySelectorAll and getElementsByClassName?
interview.a: querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList snapshot; getElementsByClassName returns a live HTMLCollection that updates as the DOM changes.

interview.q: Why prefer textContent over innerHTML for user data?
interview.a: textContent inserts plain text, whereas innerHTML parses HTML and can execute injected markup (XSS).

topics.title: Fetch, URL, Storage and Timers API List
topics.summary: Quick reference for fetch/Response/Headers, URL and URLSearchParams, localStorage/sessionStorage, timers and other common web globals.
topics.description:
### fetch
```js
const res = await fetch(url, { method, headers, body, signal, credentials, cache, mode });
```
| Member | Notes |
|---|---|
| `res.ok`, `res.status`, `res.statusText` | fetch **does not reject on 404/500**, check `ok` |
| `res.headers.get(name)` | `Headers` object (case-insensitive) |
| `res.json() / text() / blob() / arrayBuffer() / formData()` | body readers, **one use only** |
| `res.clone()` | read the body twice |
| `res.body` | ReadableStream |
| `AbortController` + `signal` | cancel; `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` auto-abort |
| `new Request(url, init)` / `new Response(body, init)` | constructors (Service Workers, tests) |
| `FormData`, `Blob`, `File`, `URLSearchParams` | request bodies |

### URL and URLSearchParams
`new URL(str, base)` with `href`, `origin`, `protocol`, `host`, `hostname`, `port`, `pathname`, `search`, `hash`, `searchParams`. Methods: `get`, `getAll`, `set`, `append`, `delete`, `has`, `toString`, iteration, `sort`. Static `URL.canParse(str)` and `URL.createObjectURL(blob)`.

### Storage
| API | Lifetime | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| `localStorage` | until cleared | about 5 MB, strings only |
| `sessionStorage` | tab session | about 5 MB |
| `setItem / getItem / removeItem / clear / key(i) / length` | synchronous | |
| Cookies (`document.cookie`) | configurable | about 4 KB, sent with requests |
| IndexedDB | persistent, async | large, structured data |
| Cache API / Service Worker | offline caching | |

Store objects with `JSON.stringify`; reads return `null` when missing. The `storage` event fires in **other** tabs.

### Timers and scheduling
`setTimeout / clearTimeout`, `setInterval / clearInterval`, `requestAnimationFrame / cancelAnimationFrame`, `requestIdleCallback`, `queueMicrotask(fn)`, `structuredClone`, `performance.now()`, `crypto.randomUUID()`, `crypto.getRandomValues(arr)`, `navigator.clipboard`, `navigator.onLine`.
keyPoints: fetch only rejects on network failure; always check response.ok.
A response body can be read once; clone it to read twice.
AbortSignal.timeout(ms) gives a built-in timeout for requests.
localStorage is synchronous, string-only and shared across tabs of the same origin.
queueMicrotask and requestAnimationFrame schedule work at different phases of the event loop.
pitfalls: Sending JSON needs both JSON.stringify(body) and the Content-Type: application/json header.
Never store secrets or tokens in localStorage if XSS is a risk.

examples.title: Parsing and storage helpers
examples.explanation: Uses a Map-backed storage shim so it also runs in Node.

interview.q: Does fetch reject on a 404 response?
interview.a: No. It only rejects on network errors; check response.ok or response.status yourself.

interview.q: What is the difference between localStorage and sessionStorage?
interview.a: localStorage persists until cleared and is shared across tabs of an origin; sessionStorage lives only for the tab session.

topics.title: Object.groupBy and Map.groupBy (ES2024)
topics.summary: Group an iterable by a key function natively, returning either a plain null-prototype object or a Map.
topics.description:
**Support:** ES2024. Available in Node 21+, Chrome 117+, Firefox 119+, Safari 17.4+. Older runtimes need a `reduce` fallback.

`Object.groupBy(items, callback)` loops over any iterable, calls `callback(item, index)` to get a key, and returns an object whose properties are arrays of the items sharing that key. `Map.groupBy` does the same but returns a `Map`, so keys can be **any value** (objects, numbers, booleans) instead of being converted to strings.

### Key facts
| | `Object.groupBy` | `Map.groupBy` |
|---|---|---|
| Result | object with `null` prototype | `Map` |
| Key types | strings or symbols (others converted) | any value, compared with SameValueZero |
| Key order | insertion order, but integer-like keys come first | insertion order |
| Use for | JSON-like output | numeric/object keys, ordered results |

- The object has **no prototype**, so keys like `toString` or `constructor` are safe, but you cannot call `result.hasOwnProperty()`. Use `Object.hasOwn(result, key)`.
- Groups keep the original item order.
- Works with arrays, Sets, generators and other iterables.
- It does not mutate the input and does not copy items (shallow references).

### Replaces
The classic `reduce` pattern: `arr.reduce((g, x) => ((g[f(x)] ??= []).push(x), g), {})`. The native method is shorter and avoids prototype-pollution pitfalls with keys such as `__proto__`.

### Typical uses
Group orders by status, products by category, events by day, or bucket numbers into ranges (return a label from the callback).
keyPoints: Object.groupBy returns a null-prototype object of arrays; Map.groupBy returns a Map.
Use Map.groupBy when keys are not strings.
The callback receives (item, index).
Group order inside each bucket matches the original order.
Standardised in ES2024; older engines need a fallback.
pitfalls: Calling result.hasOwnProperty fails because the object has no prototype.
Integer-like keys in an object are reordered to the front regardless of insertion order.

examples.title: Grouping with both APIs
examples.explanation: Needs Node 21+ (Node 24 is fine).

interview.q: Why does Object.groupBy return an object with a null prototype?
interview.a: So that group names like constructor or __proto__ cannot clash with inherited properties.

interview.q: When would you use Map.groupBy instead?
interview.a: When the grouping key is not a string, such as a number, boolean or object, or when you want guaranteed insertion order.

topics.title: Non-mutating Array Methods: toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced, with (ES2023)
topics.summary: Copy-then-change array methods plus findLast, at and flat tools that make immutable updates easy.
topics.description:
**Support:** ES2023. Node 20+, Chrome 110+, Firefox 115+, Safari 16+. TypedArrays have `toSorted`, `toReversed` and `with` too.

The old `sort`, `reverse` and `splice` mutate the original array, which causes bugs in React state, Redux reducers and shared data. ES2023 adds **change-by-copy** versions that return a modified copy and leave the source untouched.

| Mutating | Copying version | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `arr.sort(cmp)` | `arr.toSorted(cmp)` | still needs a comparator for numbers |
| `arr.reverse()` | `arr.toReversed()` | |
| `arr.splice(i, d, ...items)` | `arr.toSpliced(i, d, ...items)` | returns the **new array**, not the removed items |
| `arr[i] = v` | `arr.with(i, v)` | throws `RangeError` if the index is out of range |

### Related search helpers
- `findLast(fn)` and `findLastIndex(fn)` (ES2023) search from the end.
- `at(-1)` (ES2022) reads from the end.
- `Array.prototype.group` was **not** shipped; use `Object.groupBy`.

### Sparse arrays
The copying methods read holes as `undefined` and always produce dense arrays.

### Remember
These make a **shallow** copy: objects inside are still shared. They are O(n) per call, so avoid in tight loops over huge arrays; use them where clarity and immutability matter.
keyPoints: toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced and with return new arrays and leave the source unchanged.
toSpliced returns the modified copy, unlike splice which returns removed items.
with(i, v) replaces one element immutably and throws RangeError for invalid indexes.
findLast and findLastIndex search from the end.
Copies are shallow; nested objects are shared.
pitfalls: toSorted without a comparator still sorts numbers as strings.
Old runtimes (Node 18 and below) lack these methods; polyfill or transpile.

examples.title: Immutable updates
examples.explanation: Original array is never changed.

interview.q: What does toSpliced return compared with splice?
interview.a: toSpliced returns the new modified array without changing the original; splice mutates and returns the removed elements.

interview.q: Why are these methods useful in React?
interview.a: State must not be mutated; copying methods allow sorting or updating items without touching the previous state object.

topics.title: Promise.withResolvers, Promise.try, Array.fromAsync
topics.summary: Newer async helpers that remove boilerplate: externally resolved promises, safe sync-or-async wrapping, and collecting async iterables.
topics.description:
### Promise.withResolvers (ES2024)
Before: `let resolve, reject; const promise = new Promise((res, rej) => { resolve = res; reject = rej; });`
Now: `const { promise, resolve, reject } = Promise.withResolvers();`. Great for turning event callbacks, queues and "wait until X happens" flows into promises. Node 22+, modern browsers.

### Promise.try (ES2025)
`Promise.try(fn, ...args)` runs `fn` immediately (synchronously) and returns a promise. A synchronous throw becomes a rejection, and a normal return value (or returned promise) is wrapped. It fixes the classic bug where `new Promise(r => r(fn()))` or `Promise.resolve().then(fn)` either delays the call or leaks sync errors. Available in Node 24 (V8 12.8+) and current browsers.

### Array.fromAsync
`await Array.fromAsync(asyncIterable, mapFn)` collects an async iterable (or a sync iterable of promises) into an array. It awaits each element **sequentially**, unlike `Promise.all(array)`. Shipped in all current engines since about 2023-24 (Node 22+).

### Related existing features
- `Promise.any`, `allSettled` (ES2020-21) and `for await...of` (ES2018).
- `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` and `AbortSignal.any([...])` for cancellation (web platform, Node 20+).
- `await` at the top level of modules (ES2022).

### Use cases
Test helpers, deferred values, event-to-promise adapters, wrapping library functions that may be sync or async, and reading streams into arrays.
keyPoints: Promise.withResolvers returns { promise, resolve, reject } without an executor closure.
Promise.try turns synchronous throws into rejections and runs the function immediately.
Array.fromAsync collects async iterables into an array, awaiting sequentially.
All three are available in Node 24 and current evergreen browsers.
AbortSignal.timeout complements them for cancellation.
pitfalls: Promise.try calls the function synchronously, unlike Promise.resolve().then(fn).
Array.fromAsync is sequential; use Promise.all for parallel awaiting.

examples.title: Deferred, try and fromAsync
examples.explanation: Three helpers in one script.

interview.q: What problem does Promise.try solve?
interview.a: It lets you start a function that may be sync or async and always get a promise, with synchronous exceptions converted to rejections, while still running the function immediately.

interview.q: How does Array.fromAsync differ from Promise.all?
interview.a: fromAsync consumes an async iterable one element at a time; Promise.all awaits an existing array of promises concurrently.

topics.title: Set Methods: union, intersection, difference and more (ES2025)
topics.summary: Seven new Set methods that finally give set algebra natively, with notes on set-like arguments and support.
topics.description:
**Support:** ES2025. Node 22+, Chrome 122+, Firefox 127+, Safari 17+.

Before ES2025 you had to write `new Set([...a].filter(x => b.has(x)))`. Now `Set.prototype` has:

| Method | Returns | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `a.union(b)` | new Set | in a or b |
| `a.intersection(b)` | new Set | in both |
| `a.difference(b)` | new Set | in a but not b |
| `a.symmetricDifference(b)` | new Set | in exactly one |
| `a.isSubsetOf(b)` | boolean | every item of a is in b |
| `a.isSupersetOf(b)` | boolean | a contains every item of b |
| `a.isDisjointFrom(b)` | boolean | no shared items |

### Details
- Methods are **non-mutating**; they return a new `Set` and leave both inputs alone.
- The argument only needs to be **set-like**: an object with `size`, `has()` and `keys()`. A `Map` qualifies (its keys are used), an `Array` does **not** and throws a `TypeError`.
- The result order follows spec rules (items from `a` first for union; for `intersection` order depends on which set is smaller).
- Equality is SameValueZero: `NaN` equals `NaN`, objects by reference.

### Use cases
Permissions (`required.isSubsetOf(granted)`), tag filtering, diffing selected ids, removing duplicates between lists.

### Not included
There is no in-place mutation variant (no `unionWith`); use `for (const x of b) a.add(x)` for that.
keyPoints: Seven new methods: union, intersection, difference, symmetricDifference, isSubsetOf, isSupersetOf, isDisjointFrom.
They return new Sets; they never mutate.
The argument must be set-like (size, has, keys); arrays are rejected.
A Map can be passed as a set-like argument.
Part of ES2025 and available in Node 22+.
pitfalls: Passing an array throws a TypeError; wrap it with new Set(array).
Do not depend on exact result ordering of intersection across engines.

examples.title: Set algebra
examples.explanation: Runs on Node 22+.

interview.q: Do the new Set methods mutate the Set?
interview.a: No. They return a new Set (or a boolean for the is* methods) and leave the originals unchanged.

interview.q: What does set-like mean for the argument?
interview.a: An object with a numeric size property and has() and keys() methods; arrays do not qualify.

topics.title: Iterator Helpers: map, filter, take, drop, flatMap, toArray (ES2025)
topics.summary: Lazy array-like methods on iterators and generators, so you can process infinite or huge sequences without building arrays.
topics.description:
**Support:** ES2025. Node 22+ (V8 12+), Chrome 122+, Firefox 131+, Safari 18.4+.

Arrays have `map` and `filter`, but iterators (generators, `Map.prototype.entries()`, `Set.prototype.values()`...) did not. ES2025 adds a global `Iterator` and these methods on `Iterator.prototype`:

| Method | Returns | Lazy? |
|---|---|---|
| `map(fn)`, `filter(fn)` | iterator | yes |
| `take(n)`, `drop(n)` | iterator | yes |
| `flatMap(fn)` | iterator (fn returns an iterable) | yes |
| `toArray()` | array | consumes |
| `forEach(fn)` | undefined | consumes |
| `reduce(fn, init)` | value | consumes |
| `some`, `every`, `find` | boolean / item | stops early |
| `Iterator.from(x)` | wraps any iterable or iterator | - |

### Why lazy matters
`naturals().filter(isEven).map(square).take(3).toArray()` processes only as many numbers as needed, even though `naturals()` is infinite. With arrays you would need the whole array first.

### Details
- Each helper returns a new iterator that is itself iterable and has the helpers, so chains work.
- Callbacks receive `(value, counter)`.
- Values are consumed once; an iterator cannot be rewound.
- `take`, `find`, `some` and `every` call `return()` on the source to release resources.
- Async iterator helpers are a separate proposal and are **not** available yet.
- `Iterator` can be extended: `class MyIt extends Iterator { next() {...} }` gains all helpers.
keyPoints: Iterator helpers run lazily and process one item at a time through the chain.
take and drop let you slice infinite generators.
toArray, forEach, reduce, some, every and find consume the iterator.
Iterator.from wraps plain iterators so they gain the helper methods.
Async iterator helpers are not part of ES2025.
pitfalls: An iterator is exhausted after one pass; calling toArray twice gives an empty array the second time.
Helpers are not available on arrays themselves; call arr.values() first.

examples.title: Lazy pipeline over an infinite generator
examples.explanation: Node 22+.

interview.q: What is the advantage of iterator helpers over array methods?
interview.a: They are lazy: they pull one value at a time, so you can work with infinite generators and avoid creating intermediate arrays.

interview.q: Can you reuse an iterator after toArray()?
interview.a: No, iterators are single-pass; after being consumed they are done.

topics.title: Modern RegExp: v flag, duplicate named groups, inline modifiers, RegExp.escape
topics.summary: Newer regex features: unicodeSets (v), set subtraction and intersection, duplicate named groups, (?i:) modifiers, and RegExp.escape.
topics.description:
Regex gained several features after named groups and lookbehind (ES2018). Check engine support in older environments.

| Feature | Version | Node 24 |
|---|---|---|
| `d` flag (match indices) | ES2022 | yes |
| `v` flag (unicodeSets) | ES2024 | yes |
| Duplicate named groups (in different alternatives) | ES2025 | yes |
| Inline modifiers `(?i:...)`, `(?-i:...)` | ES2025 | yes |
| `RegExp.escape(str)` | ES2025 | yes (V8 13.6) |

### The `v` flag
An upgrade to `u`. In a character class you can use:
- **Set subtraction**: `[\p{L}--[a-z]]` letters except lowercase ASCII.
- **Intersection**: `[\p{Script=Greek}&&\p{Letter}]`.
- **Nested classes**: `[[a-z]--[aeiou]]` consonants.
- **String properties** such as `\p{RGI_Emoji}` (matches whole emoji sequences).
- Stricter syntax: characters like `(`, `)`, `[`, `{`, `}`, `/`, `-`, `|` must be escaped inside classes.
You cannot combine `u` and `v`.

### Duplicate named groups
`/(?<y>\d{4})-\d\d|\d\d-(?<y>\d{4})/` lets the same name appear in different alternatives; whichever branch matched fills `groups.y`.

### Modifiers
`(?i:abc)def` makes only `abc` case-insensitive; `(?-i:...)` turns it off inside an `i` regex. Supported flags: `i`, `m`, `s`.

### RegExp.escape
Escapes text so it can be used literally in a regex: `new RegExp(RegExp.escape(userInput))`. Replaces homemade escapers.

### Also useful
The `d` flag gives `match.indices` with start/end positions for every group.
keyPoints: The v flag adds set subtraction (--), intersection (&&) and emoji string properties.
Duplicate named groups are allowed in separate alternatives.
(?i:...) applies a flag to only part of a pattern.
RegExp.escape safely escapes user text for literal matching.
u and v cannot be used together.
pitfalls: Under the v flag, unescaped special characters inside classes are syntax errors.
Older browsers lack v flag, modifiers and RegExp.escape; feature-detect with try/new RegExp.

examples.title: Four modern regex features
examples.explanation: Verified on Node 24.

interview.q: What does the v flag add over u?
interview.a: Set operations (subtraction and intersection) inside character classes, nested classes and properties of strings such as emoji sequences, with stricter syntax.

interview.q: Why use RegExp.escape?
interview.a: It escapes regex special characters in user-provided text so it matches literally and safely.

topics.title: using and Explicit Resource Management
topics.summary: Automatic cleanup with using and await using, Symbol.dispose, and DisposableStack. Stage 3 proposal, supported in Node 24 and Chrome 134+.
topics.description:
**Status (be careful):** Explicit Resource Management is a **TC39 Stage 3** proposal at the time of writing, not yet part of the ECMAScript spec. V8 ships it in **Chrome 134+ and Node 24**, and TypeScript 5.2+ and Babel can compile it. Firefox and Safari support is still arriving, so check before using it in browser code.

### The idea
A `using` declaration disposes a resource automatically when the block ends, whether it ends normally, by `return`, `break` or by throwing, like Python's `with` or C#'s `using`. It replaces `try/finally` boilerplate.

```js
{
  using file = openFile();       // calls file[Symbol.dispose]() at block exit
  await using db = await connect(); // calls db[Symbol.asyncDispose]()
}
```

### Pieces
| Piece | Role |
|---|---|
| `Symbol.dispose` | method name for sync cleanup |
| `Symbol.asyncDispose` | method name for async cleanup (awaited) |
| `using x = v` | block-scoped, `const`-like binding; `null`/`undefined` allowed |
| `await using x = v` | async disposal; allowed in async functions and modules |
| `DisposableStack` / `AsyncDisposableStack` | collect many cleanups: `use()`, `adopt()`, `defer()`, `dispose()` |
| `SuppressedError` | thrown when disposal fails while another error is propagating |

### Rules
- Resources dispose in **reverse order** of declaration.
- The value must have the dispose method, otherwise a `TypeError` is thrown at the declaration.
- Errors thrown by several disposers are combined into a `SuppressedError`.
