Object.entries(arr) vs arr.entries(): the second returns an iterator, not an array.
topics.title: Array Errors: "Reduce of empty array", map/forEach not a function, not extensible
topics.summary: Common array-related messages and how to avoid them.
topics.description:
| Message | Why | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `Reduce of empty array with no initial value` | `[].reduce((a, b) => a + b)` | provide an initial value: `.reduce(fn, 0)` |
| `x.map is not a function` | `x` is an object, string, Set, NodeList, `undefined` | `Array.isArray(x)`, `Array.from(x)`, `[...x]` |
| `x.forEach is not a function` | same: `x` is not an array | convert first |
| `Array.prototype.map called on null or undefined` | `Array.prototype.map.call(null, fn)` | pass a real array |
| `Invalid array length` | negative / fractional / too large length | validate |
| `Cannot add property 1, object is not extensible` | `push` onto a frozen or sealed array | copy: `[...arr, x]` |
| `Cannot assign to read only property '0' of object '[object Array]'` | writing to a frozen array in strict mode | copy first |
| `Cannot delete property '1' of [object Array]` | `pop()` / `delete` on frozen array | copy first |
| `Invalid index : 5` | `arr.with(5, x)` out of range | check `index < length` |
| `The comparison function must be either a function or undefined: x` | `sort("x")` or `sort(null)` | pass a function |
| `Iterator value 1 is not an entry object` | `Object.fromEntries([1])` / `new Map([1])` | pass `[k, v]` pairs |
| `Spread syntax requires ...iterable[Symbol.iterator] to be a function` | spread of non-iterable in a call | convert |
| `undefined is not iterable (cannot read property Symbol(Symbol.iterator))` | destructuring/spread of `undefined` | default `= []` |

### Reduce of empty array
`reduce` without a second argument uses the first element as the starting accumulator. An empty array has no first element, so it throws. **Always give an initial value** unless you are sure the array is non-empty.

### "x.map is not a function" - API data
The most common real cause is an API returning `{ items: [...] }` or `{ error: "..." }` while you call `data.map`. Check the actual shape (`console.log(data)`), normalise at the boundary: `const list = Array.isArray(data) ? data : data.items ?? []`.

### Other array gotchas that look like errors
- `arr[arr.length]` is `undefined`, not an error (off-by-one).
- `sort()` without comparator sorts numbers as strings (`[10, 2].sort()` → `[10, 2]`).
- `arr.length = 0` clears the array in place.
keyPoints: Always pass an initial value to reduce: arr.reduce(fn, 0).
x.map is not a function nearly always means x is not an array (check the API shape).
Frozen/sealed arrays reject push/pop/assignment: copy with spread.
sort(compareFn) accepts only a function or undefined.
NodeList and Set need Array.from(...) before using map/filter.

examples.title: Trigger and fix
NodeList-like and Set values
Immutable updates avoid "not extensible"

interview.q: Why does [].reduce(fn) throw?
interview.a: Without an initial value reduce takes the first element as the accumulator; an empty array has none, so it throws TypeError: Reduce of empty array with no initial value.

interview.q: Why do I get "map is not a function" on data from an API?
interview.a: The data is not an array (often an object wrapper like { data: [...] } or an error object). Inspect the shape and normalise it.

interview.q: How do you add to a frozen array?
interview.a: You can't mutate it; create a new array with spread, concat or the immutable methods (toSorted, with, toSpliced).

pitfalls: Object.freeze is shallow - nested objects remain mutable.
Frozen state objects often cause errors only in strict-mode code paths, so tests may pass while production fails.
topics.title: Property Errors: read only, not extensible, redefine, getter-only
topics.summary: Messages from frozen, sealed and accessor properties: "Cannot assign to read only property", "Cannot add property", "Cannot redefine property".
topics.description:
Property attributes (`writable`, `configurable`, `enumerable`) and object integrity levels (`preventExtensions`, `seal`, `freeze`) control what you may do with an object. Violations are **silent in sloppy mode** but throw `TypeError` in **strict mode** (modules and classes are always strict).

| Message | Why | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `Cannot assign to read only property 'a' of object '#<Object>'` | write to a non-writable property (frozen, `writable:false`, `Math.PI`, `NaN`) | copy the object, or define it writable |
| `Cannot add property b, object is not extensible` | new key on a frozen/sealed/prevented object | add before freezing, or copy |
| `Cannot delete property 'a' of #<Object>` | delete on a frozen/sealed object, non-configurable property | do not delete |
| `Cannot set property a of #<Object> which has only a getter` | assigning to an accessor without a setter | add `set a(v)` |
| `Cannot redefine property: x` | `defineProperty` on a non-configurable property | define as `configurable: true` |
| `Cannot create property 'x' on string 'abc'` | setting a property on a primitive in strict mode | primitives are immutable |
| `Cannot assign to read only property 'length' of string 'abc'` | writing `str.length` | strings are immutable |
| `Cannot define property x, object is not extensible` | `defineProperty` on a non-extensible object | |
| `Cannot assign to read only property 'name' of function` | writing `fn.name` | use `defineProperty` |

### Where it hides
- **Redux / React state** that was frozen (Immer, `Object.freeze` in dev mode): mutate a copy instead.
- **Imported ES module bindings** are read-only: `import { x } from "./m"; x = 1` throws `Assignment to constant variable`.
- `Object.freeze` is shallow - nested objects can still change.
- Third-party objects (`window.location` pieces, `Math`, `Intl` constants).

### Sloppy vs strict
In sloppy mode `frozen.a = 2` does nothing silently, which hides bugs; in strict mode you get the TypeError. That is one more reason to use modules/strict mode.

### Check before writing
`Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(obj, "a")` shows `writable` / `configurable` / `get` / `set`. `Object.isFrozen(obj)`, `Object.isSealed`, `Object.isExtensible`.
keyPoints: Strict mode (modules, classes) throws on writes that sloppy mode ignores silently.
freeze = no add/remove/change; seal = no add/remove but values may change; preventExtensions = no add.
Accessor without a setter: assignment throws in strict mode.
Non-configurable properties cannot be redefined or deleted.
Fix by copying: { ...obj, a: 2 } or structuredClone.

examples.title: Strict-mode property errors
Inspect before writing

interview.q: Why does writing to a frozen object throw only sometimes?
interview.a: In sloppy mode the write is silently ignored; in strict mode (modules, classes, "use strict") it throws TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property.

interview.q: Does Object.freeze make nested objects immutable?
interview.a: No. It is shallow; freeze nested objects recursively or use immutable data structures.

interview.q: What is "Cannot set property x of #<Object> which has only a getter"?
interview.a: You assigned to an accessor property defined with only get. Define a setter or stop writing to it.

pitfalls: Object.create(null) objects have no toString: string concatenation throws.
"key" in array checks indexes, not values: use includes().
topics.title: Object API Errors: defineProperty, prototypes, instanceof, in, WeakMap, Proxy
topics.summary: Messages from Object.defineProperty, setPrototypeOf, the in and instanceof operators, WeakMap keys, Proxy and Reflect.
topics.description:
These errors come from the reflective / meta-programming parts of the language.

| Message | Why | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `Object.defineProperty called on non-object` | first argument is a primitive or `undefined` | pass an object |
| `Property description must be an object: 1` | third argument is not an object | pass `{ value, writable... }` |
| `Getter must be a function: 1` | `{ get: 1 }` | pass a function |
| `Invalid property descriptor. Cannot both specify accessors and a value or writable attribute` | mixing `get` with `value` | choose one style |
| `Object prototype may only be an Object or null: 1` | `Object.create(1)` / `setPrototypeOf({}, 1)` | object or `null` |
| `Cyclic __proto__ value` | prototype chain would loop | fix the chain |
| `Right-hand side of 'instanceof' is not callable` | `x instanceof {}` | use a constructor |
| `Right-hand side of 'instanceof' is not an object` | `x instanceof 5` | |
| `Cannot use 'in' operator to search for 'a' in abc` | `"a" in "abc"` (right side primitive) | `includes` / wrap in `Object()` |
| `Invalid value used as weak map key` | `new WeakMap().set(1, 1)` | keys must be objects (or non-registered symbols) |
| `Invalid value used in weak set` | `WeakSet.add("a")` | objects only |
| `WeakRef: invalid target` | `new WeakRef(1)` | object target |
| `Cannot create proxy with a non-object as target or handler` | `new Proxy({}, null)` | pass objects |
| `Cannot perform 'get' on a proxy that has been revoked` | used after `revoke()` | do not use after revoke |
| `Reflect.ownKeys called on non-object` | `Reflect` with primitive | wrap or check |
| `Cannot convert object to primitive value` | `Object.create(null)` in string/number context | define `toString` |
| `'get' on proxy: property 'x' is a read-only and non-configurable data property...` | Proxy invariant violated | respect invariants |

### Reading a descriptor error
Object descriptors have two flavours: **data** (`value`, `writable`) and **accessor** (`get`, `set`). They cannot be combined. `configurable` and `enumerable` apply to both.

### Prototype safety
`Object.create(null)` makes a truly empty dictionary: no `toString`, so `"" + obj` throws `Cannot convert object to primitive value`. Great for lookups, but remember to define what you need.

### Tip
Many of these messages name the **argument position** of the wrong value, so the fix is to read the docs for the function's parameter list and verify each argument's type.
keyPoints: defineProperty needs an object target and an object descriptor; data and accessor styles cannot mix.
Prototypes may only be objects or null.
The right side of in must be an object; the right side of instanceof must be callable.
WeakMap/WeakSet/WeakRef accept only objects (and non-registered symbols).
Proxy needs object target and handler, and cannot be used after revoke().

interview.q: What is the difference between a data and an accessor descriptor?
interview.a: A data descriptor has value and writable; an accessor descriptor has get and/or set. A single descriptor cannot contain both kinds.

interview.a: Objects (and non-registered symbols). Primitives like numbers and strings throw TypeError: Invalid value used as weak map key.

topics.title: Regex, String, Date and URL Messages
topics.summary: Invalid regular expression, matchAll/replaceAll flags, Invalid URL, Invalid Date and similar text-related errors.
topics.description:
### Regular expressions
Invalid patterns throw `SyntaxError` in the form `Invalid regular expression: /pattern/: reason` (as the newest V8 prints it).

| Reason | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `Unterminated group` | `(abc` | close with `)` |
| `Unterminated character class` | `[a-z` | close with `]` |
| `Nothing to repeat` | `*abc`, `+`, `?` at the start; `a**` | add something before the quantifier, or escape `\*` |
| `\ at end of pattern` | `new RegExp("\\")` (one backslash) | double escapes in strings: `"\\\\"` |
| `numbers out of order in {} quantifier` | `a{2,1}` | min <= max |
| `Duplicate capture group name` | `(?<n>a)(?<n>b)` | unique names |
| `Invalid flags supplied to RegExp constructor 'z'` | unknown flag | `dgimsuvy` only |
| `Invalid regular expression flags` | same, in a literal `/a/zz` | |

### String methods that reject RegExp
- `String.prototype.matchAll called with a non-global RegExp argument` - add the `g` flag.
- `String.prototype.replaceAll called with a non-global RegExp argument` - add `g` or use `replace`.
- `First argument to String.prototype.startsWith must not be a regular expression` - pass a string.

### Date and URL
| Message | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `Invalid time value` | formatting an invalid `Date` | validate |
| `Invalid Date` (not an error, a string) | `String(new Date("x"))` | check `isNaN(date)` |
| `Invalid URL` | `new URL("abc")`, missing scheme | give a base: `new URL("/path", location.origin)` |
| `Failed to construct 'URL': Invalid URL` | browser wording of the same error | same |
| `URI malformed` | bad percent-encoding | see URIError |
| `Invalid count value: -1` | `repeat(-1)` | |

### ReDoS - catastrophic backtracking
A pattern like `/(a+)+$/` against `"aaaa...b"` takes exponential time and freezes the page. It does not throw; it hangs. Avoid nested quantifiers, validate input length first, or use safer parsing.

### Escaping user input
When building a RegExp from user text, escape special characters: `s.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, "\\$&")`. Otherwise a search for `(` throws `Unterminated group`.
keyPoints: RegExp errors are SyntaxErrors with a reason after the pattern (Unterminated group, Nothing to repeat...).
matchAll and replaceAll with a regex need the g flag.
new URL(relative) needs a base; invalid input throws TypeError: Invalid URL.
Escape user input before putting it in new RegExp().
Nested quantifiers cause catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS), a hang rather than an error.

interview.a: replaceAll requires the g flag when given a RegExp, otherwise it throws TypeError. Add g or use replace for the first match.

interview.a: Characters like ( [ * + ? have special meaning. Unescaped they can throw SyntaxError or change the pattern. Escape them (or use includes for plain text).

interview.q: What is catastrophic backtracking?
interview.a: A regex with nested quantifiers can take exponential time on certain inputs, freezing the thread. Avoid ambiguous patterns and limit input length.

topics.title: Browser Messages: "Failed to execute 'x' on 'Y'", "Failed to fetch", "Illegal invocation"
topics.summary: How to read the "Failed to ..." family of messages thrown by DOM and Web APIs, and why browsers word them differently.
topics.description:
Errors thrown by **browser (Web IDL) APIs** have a recognisable shape:

`Failed to execute '<method>' on '<Interface>': <reason>`
`Failed to construct '<Interface>': <reason>`
`Failed to read the '<property>' property from '<Interface>': <reason>`
`Failed to set the '<property>' property on '<Interface>': <reason>`

They are usually a `TypeError` (wrong argument count/type) or a `DOMException` (see the DOMException reference). Read the three parts: **what you called, on which object, and why it was rejected**.

| Message | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `Failed to execute 'querySelector' on 'Document': '##' is not a valid selector.` | invalid CSS selector (DOMException SyntaxError) | escape IDs with `CSS.escape()` |
| `Failed to execute 'appendChild' on 'Node': parameter 1 is not of type 'Node'.` | passed a string/null/jQuery object | pass a Node, use `append` for text |
| `Failed to execute 'removeChild' on 'Node': The node to be removed is not a child of this node.` | wrong parent (NotFoundError) | use `node.remove()` |
| `Failed to execute 'fetch' on 'Window': Failed to parse URL from /x` | invalid URL (often in Node) | use absolute URL |
| `Failed to execute 'atob' on 'Window': The string to be decoded is not correctly encoded.` | not Base64 | validate / use URL-safe replace |
| `Failed to execute 'getImageData' on 'CanvasRenderingContext2D': The canvas has been tainted by cross-origin data.` | cross-origin image on canvas | CORS image + `crossOrigin="anonymous"` |
| `Failed to construct 'URL': Invalid URL` | no scheme / base | add base |
| `Failed to construct 'Worker': Script at 'file:///...' cannot be accessed from origin 'null'` | opened via `file://` | serve over HTTP |
| `Failed to read the 'localStorage' property from 'Window': Access is denied for this document.` | storage blocked (SecurityError) | try/catch |
| `Failed to execute 'setItem' on 'Storage': Setting the value of 'x' exceeded the quota.` | QuotaExceededError | free space |
| `TypeError: Failed to fetch` | network down, CORS blocked, DNS, mixed content, adblock | see fetch topics |
| `Illegal invocation` | method used without its object | `.bind(document)` |

### Browser differences
| Chrome | Firefox | Safari |
|---|---|---|
| `Failed to fetch` | `NetworkError when attempting to fetch resource.` | `Load failed` |
| `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'x')` | `can't access property "x", obj is undefined` | `undefined is not an object (evaluating 'obj.x')` |
| `x is not a function` | `x is not a function` | `x is not a function. (In 'x()', 'x' is undefined)` |
Never match on message text across browsers - use `name` and your own error classes.
keyPoints: The pattern is: Failed to <verb> <method> on <Interface>: <reason> - read the reason.
Chrome says "Failed to fetch", Firefox "NetworkError when attempting to fetch resource", Safari "Load failed".
Use node.remove() instead of parent.removeChild(node) to avoid NotFoundError.
Wrap storage, clipboard and permission APIs in try/catch.
Messages differ per browser - branch on e.name or your own classes.

topics.description:
Use this as a **first-aid index**. Find the message, learn the type and the first thing to check.

| # | Message | Type | First thing to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'x') | TypeError | the value BEFORE the dot is undefined |
| 2 | Cannot read properties of null (reading 'x') | TypeError | element not found / null from API |
| 3 | Cannot set properties of undefined (setting 'x') | TypeError | parent object missing |
| 4 | x is not a function | TypeError | spelling, import, await |
| 5 | x is not a constructor | TypeError | arrow function / wrong import |
| 6 | x is not defined | ReferenceError | typo, scope, missing script |
| 7 | Cannot access 'x' before initialization | ReferenceError | move declaration up (TDZ) |
| 8 | Assignment to constant variable. | TypeError | const reassigned |
| 9 | x is not iterable | TypeError | plain object / undefined in spread or for-of |
| 10 | Cannot destructure property 'a' of 'undefined' as it is undefined. | TypeError | default parameter |
| 11 | Cannot convert undefined or null to object | TypeError | Object.keys(null) |
| 12 | Unexpected token '<' (script) | SyntaxError | server sent HTML |
| 13 | Unexpected token '<', "<!DOCTYPE "... is not valid JSON | SyntaxError | API returned HTML |
| 14 | Unexpected end of JSON input | SyntaxError | empty body |
| 15 | "undefined" is not valid JSON | SyntaxError | parsing undefined |
| 16 | Converting circular structure to JSON | TypeError | object cycle |
| 17 | Maximum call stack size exceeded | RangeError | recursion without base case |
| 18 | Invalid array length | RangeError | negative / fractional length |
| 19 | Invalid time value | RangeError | invalid Date |
| 20 | toFixed() digits argument must be between 0 and 100 | RangeError | digits |
| 21 | Class constructor X cannot be invoked without 'new' | TypeError | add new |
| 22 | Must call super constructor in derived class... | ReferenceError | super() first |
| 23 | Cannot mix BigInt and other types | TypeError | convert explicitly |
| 24 | Illegal invocation | TypeError | lost this on a browser method |
| 25 | Failed to execute 'x' on 'Y' | TypeError / DOMException | read the reason |
| 26 | Unexpected identifier | SyntaxError | missing operator/comma |
| 27 | Invalid or unexpected token | SyntaxError | unterminated string, bad character |
| 28 | missing ) after argument list | SyntaxError | check commas/parentheses |
| 29 | Unexpected end of input | SyntaxError | unclosed bracket |
| 30 | Cannot use import statement outside a module | SyntaxError | type="module" |
| 31 | await is only valid in async functions... | SyntaxError | add async |
| 32 | Identifier 'x' has already been declared | SyntaxError | duplicate let/const |
| 33 | Illegal return statement | SyntaxError | return outside function |
| 34 | Rest parameter must be last formal parameter | SyntaxError | reorder |
| 35 | Invalid regular expression: ... | SyntaxError | regex syntax |
| 36 | Reduce of empty array with no initial value | TypeError | pass initial value |
| 37 | Object.defineProperty called on non-object | TypeError | first arg object |
| 38 | Cannot redefine property: x | TypeError | configurable false |
| 39 | Cannot assign to read only property 'x' of object | TypeError | frozen / strict mode |
| 40 | Failed to fetch | TypeError | CORS, offline, mixed content |
| 41 | Uncaught (in promise) | any | missing catch on a promise |
| 42 | ResizeObserver loop completed with undelivered notifications. | benign | layout loop; usually safe to ignore |

### Workflow for any message
1. Read the **type** (what class of problem), then the **message**, then the **file:line** in the stack.
2. Reproduce with the smallest input; log the value just before the failing line.
3. Fix the *cause* (missing data, wrong type), not the symptom (try/catch).

Most TypeErrors are "the value before the dot is not what you assumed".

interview.q: What happens if both try and finally contain return?

topics.title: throw, Rethrow and Error Propagation
topics.summary: How throw unwinds the call stack, when to rethrow, and how to keep the original stack trace.
topics.description:
### throw
`throw expression` stops the current function immediately. The engine **unwinds the call stack** frame by frame looking for a `catch`. If it reaches the top without finding one the error is **uncaught**: browsers log `Uncaught Error: ...` and fire the global `error` event; Node.js prints the stack and exits with code 1.

You can throw any value, but throw `Error` objects (or subclasses) so that you get `name`, `message` and `stack`.

### Propagation
Errors travel upward through callers; every function on the way is *skipped*, which is why you rarely need `try/catch` everywhere. **Catch where you can do something useful**: show a message, retry, fall back, or add context. Low-level functions should usually throw; the top-level code (UI event handler, request handler, `main()`) decides what to do.

### Rethrow patterns
| Pattern | Code | When |
|---|---|---|
| Pure rethrow | `catch (e) { cleanup(); throw e; }` | you only need side effects; stack is preserved |
| Conditional rethrow | `if (!(e instanceof Expected)) throw e;` | handle one kind only |
| Wrap and rethrow | `throw new AppError("Load failed", { cause: e })` | add context, keep the original in `cause` |
| Log and rethrow | `console.error(e); throw e;` | at boundaries only; risk of duplicate logs |

`throw e` keeps the **original stack** (the stack is captured when the Error is *created*, not when thrown). Creating a new error loses the original stack unless you pass `cause`.

### throw in expressions (workaround)
There is no throw expression yet; use a helper: `const required = (name) => { throw new Error(name + " is required"); };` then `function f(a = required("a")) {}`.

### Errors in different places
| Where | How it surfaces |
|---|---|
| Synchronous code | caught by surrounding `try/catch` |
| `async` function | becomes a **rejected promise** |
| Promise callback (`then`) | rejects the derived promise |
| Event handler / timer | global `error` event / uncaught exception |
keyPoints: throw unwinds the stack until a catch is found; otherwise the error is uncaught.
Throw Error objects; the stack is recorded at creation time.
Catch only where you can act; let low-level functions throw.
Rethrow with throw e to keep the stack, or wrap with { cause } to add context.
In async functions a throw becomes a rejected promise.

interview.q: Where is the stack trace of an error captured?
interview.a: When the Error object is created (new Error), not when it is thrown. So rethrowing the same object keeps the original stack.

interview.q: Why wrap an error with cause?
interview.a: To add context (what operation failed) while preserving the low-level error and its stack for debugging.

interview.q: What happens to an error thrown inside an async function?
interview.a: The function returns a rejected promise with that error; it must be handled with await in try/catch or .catch().

topics.title: Custom Error Classes
topics.summary: Create your own Error subclasses with names, codes and extra data - and avoid the common pitfalls.
topics.description:
Built-in types cannot express your domain: "user not found", "payment declined", "validation failed". **Custom errors** give each situation a class that callers can test with `instanceof` and that carries useful data.

### Basic pattern
```js
class AppError extends Error {
  constructor(message, options = {}) {
    super(message, options);              // passes cause along
    this.name = this.constructor.name;     // "AppError" / subclass name
    this.code = options.code;
    if (Error.captureStackTrace) Error.captureStackTrace(this, this.constructor); // V8: clean stack
  }
}
class NotFoundError extends AppError {}
```

### Details that matter
- Call `super(message)` first; it sets `message` and the `stack`.
- Set `this.name` - otherwise it stays `"Error"` in logs. Using `this.constructor.name` breaks after **minification** (names are mangled) - set a literal string for server-visible names.
- `Error.captureStackTrace(this, ctor)` is V8-only (Chrome, Node, Edge). It hides the constructor frames from the trace.
- Add **machine-readable** fields: `code` (`"E_NOT_FOUND"`), `status` (`404`), `details`.
- `JSON.stringify(err)` returns `{}` for errors; implement `toJSON()` to log/send them.
- Use the class hierarchy to build categories: `AppError → HttpError → NotFoundError`.
- `instanceof` works for classes in the same realm; for cross-realm checks add a `Symbol.hasInstance` or compare `name` / `code`.
- In old ES5 transpilers (Babel 5, TypeScript targeting ES5) `extends Error` broke `instanceof`; with modern targets this is solved. If needed call `Object.setPrototypeOf(this, new.target.prototype)`.

### When to create a class
When callers need to *react differently* (retry vs show message vs report). Do not create one class per message string. Typical set: `ValidationError`, `NotFoundError`, `AuthError`, `NetworkError` (with `status`), `TimeoutError`.

Set name explicitly - it defaults to "Error".
Add code/status/details fields for programmatic handling.
Implement toJSON because JSON.stringify(err) gives {}.
Error.captureStackTrace is V8-only: feature-test it.

interview.a: name defaults to "Error" (inherited), so logs and err.toString() would not show your type. Setting name makes the type visible without checking the constructor.

interview.q: What does Error.captureStackTrace do?
interview.a: A V8 API that records a stack trace on the given object and can omit frames above a constructor function, so your error class constructor is not part of the trace.

interview.q: When should you create a custom error class?
interview.a: When callers need to handle the situation differently (retry, show a message, log as bug). Use a code or status field for details instead of a new class per message.

topics.title: error.cause: Wrapping and Chaining Errors
topics.summary: Keep the root cause while adding context at every layer, then log the whole chain.
topics.description:
Real failures happen in layers: *the database failed* → *the repository could not load the user* → *the request handler could not render the page*. If every layer rethrows a new Error with only its own message, the root cause is lost. The ES2022 **cause** option chains them:

```js
try {
  await db.query(sql);
} catch (err) {
  throw new Error("Could not load user " + id, { cause: err });
}
```

### Rules
- `cause` can be **any value**, but usually the original error object.
- It is stored as a non-enumerable own property: `err.cause`.
- Use it at **layer boundaries**: translate a low-level error into a domain error, but keep the low-level one.
- The new message should say **what you were trying to do** ("Could not load user 7"), not repeat the inner message.
- The inner error keeps its own `stack`, so debugging shows both places.

### Reading a chain
```js
function* chain(err) { while (err) { yield err; err = err.cause; } }
```
Logging libraries and DevTools show the cause automatically: Chrome prints `Caused by: ...` below the stack; Node's `console.error` prints `[cause]: ...`.

### What not to do
- Do not append the inner message into the outer message (`"Failed: " + e.message`) - that loses type, stack and code.
- Do not create very long chains of identical messages; each layer should add distinct information.
- Avoid cycles (an error that is its own cause) - walking the chain would loop forever; guard with a `Set`.

### Support
Chrome 93+, Firefox 91+, Safari 15+, Node 16.9+. For older environments define a manual `this.cause = cause` in your custom base class.
keyPoints: new Error(message, { cause: original }) keeps the root cause.
cause is non-enumerable; read err.cause, not Object.keys.
Add context at layer boundaries (what you were trying to do).

interview.q: What problem does error.cause solve?
interview.a: It preserves the original error when you translate or wrap it, so higher layers get a meaningful message and developers still see the root cause and its stack.

interview.q: How do you print the whole chain?

topics.title: Handling Multiple Errors: AggregateError, Promise.any and Collecting Failures
topics.summary: Report all failures at once: validation collectors, Promise.any, and turning allSettled results into one AggregateError.
topics.description:
Sometimes the correct response to failure is not to stop at the first problem, but to **collect all of them**.

### Where multiple errors appear
1. **Validation** - show every invalid field at once, not one per submit.
2. **Parallel tasks** - upload 5 files; report which failed.
3. **Redundant sources** - try 3 mirrors; fail only if all fail (`Promise.any`).
4. **Cleanup** - closing several resources where more than one close can fail.

### Tools
| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `new AggregateError(errors, message)` | one error holding `err.errors` |
| `Promise.any` | first success wins; rejects with `AggregateError` when all fail |
| `Promise.allSettled` | never rejects; returns `{status, value/reason}` per promise |
| plain array | collect errors yourself and throw at the end |

### The collector pattern
```js
const errors = [];
for (const item of items) {
  try { process(item); } catch (e) { errors.push(e); }
}
if (errors.length) throw new AggregateError(errors, errors.length + " items failed");
```
This is the *"continue on error, report at the end"* strategy, common in batch jobs, linters and form validation.

### allSettled → AggregateError
```js
const results = await Promise.allSettled(tasks);
const failed = results.filter(r => r.status === "rejected").map(r => r.reason);
if (failed.length) throw new AggregateError(failed, "Some tasks failed");
```

### Design tips
- Decide per feature: **fail fast** (`Promise.all`) when one failure makes the rest pointless; **collect** when partial success is useful.
- Keep the `errors` array items meaningful (include which input failed, e.g. `cause` or `item` field).
- Log the individual errors, not just the aggregate message ("All promises were rejected" says nothing).

Promise.allSettled never rejects; convert failures to an AggregateError if needed.

Choose fail-fast vs collect-all deliberately.

interview.q: When would you collect errors instead of failing fast?
interview.a: When partial results are valuable or users benefit from seeing every problem: form validation, batch imports, linters, parallel uploads.

interview.a: all rejects on the first failure and discards other results; allSettled waits for everything and returns an array describing each outcome, never rejecting.

interview.q: What is inside an AggregateError from Promise.any?
interview.a: An errors array with the rejection reasons in input order and the message "All promises were rejected".

topics.title: Error Handling Strategies: Fail Fast, Wrap, Retry, Fallback
topics.summary: Choose the right response to each failure: fail fast, add context, retry with backoff, fall back or degrade gracefully.
topics.description:
Catching an error is not a strategy. Decide **what the program should do** for each kind of failure.

| Strategy | Use when | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Fail fast** | invalid state would corrupt data or hide bugs (programmer errors) | throw on invalid argument, `assert` |
| **Wrap with context** | crossing a layer boundary | `new Error("Load user failed", {cause})` |
| **Retry** | *transient* failures: network blips, `503`, `429`, timeouts | retry 3 times with exponential backoff + jitter |
| **Fallback / default** | non-critical feature | cached value, default avatar, empty list |
| **Graceful degradation** | part of the page can fail | show widget error, keep the page |
| **Circuit breaker** | a dependency is down | stop calling for N seconds |
| **Report and continue** | background or analytics tasks | log to monitoring |
| **Crash and restart** | unrecoverable server state | process manager restarts |

### Operational vs programmer errors
- **Operational** errors are expected in a correct program: network down, file missing, invalid user input. Handle them.
- **Programmer** errors are bugs: `undefined is not a function`, wrong arguments. Do **not** retry or hide them - fix the code, and let tests/monitoring find them.

### Retry rules
1. Retry only *idempotent* operations (GET, or POST with an idempotency key).
2. Retry only *transient* errors (network error, 5xx, 429, 408), never 4xx validation errors.
3. Use **exponential backoff** (200ms, 400ms, 800ms...) with **jitter** (random part) to avoid thundering herds.
4. Set a maximum attempts / total time. Respect `Retry-After`.

### Timeouts
Every network call needs a timeout (`AbortSignal.timeout(5000)`), otherwise "no error" can mean "hangs forever".

### User-facing messages
Show a short friendly message ("Could not save. Try again."), log technical details separately, and never show raw stack traces or SQL errors to users.
keyPoints: Decide per error: fail fast, wrap, retry, fallback, degrade or report.
Retry only transient failures of idempotent operations, with backoff and jitter.
Do not retry or swallow programmer errors; fix them.
Always set timeouts on network calls.
Separate user messages from technical logs.

interview.q: What is the difference between operational and programmer errors?
interview.a: Operational errors come from the environment (network, disk, invalid input) and must be handled. Programmer errors are bugs (wrong types, undefined access) and should be fixed, not retried or swallowed.

interview.q: Why add jitter to exponential backoff?
interview.a: Without randomness, many clients retry at the same moments and hit the recovering server together. Jitter spreads retries out.

interview.q: Which operations are safe to retry?
interview.a: Idempotent ones (GET, PUT, DELETE, or POST with an idempotency key) and only for transient failures such as network errors, 5xx, 429 or 408.

topics.title: Validation Errors, Assertions and Invariants
topics.summary: Validate input at the boundary, report all problems with useful messages, and use assertions for impossible states.
topics.description:
### Validate at the boundary
Data arrives from users, URLs, storage, APIs and other modules. Validate it **once, at the edge**; inside the app, trust the validated shape.

Good validation errors are:
- **Specific** - say which field and what rule: `"age must be an integer between 0 and 120, got 'abc'"`.
- **Structured** - `{ field, code, message }` so the UI can highlight the field.
- **Complete** - collect all problems, not just the first one (see AggregateError).
- **Safe** - never echo secrets (passwords, tokens).

### ValidationError class
```js
class ValidationError extends Error {
  constructor(issues) {
    super(issues.length + " validation issue(s)");
    this.name = "ValidationError";
    this.issues = issues;          // [{ field, message }]
  }
}
```

### Assertions (invariants)
An **assertion** states "this must be true if the program is correct". If it is false, it is a **bug**, not a user mistake.
```js
function assert(condition, message = "Assertion failed") {
  if (!condition) throw new Error(message);
}
```
- Use assertions for **programmer errors** and internal invariants (`assert(Array.isArray(list))` in a private function).
- Use validation errors for **user/external** data.
- `console.assert(cond, msg)` only logs - it does not throw.
- Node has `assert` (`node:assert`); in the browser write your own or use libraries (Zod, Yup, Valibot, Joi, Ajv).

### Type checks
`typeof x === "string"`, `Array.isArray`, `Number.isFinite`, `Number.isInteger`, `x instanceof Date && !isNaN(x)`. Beware `typeof null === "object"` and `NaN`.

### Exhaustiveness
In a `switch` over known values add a default that throws: `default: throw new Error("Unhandled case: " + x)` - future values then fail loudly.
keyPoints: Validate untrusted data once at the boundary and return structured issues.
Collect all validation problems; each with field and message.
Assertions are for impossible states (bugs), validation for bad input.
console.assert logs only; it does not throw.
Add a throwing default to switch statements over closed sets.

interview.q: When should you use an assertion instead of a validation error?
interview.a: Assertions check internal invariants that only a bug can violate. External or user data can legitimately be wrong, so it gets validation with friendly structured errors.

interview.q: Does console.assert throw?
interview.a: No. It logs an error message to the console when the condition is false and execution continues.

interview.q: Why validate again on the server?
interview.a: Client-side checks can be bypassed; the server is the trust boundary and must never assume validated input.

interview.q: Result pattern vs exceptions - when to choose which?
interview.a: Use Results for expected, recoverable failures that the immediate caller should handle (validation, parsing, not found). Use exceptions for unexpected failures and when handling happens far from the failure.

interview.q: What is the downside of returning [error, data]?
interview.a: Nothing forces the caller to check error, and both values can be misused. A tagged union (ok flag) with type checking is safer.

interview.q: What is Either?
interview.a: A type with two cases, Left (failure) and Right (success), plus operations like map and flatMap that only run on Right.

topics.title: Global Handlers, Logging and Monitoring
topics.summary: Catch what try/catch cannot: window.onerror, unhandledrejection, error boundaries, Node process events and error reporting.
topics.description:
Some errors escape every `try/catch`. Production apps add a **safety net** that records them.

### Browser
| Hook | Fires for |
|---|---|
| `window.addEventListener("error", e => ...)` / `window.onerror` | uncaught synchronous exceptions, **resource load errors** (img/script; use capture phase `true`) |
| `window.addEventListener("unhandledrejection", e => ...)` | promise rejected with no handler; `e.reason` is the error; `e.preventDefault()` silences the console |
| `window.addEventListener("rejectionhandled", ...)` | a late handler was attached |
| `securitypolicyviolation` | CSP violations |
| `console.error` hooks, `reportError(err)` | manual reporting through the same path as uncaught errors |

### Node.js
- `process.on("uncaughtException", (err, origin) => ...)` - log, then **exit**; the process may be in an unknown state.
- `process.on("unhandledRejection", (reason, promise) => ...)` - since Node 15 unhandled rejections crash by default.
- Frameworks: Express error middleware `(err, req, res, next)`.

### Error boundaries (React concept)
A component that catches errors thrown **while rendering** its children and shows a fallback UI instead of unmounting the whole app. They are class components using `static getDerivedStateFromError` and `componentDidCatch(error, info)` (or the `react-error-boundary` library). They do **not** catch event-handler, async or server errors.

### What to log
Message, stack, error type, **release/version**, URL, user id (anonymised), browser, breadcrumbs (last clicks/requests). Services such as Sentry, Datadog or Rollbar collect this and use **source maps** to de-minify stack traces.

### Good practices
1. **Rate-limit and de-duplicate** reports (one error in a loop can send thousands).
2. Use `navigator.sendBeacon` so reports survive page unload.
3. Never log secrets or personal data; scrub URLs and bodies.
4. Ignore known noise (browser extensions, `ResizeObserver loop`, "Script error.").
5. Show users a friendly fallback, not a blank page.
keyPoints: window error + unhandledrejection catch what try/catch cannot.
Node: uncaughtException/unhandledRejection are for logging and graceful shutdown, not recovery.
React error boundaries catch render errors only, not event handlers or async code.
De-duplicate and rate-limit reports; use sendBeacon; scrub personal data.
Upload source maps so minified stacks are readable in monitoring tools.

interview.q: Why do you need unhandledrejection if you use window.onerror?
interview.a: Rejected promises without a handler do not raise a normal error event; they fire unhandledrejection instead.

interview.q: What do React error boundaries not catch?
interview.a: Errors in event handlers, asynchronous code (setTimeout, promises), server-side rendering and errors thrown in the boundary itself.

interview.q: Why should a Node process exit after uncaughtException?
interview.a: The error left the program in an unknown state (open handles, half-written data). Log it and restart under a process manager.

topics.title: Reading Stack Traces and Source Maps
topics.summary: Understand each line of err.stack, async frames, minified code and how source maps restore the original file and line.
topics.description:
A **stack trace** lists the functions that were active when the error object was created, from the most recent call at the top to the entry point at the bottom.

```text
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')
    at getName (app.js:12:20)
    at renderUser (app.js:25:10)
    at HTMLButtonElement.<anonymous> (app.js:40:5)
```

### How to read it
1. **First line** = `name: message`.
2. **Each `at` line** = function name, file, line, **column**.
3. The **first frame in your own code** (not in a library, not in `node_modules`) is usually where to start.
4. `<anonymous>` = an unnamed function; name your callbacks to get readable traces.
5. Frames such as `at new Promise (<anonymous>)`, `at async fn` show async chains (V8 "async stack traces").

### Differences between engines
| Engine | Frame format |
|---|---|
| V8 (Chrome, Node, Edge) | `at fn (file:line:col)` |
| Firefox / Safari | `fn@file:line:col` |
The format is **not standardised**; use a library (e.g. `error-stack-parser`) if you must parse it.

### Limits
`Error.stackTraceLimit` (V8, default 10) controls how many frames are kept. Set `Infinity` while debugging deep call stacks. `Error.captureStackTrace(obj)` creates a stack on any object.

### Source maps
Production code is minified and bundled, so a stack like `at t (main.4f3a.js:1:53284)` is useless. A **source map** (`main.4f3a.js.map`) maps each position back to the original file, line and name.
- Build tools (Vite, webpack, esbuild) emit them with `sourcemap: true`.
- Browsers load them in DevTools via the comment `//# sourceMappingURL=main.js.map`.
- Monitoring services (Sentry etc.) use **uploaded** maps so you do not need to expose them publicly.
- Hidden source maps (`"hidden-source-map"`) are not referenced in the bundle, so public users cannot read your original source.
- The map must match the **exact build** (use content-hash filenames and release tags).

### Async stack traces
Chrome DevTools can show "async" frames across `await` and promise chains. Always `await` (or return) promises: a lost promise loses its stack.
keyPoints: Read from the top: message first, then the first frame in your own code.
Format differs per engine (V8: "at fn (file:line:col)", Firefox/Safari: "fn@file:line:col").

The stack is captured where the error is created, not where it is caught.

interview.q: What is a source map?

topics.title: Debugging Workflow: Console, Breakpoints, debugger and DevTools
topics.summary: A repeatable method to find a bug: reproduce, isolate, inspect with console and breakpoints, fix, and verify.
topics.description:
Debugging is a **process**, not a guess.

### The loop
1. **Reproduce** reliably. Write down the exact steps and the input.
2. **Read the error**: type, message, first frame in your code.
3. **Isolate**: reduce the problem (comment out code, binary search, minimal example).
4. **Hypothesise** the cause, then **test** it with a log or breakpoint.
5. **Fix** the cause, not the symptom.
6. **Verify** and add a test so it cannot return.

### Console tools
| Method | Use |
|---|---|
| `console.log(obj)` | quick values (objects are live references - expand shows *current* state; use `structuredClone` or `JSON.stringify` for a snapshot) |
| `console.error / warn / info` | severity filters |
| `console.table(arr)` | arrays of objects as a table |
| `console.dir(obj, {depth})` | deep objects |
| `console.group / groupEnd` | nested output |
| `console.time("x") / timeEnd("x")` | measure duration |
| `console.trace()` | print the current call stack |
| `console.assert(cond, msg)` | log only when false |
| `console.count(label)` | how many times a line runs |
Label logs (`console.log("user:", user)`) and use `%o`, `%c` formats if needed.

### Breakpoints (DevTools: Sources panel)
- **Line breakpoint** - click the line number; **conditional** (right click: `i > 100`); **logpoint** (prints without editing code).
- `debugger;` statement - pauses when DevTools is open. Remove before commit.
- **Pause on exceptions** (the pause icon): stops at the throw, including *caught* exceptions.
- **DOM breakpoints** (subtree/attribute/removal), **XHR/fetch breakpoints**, **event listener breakpoints** (click, keydown).
- While paused: **Scope** (variables), **Call stack**, **Watch** expressions, step over (F10), into (F11), out (Shift+F11), continue (F8).
- **Blackbox** library scripts so stepping skips them.

### Other panels
**Network** (status, payload, headers, timing, "Preserve log"), **Application** (storage, service workers), **Performance** and **Memory** (profiles), **Console** "Issues" tab (CORS, CSP, deprecations).

### Node.js
`node --inspect-brk app.js` then attach DevTools (`chrome://inspect`) or use the VS Code debugger with a launch configuration.

### Tricks
Binary search through `git bisect`, rubber-duck explanation, checking assumptions (is the value really what I think? is the code even running? is it the latest build, not cache?).

Use console.table/dir/time/trace/assert, not just console.log.

Check the Network tab and Issues tab for CORS/HTTP problems.

topics.title: Error Handling Anti-patterns
topics.summary: The mistakes that make bugs invisible: empty catch, swallowing, string throws, over-catching and more - with fixes.
topics.description:
These habits turn small bugs into hours of debugging.

| Anti-pattern | Why it hurts | Better |
|---|---|---|
| **Empty catch** `catch (e) {}` | error disappears; app continues in a broken state | handle it, or at least log; comment why ignoring is safe |
| **Log and continue** only `console.log(e)` | user sees nothing, logs unseen | show feedback, report to monitoring |
| **Catch-all around everything** | hides unrelated bugs | small try blocks, rethrow unknown errors |
| **Throwing strings** `throw "bad"` | no stack, no type | `throw new Error("bad")` |
| **Rethrow with new message only** `throw new Error(e.message)` | loses stack and type | `{ cause: e }` |
| **Return in finally** | swallows errors | cleanup only |
| **Exceptions for control flow** | slow, confusing | use return values / conditions |
| **Matching message text** | brittle across versions/locales | classes, `code`, `name` |
| **Forgotten await / floating promise** | rejection never caught | `await`, `.catch`, lint rule `no-floating-promises` |
| **async inside forEach** `items.forEach(async ...)` | errors and completion not awaited | `for...of` or `Promise.all(map(...))` |
| **try/catch around async call without await** | does not catch | `await` inside try |
| **Promise constructor anti-pattern** wrapping an existing promise in `new Promise` | errors lost if you forget reject | return the promise |
| **Showing raw errors to users** | leaks internals/security info | friendly message + log id |
| **Catching `Error` for validation of known data** | slow and noisy | validate first |
| **Retrying everything** | duplicates payments, hammers servers | retry only idempotent + transient |
| **Not cleaning up** | leaks (timers, connections) | `finally` |
| **Swallowing `unhandledrejection` with `preventDefault()` everywhere** | hides real bugs | only after reporting |
| **Using `window.onerror` return true** blindly | hides errors in dev | report, keep default behaviour in dev |

### Checklist for each catch block
1. What exactly can fail here, and do I **expect** it?
2. Can I **recover**? If not, rethrow (with context).
3. Does the **user** know something went wrong?
4. Is the error **recorded** somewhere with enough context?
5. Did I **clean up** resources (finally)?
6. Is the error handling **tested** (failing path)?
keyPoints: Never leave a catch block empty without a comment explaining why.
Handle what you expect, rethrow what you do not.
Do not throw strings; keep stack and type when wrapping (cause).
Await promises; avoid async callbacks in forEach.
Test the failure paths, not only the happy path.

interview.q: Why is async inside forEach a problem?
interview.a: forEach ignores returned promises. The loop finishes immediately, errors are not propagated and you cannot await completion. Use for...of or Promise.all with map.

interview.q: What should every catch block answer?
interview.a: What failed, can I recover, does the user know, is it logged with context, and is cleanup done.

topics.title: Promise Rejections and "Uncaught (in promise)"
topics.summary: How promises fail, what an unhandled rejection is, and how errors flow through then, catch and finally.
topics.description:
A promise is **rejected** when the function passed to `new Promise` calls `reject(reason)`, when it `throw`s, or when an `async` function throws. A rejection is an *asynchronous error*: it is not delivered to `try/catch` around the call, but to a **rejection handler**.

### Where rejections are handled
```js
promise
  .then(onFulfilled, onRejected)   // 2nd argument handles only the previous promise
  .catch(onRejected)               // handles errors from everything above
  .finally(cleanup);               // runs either way; passes the result through
```

### Error flow rules
1. A `throw` inside `then` turns the **returned** promise into a rejection.
2. `catch` **recovers**: whatever it returns becomes a fulfilled value for the next `then`. Rethrow (`throw e`) to keep failing.
3. `finally` cannot change the value, but a throw inside `finally` replaces the result with the new rejection.
4. Always `return` the inner promise in a `then`, or errors escape the chain ("floating promise").

### Unhandled rejections
If a rejected promise has **no handler** by the time the microtask queue drains, the host reports it:
- Browser console: `Uncaught (in promise) Error: message` and the `unhandledrejection` event (`event.reason`).
- Node.js 15+: prints the error and **terminates** the process (`ERR_UNHANDLED_REJECTION`).
- If a handler is attached later, a `rejectionhandled` event fires.

### Common causes
- Calling an async function without `await` or `.catch` (**fire and forget**).
- `new Promise(async (resolve) => { ... })` - a throw inside the async executor is never connected to the promise.
- Forgetting `return` inside `then`.
- `setTimeout(() => { throw ... })` is not a promise error at all - it is an uncaught exception.

### Fix
End every chain with a `catch` (or `await` in a `try/catch`), and add a global `unhandledrejection` listener as a safety net that reports to your logging service.
keyPoints: A rejection is delivered to .catch / the second then argument, not to a surrounding try/catch (unless awaited).
catch returns a fulfilled promise: rethrow if you cannot handle the error.
"Uncaught (in promise)" = a rejected promise with no handler.
Node 15+ crashes on unhandled rejections; browsers fire unhandledrejection.
Always return promises inside then and end chains with catch.

examples.title: Error flow through a chain
examples.code:
Promise.resolve(1)
  .then((v) => { console.log("then 1:", v); throw new Error("boom in then"); })
  .then(() => console.log("skipped"))
  .catch((e) => { console.log("catch:", e.message); return "recovered"; })
  .then((v) => console.log("then after catch:", v))
  .finally(() => console.log("finally runs"))
  .then(() => { throw new TypeError("second failure"); })
  .catch((e) => console.log("caught again:", e.name));

interview.q: What does "Uncaught (in promise)" mean?
interview.a: A promise was rejected and no rejection handler was attached, so the error reached the global unhandledrejection handling.

interview.q: Does catch() stop the chain?
interview.a: No. catch returns a new promise that fulfils with the handler's return value, so later thens run. Rethrow to keep the chain rejected.

interview.q: Why is new Promise(async ...) an anti-pattern?
interview.a: Errors thrown in the async executor reject the executor's own promise, not the outer one, so they are lost and the promise may never settle.

interview.q: What is the difference between return promise and return await promise in a try block?
interview.a: Plain return passes the promise to the caller before it settles, so the local catch will not run on rejection. return await waits inside the try, so the catch handles it.

interview.q: Why shouldn't you use async callbacks in forEach?
interview.a: forEach ignores the returned promises, so it does not wait and errors become unhandled. Use for...of with await or Promise.all(items.map(...)).

interview.q: How do you handle errors in async event handlers?

Promise.all loses information about the other failures.
topics.title: Promise.all vs allSettled vs race vs any: Error Behaviour
topics.summary: Pick the right combinator by how it treats failures: fail-fast, collect all, first settled or first success.
topics.description:
The four combinators differ mainly in **how they react to rejection**.

| Combinator | Fulfils when | Rejects when | Rejection value |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Promise.all` | all fulfil → array of values | **first** rejection (fail-fast) | that single reason |
| `Promise.allSettled` | all settle → array of `{status, value/reason}` | **never** | - |
| `Promise.race` | first promise settles (fulfilled) | first settled promise is rejected | that reason |
| `Promise.any` | **first fulfilment** | **all** reject (or empty array) | `AggregateError` |

### Choosing
- Need everything or nothing (page needs user **and** settings)? → `all`.
- Want a report for every item (bulk upload, health checks)? → `allSettled`.
- Timeouts: `race([request, timeout])` (but also abort the request!).
- Fastest of redundant sources (mirrors, CDNs)? → `any`.

### Details
- With `all`, the other promises **keep running** after one rejection. Their later rejections are handled (no warning) but side effects still happen. Use an `AbortController` to cancel.
- `all` preserves **input order** in the result, not completion order.
- `race([])` never settles; `all([])` resolves `[]`; `any([])` rejects with an empty `AggregateError`.
- Non-promise values are treated as already fulfilled.
- `allSettled` results: `{ status: "fulfilled", value }` or `{ status: "rejected", reason }` - **reason is whatever was thrown**, not necessarily an Error.

### Handling allSettled results
```js
const results = await Promise.allSettled(tasks);
const ok = results.filter(r => r.status === "fulfilled").map(r => r.value);
const failed = results.filter(r => r.status === "rejected").map(r => r.reason);
```
Use `failed.length` to decide: show partial results, retry only the failed ones, or throw an `AggregateError`.
keyPoints: all = fail-fast; allSettled = never rejects; race = first to settle; any = first success.
Promise.any rejects with AggregateError only if everything fails.
Other promises keep running after all/race settle: cancel with AbortController.
allSettled results have status and value or reason.
Empty arrays: all resolves [], any rejects, race never settles.

examples.title: Side by side
Timeout with race and cancellation
Separate successes and failures

interview.q: When would you pick allSettled over all?
interview.a: When partial success is acceptable and you need to know the outcome of every promise, such as batch uploads or multi-source dashboards.

interview.q: What does Promise.race do with a rejection?
interview.a: If the first promise to settle is rejected, race rejects with that reason. Later results are ignored.

interview.q: Does Promise.all cancel the remaining promises after one rejects?
interview.a: No. They continue running; only their results are ignored. Use AbortController to actually cancel work.

topics.title: fetch Errors: Network Failure vs HTTP Status
topics.summary: fetch only rejects on network-level failure. A 404 or 500 is a successful promise - check response.ok yourself.
topics.description:
The most important fetch fact: **`fetch()` does not reject on HTTP error statuses.** It rejects only when the request could not be completed at all.

| Situation | What fetch does |
|---|---|
| Server replied `200` | resolves, `response.ok === true` |
| Server replied `404` / `500` | **resolves**, `response.ok === false`, `response.status` is set |
| Network down, DNS failure, connection refused, CORS blocked, mixed content blocked, adblocker, invalid URL | **rejects** with `TypeError` (`Failed to fetch` in Chrome) |
| `AbortController.abort()` | rejects with `DOMException AbortError` |
| `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` elapsed | rejects with `DOMException TimeoutError` |
| Body parse fails (`res.json()` on HTML) | `res.json()` rejects with `SyntaxError` |

### Browser wording of the network TypeError
Chrome `TypeError: Failed to fetch` · Firefox `TypeError: NetworkError when attempting to fetch resource.` · Safari `TypeError: Load failed` · Node `TypeError: fetch failed` (with `cause`). The **reason is hidden on purpose** for security: open the Network and Console tabs to see whether it is CORS, DNS, offline or blocked.

### Robust wrapper
```js
class HttpError extends Error {
  constructor(res) { super("HTTP " + res.status + " " + res.statusText); this.name = "HttpError"; this.status = res.status; this.response = res; }
}
async function request(url, options) {
  const res = await fetch(url, options);       // TypeError on network failure
  if (!res.ok) throw new HttpError(res);       // convert HTTP errors to exceptions
  return res;
}
```
Then callers use `catch (e)` with `e instanceof HttpError` vs `e instanceof TypeError` vs `e.name === "AbortError"`.

### Other things to remember
- The body can be read **once** (`Body is unusable` / `body stream already read`): use `res.clone()` before reading twice.
- `204 No Content` has no body: do not call `res.json()`.
- Cookies are not sent cross-origin unless `credentials: "include"` (and CORS allows it).
- Check `navigator.onLine` only as a hint; the request is the real test.
keyPoints: fetch resolves for 404/500: always check response.ok or status.
It rejects with TypeError for network-level failures (offline, CORS, DNS, mixed content).
The message differs by browser; the reason is intentionally hidden - use DevTools.
A response body can be consumed only once; use clone().
Wrap fetch to throw an HttpError for non-OK responses.

interview.q: Does fetch reject on a 404 response?
interview.a: No. It resolves with response.ok === false. You must check ok or status and throw yourself.

interview.q: What causes "TypeError: Failed to fetch"?
interview.a: A network-level failure: offline, DNS error, server unreachable, CORS block, mixed content, certificate error or a blocking extension. The browser hides the exact reason from JavaScript.

interview.q: Why does reading a response twice fail?
interview.a: The body is a stream that can be consumed once. Use response.clone() before reading, or read it once and reuse the result.

pitfalls: Redirecting to login on 403 creates login loops for users who simply lack permission.
Retrying POST without an idempotency key can create duplicates.
topics.title: Handling 401, 403, 404, 429 and 500 Responses
topics.summary: What each common HTTP error means for your UI and what the client should do: login, hide, retry, back off, report.
topics.description:
Turn status codes into **decisions**, not just messages.

| Status | Meaning | Client should |
|---|---|---|
| `400 Bad Request` | invalid syntax/params | fix the request (bug) or show field errors |
| `401 Unauthorized` | not authenticated / token expired | refresh token once, else go to login |
| `403 Forbidden` | authenticated but not allowed | show "no permission"; do **not** retry; do not redirect to login |
| `404 Not Found` | resource does not exist | show not-found UI, or treat as empty result |
| `408 Request Timeout` | server waited too long | retry |
| `409 Conflict` | version/state conflict | reload data, merge, ask user |
| `413 Payload Too Large` | file/body too big | tell user the limit |
| `422 Unprocessable Entity` | validation failed | show per-field errors from the body |
| `429 Too Many Requests` | rate limited | wait for `Retry-After`, back off; slow down |
| `500 Internal Server Error` | server bug | show generic error, report; retry only if idempotent |
| `502/503/504` | gateway / overloaded / timeout | retry with backoff; show "try later" |

### Token refresh without a stampede
When several requests fail with `401` at once, refresh the token **once** and let the others wait for the same promise ("single-flight"), then retry each request once. If the refresh also fails, log the user out.

### Read the error body
APIs usually send details: `{ "error": "email_taken", "message": "..." }`. Parse it defensively (the body may be HTML from a proxy).

### Design tips
- Map status → typed error classes (`AuthError`, `NotFoundError`, `RateLimitError`) in one place (an API client), not in every component.
- Respect `Retry-After` (seconds or an HTTP date).
- Never retry `4xx` (except `408`, `429`).
- Show friendly messages; log request id (`x-request-id`) for support.
- Use `fetch` interceptors / a thin wrapper so behaviour is consistent.
keyPoints: 401 = who are you? (refresh/login); 403 = you may not (show permission message).
429: honour Retry-After and back off; 5xx/408: retry with backoff.
Do not retry other 4xx errors; they will fail again.
Refresh tokens with a single in-flight promise to avoid a stampede.
Centralise status handling in an API client.

interview.a: 401 means the client is not authenticated (missing/expired credentials) and may retry after logging in. 403 means the server knows who you are but refuses; logging in again will not help.

interview.q: How do you handle many parallel requests that get 401?
interview.a: Refresh the token once using a shared in-flight promise, make the other requests wait for it, then retry each once. If refresh fails, sign the user out.

interview.q: Which statuses should be retried?
interview.a: Transient ones: 408, 429 (after Retry-After), 500/502/503/504 for idempotent requests, with exponential backoff and a limit.

pitfalls: A server error (500) without CORS headers also looks like a CORS error in the console.
Allow-Origin: * together with credentials is rejected by browsers.
topics.title: CORS Errors Explained and Fixed
topics.summary: Why "blocked by CORS policy" happens, how preflight works, and what the server (not the frontend) must change.
topics.description:
**CORS** (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser security rule: JavaScript on `https://app.com` may read a response from `https://api.com` only if the API **opts in** with response headers. An **origin** = scheme + host + port (`http://localhost:3000` and `http://localhost:5000` are different origins).

The error you see in Chrome:
`Access to fetch at 'https://api.com/data' from origin 'https://app.com' has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource.`
In JavaScript this is only `TypeError: Failed to fetch` - the details are in the **Console**.

### Important truths
- CORS is enforced by the **browser**. The request often reaches the server; the browser then refuses to give the response to your script. Curl/Postman/servers are not affected.
- It **cannot be fixed in frontend code**. Fix it on the server (or use a proxy).
- `fetch(url, { mode: "no-cors" })` does not fix it; it returns an **opaque** response you cannot read.

### Simple vs preflighted requests
"Simple" requests (`GET/POST` with basic headers and `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` or `text/plain`) are sent directly. Everything else (JSON `Content-Type`, `Authorization` header, `PUT/DELETE/PATCH`) triggers a **preflight**: the browser first sends an `OPTIONS` request and the server must answer with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` (and `204/200`).

### Common messages and fixes
| Message | Fix |
|---|---|
| `No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present` | add the header on the server for your origin |
| `Response to preflight request doesn't pass access control check: It does not have HTTP ok status` | handle `OPTIONS` and return `204` (also before auth middleware) |
| `Request header field authorization is not allowed by Access-Control-Allow-Headers in preflight response` | add the header name to `Allow-Headers` |
| `The value of the 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header must not be the wildcard '*' when the request's credentials mode is 'include'` | send the exact origin and `Allow-Credentials: true` |
| `Method PUT is not allowed by Access-Control-Allow-Methods` | add the method |
| `has been blocked by CORS policy: The request client is not a secure context...` / Private Network Access | HTTPS or private network headers |

### Development workaround
Use a dev-server **proxy** (Vite `server.proxy`, CRA `proxy`) so the browser talks to the same origin, and forward to the API. Production: same origin via reverse proxy, or configure CORS properly.
keyPoints: CORS is enforced by browsers; fix it on the server with Access-Control-* headers.
Origin = scheme + host + port.
JSON bodies and Authorization headers trigger an OPTIONS preflight.
Credentials (cookies) need an exact origin, not *, plus Allow-Credentials: true.
no-cors does not make the response readable; use a proxy in development.

interview.q: Why can curl call the API but my frontend cannot?
interview.a: CORS is a browser-enforced policy. curl/Postman are not browsers and do not apply it. The browser blocks the response unless the server sends the right Access-Control-Allow-* headers.

interview.q: What is a preflight request?
interview.a: An automatic OPTIONS request the browser sends before a non-simple cross-origin request to ask whether the actual method and headers are allowed.

interview.q: Why does Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * fail with cookies?
interview.a: Credentialed requests require an exact origin and Allow-Credentials: true; the wildcard is rejected for security.

pitfalls: Hard-coded http:// URLs in config or database content break after moving to HTTPS.
Third-party snippets (analytics, widgets) often need script-src and connect-src entries.
topics.title: Mixed Content and Content-Security-Policy Errors
topics.summary: Blocked http resources on https pages, CSP violations (inline scripts, eval, third-party hosts) and how to read and fix them.
topics.description:
### Mixed content
When an **HTTPS** page loads a resource over **HTTP**, browsers treat it as insecure:
- **Active mixed content** (scripts, iframes, fetch/XHR, stylesheets) is **blocked**. Console: `Mixed Content: The page at 'https://...' was loaded over HTTPS, but requested an insecure XMLHttpRequest endpoint 'http://...'. This request has been blocked; the content must be served over HTTPS.` In JavaScript this surfaces as `TypeError: Failed to fetch`.
- **Passive** (images, audio, video) are usually auto-upgraded to HTTPS or show a warning.

Fix: use `https://` (or protocol-relative / relative URLs), serve the API over TLS, and add `Content-Security-Policy: upgrade-insecure-requests` as a safety net. A call from HTTPS to `http://localhost` is allowed by browsers (it is treated as potentially trustworthy).

### Content-Security-Policy (CSP)
A CSP header (or `<meta http-equiv>`) tells the browser which sources of scripts, styles, images, connections etc. are allowed. Violations are **blocked** and reported:
`Refused to execute inline script because it violates the following Content Security Policy directive: "script-src 'self'". Either the 'unsafe-inline' keyword, a hash ('sha256-...'), or a nonce ('nonce-...') is required to enable inline execution.`

| Console message | Meaning | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `Refused to execute inline script...` | inline `<script>` or `onclick="..."` | move to a file, or add a **nonce** / hash |
| `Refused to load the script 'https://x.com/a.js' because it violates ... "script-src"` | host not allowed | add host to `script-src` |
| `Refused to connect to 'https://api...' because it violates ... "connect-src"` | `fetch`/XHR/WebSocket blocked | add to `connect-src` |
| `Refused to evaluate a string as JavaScript because 'unsafe-eval' is not allowed...` | `eval`, `new Function`, string `setTimeout` | remove eval (EvalError in some browsers) |
| `Refused to apply inline style...` | inline `style=""` | external CSS / nonce |
| `Refused to frame 'x' because an ancestor violates "frame-ancestors"` | page cannot be embedded | adjust `frame-ancestors` |

### Debugging
Open the Console (messages name the directive), use the `securitypolicyviolation` event, or start with `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` to collect violations without breaking the site.

### Principle
Do not "fix" CSP errors with `'unsafe-inline'` / `'unsafe-eval'` / `*`; these remove the XSS protection that CSP provides.
keyPoints: HTTPS pages block HTTP scripts, iframes and fetch/XHR (active mixed content).
Mixed-content/CSP/CORS blocks all show as TypeError: Failed to fetch in JS; the Console tells why.
CSP blocks inline scripts, eval and unlisted hosts; use nonces or hashes, not unsafe-inline.
Use Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only to roll out safely.
The securitypolicyviolation event lets you log violations.

interview.q: Why does my fetch to an http:// API fail on my https:// site?
interview.a: Browsers block active mixed content. Serve the API over HTTPS (or use relative URLs behind the same HTTPS host).

interview.q: How do you allow an inline script under CSP safely?
interview.a: Add a per-response random nonce to the CSP and to the script tag (or allow its hash). Avoid unsafe-inline.

interview.q: What is Report-Only mode?
interview.a: Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only logs violations without blocking them, letting you tune a policy before enforcing it.

pitfalls: Promise.race timeouts do not cancel the request; use an abort signal.
Reusing an already aborted signal makes every new request fail immediately.
topics.title: AbortError, Cancellation and Timeouts
topics.summary: Cancel in-flight requests with AbortController, add timeouts with AbortSignal.timeout, and tell AbortError from real failures.
topics.description:
Network requests can take forever, or become irrelevant (the user typed another letter, left the page, changed tab). **AbortController** lets you cancel them.

```js
const controller = new AbortController();
fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal })
  .catch(e => { if (e.name === "AbortError") return; throw e; });
controller.abort();                 // rejects the fetch with AbortError
```

### Key facts
| API | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `controller.abort(reason?)` | signal becomes aborted; fetch rejects with `signal.reason` (default: a `DOMException` named `AbortError`) |
| `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` | auto-abort after ms with a `TimeoutError` |
| `AbortSignal.any([a, b])` | aborted when any signal aborts (user cancel + timeout) |
| `signal.throwIfAborted()` | throw `signal.reason` if aborted - use inside your own async work |
| `signal.addEventListener("abort", fn)` | cleanup hook |
| `AbortSignal.abort(reason)` | already aborted signal |

### Handling
- **AbortError is not a failure**: the user or your code cancelled. Do not show an error toast. Ignore or clean up.
- **TimeoutError is a failure**: show a message, maybe retry.
- Network error → `TypeError`. HTTP error → check `response.ok`.
- A signal can be used **once**; create a new controller for each request. Reusing an aborted signal makes new requests reject immediately.

### Typical use cases
1. **Search as you type** – abort the previous request when a new key is pressed (avoid out-of-order responses).
2. **React `useEffect` cleanup** – abort in the cleanup function to avoid state updates after unmount.
3. **Timeouts** – never leave a request without one.
4. **Navigating away** – cancel pending loads.

### Timeout without AbortSignal.timeout (older browsers)
`const c = new AbortController(); const id = setTimeout(() => c.abort(), 5000); try { ... } finally { clearTimeout(id); }`

Abort also works with `addEventListener` options (`{ signal }` removes the listener), streams and many libraries (axios supports `signal`).
keyPoints: controller.abort() makes fetch reject with DOMException AbortError.
AbortSignal.timeout(ms) produces TimeoutError; AbortSignal.any combines signals.
Do not show error UI for AbortError; it is intentional.
Use a fresh AbortController per request.
Abort previous search requests and in React effect cleanups.

examples.title: Cancelling work with a signal
Timeout versus user cancel
Search-as-you-type: keep only the latest

interview.q: Is AbortError an error you should report?
interview.a: No. It means the operation was cancelled on purpose. Ignore it (or clean up); report only real failures.

interview.q: How do you add a timeout to fetch?
interview.a: Pass signal: AbortSignal.timeout(ms), or create an AbortController and call abort() from setTimeout. Catch TimeoutError/AbortError.

interview.q: Why is Promise.race not a proper timeout?
interview.a: The losing promise keeps running; the request continues using bandwidth. An abort signal actually cancels it.

pitfalls: Proxies and SPAs may return index.html with status 200 for missing API routes.
JSON.parse on a stored "undefined" string (from localStorage.setItem(k, undefined)) throws.
topics.title: JSON Parse Errors from APIs
topics.summary: Why response.json() throws on real APIs - HTML error pages, empty bodies, wrong content-type, BOMs - and a defensive parsing helper.
topics.description:
`response.json()` fails with a `SyntaxError` whenever the body is not valid JSON. In production this is almost always **the server sent something else**.

| Symptom (Chrome) | Real cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `Unexpected token '<', "<!DOCTYPE "... is not valid JSON` | HTML page: wrong URL, 404/500 page, login redirect, SPA `index.html` fallback, proxy error | check status and `Content-Type`; fix URL / proxy |
| `Unexpected end of JSON input` | empty body: `204 No Content`, `HEAD` request, server crash mid-response, aborted request | check `res.status === 204` or `text()` is empty |
| `"undefined" is not valid JSON` | you called `JSON.parse(undefined)` (e.g. missing localStorage key shows `null` ok, but `"undefined"` string stored) | validate before parsing |
| `Unexpected token 'N', "NaN" is not valid JSON` / `Infinity` | server serialised NaN | fix server |
| `Unexpected token '﻿'...` | UTF-8 BOM at start of file | strip `﻿` |
| `Unexpected token ' in JSON` | single quotes: this is a JS object literal, not JSON | server must use `JSON.stringify` |
| `Unexpected non-whitespace character after JSON` | two JSON documents concatenated, trailing text, NDJSON | parse per line |
| `Body is unusable` | body already read | `clone()` |

### Defensive reading
1. Check `res.ok` first - an error page will not be JSON.
2. Check `Content-Type` contains `application/json` (or `+json`).
3. Read as **text once**, then decide; include a short snippet of the text in your error to debug.
4. Handle `204` / empty bodies explicitly.
5. Validate the parsed shape (is `data.items` an array?) before using it.

### Developer tips
- Open the **Network tab → Response/Preview** to see the real body.
- Beware dev-server proxies returning `index.html` for unknown `/api` paths.
- Redirects to a login page return HTML `200`: `res.redirected` and `res.url` help detect them.
- Large numbers: JSON numbers above `2^53` lose precision in `JSON.parse`; send IDs as strings.
keyPoints: "Unexpected token <" means HTML came back instead of JSON.
"Unexpected end of JSON input" means an empty body (204, aborted, crashed).
Check res.ok and Content-Type before res.json().
Read the body as text once, parse yourself, and include a snippet in the error.
Send big IDs as strings and validate the parsed shape.
